/method/.title: Method — The Booyzen Archive
blocks: how to read this archive

every claim here carries a label saying how well it is known. the labels are the point: an archive that presents testimony and documents in the same voice is not a history, it is a story with footnotes.

all seven of these family archives grade a claim with the same five words, so a level means the same thing wherever you meet it. the word is always printed next to the colour, because a reader should never have to know the palette to know the confidence.
a record was read, and it says this. the source is named.
the evidence points one way and nothing found so far points the other. not proven.
reasoned from what is known — a gap of the right size, a name in the right place — rather than witnessed in a record.
told, remembered, or written on a family chart. kept, because discarding it would lose the lead; labelled, because it is not evidence.
two sources disagree and neither has been ruled out. both are shown.

some pages carry this instead. it states the thing a reader is likely to assume — the connection that would be tidy, the identification that almost works — and says plainly that this archive does not assert it. an archive is judged as much by what it refuses to say as by what it says.
¦label what it means

¦documented a named source with a reference, and where possible the scan. most of this archive's documented claims trace to dutch reformed church registers and to cape and transvaal probate records, cited by familysearch ark.

¦inferred a reasoned conclusion drawn from documented facts, with the reasoning written out so it can be overturned. the cousin marriage, the reading of the surname distribution, and the identification of the 1820 settler are all inferences.
¦family lore told, remembered, not corroborated. kept because it is precious; labelled because pretending otherwise is how family myths become family history.
¦superseded asserted in the family record, and now displaced by a document that says otherwise.
¦disputed asserted somewhere in the record and contradicted somewhere else in it. every one is listed. disputed →

a living person (80 or younger, with no death recorded) is named with their relationships and their town and country, and nothing more. no date, no record, no source, no note and no photograph; their page is not indexed, carries no structured data and is left out of the sitemap and the search index. the test is the estate's one shared rule: age by year (this year minus the birth year), a death or burial recorded means dead, and a citation from a public record source means the person is not treated as living. a person with no birth year cannot be shown to be 80 or younger; the archive's own statement that someone is living is accepted. anyone who may be a child (under 18, or undated with a living parent) is not published at all: no page, and no name as anyone's relative.

because this line reaches the present within three generations of catherine mary sophia booyzen, a living person is part of the descent: cheryl anne lerena, david defranceski's mother, and david himself, who is named on the home page with his own places by his own choice. their siblings and other relatives are not named, and so have no page.
a removal request is honoured within days, without argument and without requiring a reason.
where this one starts

unusually well. the lerena archive began with almost nothing documented. this one begins with a myheritage tree of 15,643 people in which the booyzen line is already carried back seven generations, and in which a large proportion of births, marriages and deaths already carry a familysearch citation to an original register.
that changes the job. the work here is not to find the family. it is to test what has been assembled — because a tree that good will be believed, and parts of it are wrong.
so this archive did three things the tree does not do:
listed every contradiction rather than choosing between them silently.
tested the family testimony against outside evidence — surname distribution, cape rebel district figures, the 1820 settler record — instead of repeating it.
named what has not been searched, so the gaps are visible.
a nil return is worth nothing until you show the search works
this is the thing this archive actually does, and until today it was not written down anywhere. it arrived by being wrong six times in a week.

an index that returns nothing is making one of two statements and it does not tell you which. either the record does not exist, or your search could not have found it. those are opposite conclusions and they look identical on the screen. so a negative is not publishable until something has been run through the same search that is known to be there — a control — and come back.
¦the nil return what it actually meant

¦“148 of 184 — thirty-six not reached” all ten pages had been walked. this archive's own harvesting code required a description longer than three characters and silently dropped every row the index leaves short. a caveat that blamed the source for a hole this archive dug.
¦a register with no barrys in it the name column was blank for a whole class of entry. a filter that drops what it cannot see is indistinguishable from an archive that holds nothing.
¦barry and burgersdorp: 6,245 documents more than barry alone. naairs treats two keywords as or unless the operator is sent. a search that returns more than its own first term is not a search.

¦“luus with booyzen returns nothing” it returns nothing from the estate index, which was the only index asked. a marriage transcription holds the marriage. the sentence did not say what had been asked.

¦no kolbes, mountjoys or sliers in the cape inventories that index runs from the 1780s to the 1830s and all three families reached the cape in the nineteenth century. a zero from an index that ends before your people arrive is not a finding.

¦nothing older than the 1840s, for weeks every register in the filmed church collection begins in 1843. the registers themselves go back two centuries. it was the edge of a filming project, and it announced itself nowhere.

so the rule is: run a control, and publish it with the negative. when this archive reported that james mountjoy is not among the discharge papers at kew, it published alongside that ninety-five records for his regiment in the same series in a single page of results — because the number that makes the absence meaningful is not his, it is theirs.

the same search also turned up the reason the control mattered. the catalogue indexes the regiment as “21st dragoons (light)”, not as the newspaper wrote it and not as this archive had been writing it. one word order between a real record and a nil return.

a search that has not been controlled has not been done. it has only been attempted, and the difference between “searched and not found” and “could not search” is the most important distinction on this site.

which is why what has been read marks a row void when the search itself was faulty, and blocked when it could not run — and why a build here now refuses if a blocked row does not say what would unblock it. a negative with no control behind it is an opinion with a citation.
each was a correct answer to a question nobody asked

this one was named on 21 september 2026 by the session keeping the d’arcy archive, after the two of us had between us produced six of them in a day. it is the rule the controlled negative does not reach, because half of these never returned a nil at all. a test passed. a count came back. a confidence field said exact.

an instrument can be working perfectly and be pointed at something else. what it reports is then true, and about the wrong thing, and it arrives wearing exactly the face of an answer. a nil at least announces itself as bad news worth checking. a confident yes does not.
¦what it reported what it was actually describing

¦“345 reordered, zero content changed” a comparison that iterated the dossier dict’s keys — n, slug, mentions, pages, hits — which are identical for every person alive or dead. the reassuring answer was the only answer it could return. 345 dossiers had in fact changed content.

¦two byte-identical runs of the generator both runs read the same built site, and the generator’s input was 81% its own previous output. it proved the disk had not changed between two reads of it. generate, rebuild, generate moved all 347.

¦“0 results for westfalen” seven of the eleven records on the page were westphalian. findmypast’s place filter is not applied to that collection at all, so the zero described the filter and never touched the data.
¦three empty full-text searches http 000 — no connection. the endpoint no longer exists. three nil returns that described a hostname.

¦36 map pins stamped exact the confidence field recorded that the lookup succeeded, not that it answered the question. twenty-one places sat on the geocode for the word “england” — right country, wrong precision, and a wrong-country gate passes it cleanly.

¦“the stale index passes — we do not have that fault” written the same day as this section, and caught by it. the row was planted in public/searchindex.json and the check reads dist/searchindex.json, which had not been rebuilt. it was asked about the built copy and told about a change to the source. planted in the file the check actually reads, it fails at once and names the row.
¦a gate reporting a clean build it had been run before the row that broke it existed, and on checks that do not touch that schema. a build that did not cover the change is not a build.

¦a trap built to say how the build died it read $?, which in an exit handler is the status of the last child. right when the machine reaps the build process; wrong when the signal hits the script itself, where it is whatever finished last. so the instrument built to tell a killed build from a refusing one went silent on the one case it existed for — and it had been watched working, on the other path. the signals are trapped now, not inferred.

the test that catches every one of them is the same, and it is one question: if the thing i am looking for were definitely there, could this instrument have told me? ask a filter for something already seen with your own eyes on the page in front of you. ask a comparison to fail on a difference you planted. ask a generator to survive a rebuild, not a re-read.
none of them is a wrong answer. each is a correct answer to a question nobody asked.

and one heuristic of this archive’s own did not survive the day. “three identical failures is a fault; one is the weather” is sound for a machine under load and useless for a bug whose trigger is intermittent and whose mechanism is not. a build failure here was written off that way in the afternoon; it was a missing subshell that could have reported a killed build as build complete, and it had been there all along.
a failure that does not reproduce has not been explained. it has only been survived — and passing next time is evidence about the trigger and none at all about the mechanism.

one last thing, about why any of this got found. eight of these faults were caught in a single afternoon, and not one was caught by an audit. they were caught because two archives kept describing their own work to each other in enough detail that the other could recognise the shape of a fault it had not gone looking for. neither was checking the other. a wrong attribution, a comparison that could not fail, a trap that went silent, a stopper that stopped nothing — every one of them surfaced because somebody volunteered it first.

this archive already sets its negatives down at the same length as its finds, on the grounds that a family history publishing only its successes is not a history. the day added a second reason, and it is more selfish than the first: a fault written up as briefly as it is embarrassing is a fault nobody else can recognise in their own work. the length is what makes the shape visible from outside. that is a discipline rather than a courtesy.

and it is why the three tool faults needed somebody else at all. a claim about a family is a claim about the world, and the world can contradict it. a claim about an instrument is a claim about oneself — my filter filtered, my trap trapped, my stopper stopped — and nobody is a disinterested judge of their own competence. so the judgement never gets made, and the claim never reaches a boundary where anything would test it. somebody describing their own instrument out loud is the cheapest boundary there is.

the second half of that sentence is the d’arcy session’s, and it is the part that makes the rule usable: it says exactly what the re-run did prove, which is the thing a tired reader will otherwise take for a clean bill of health.

six of these were found by measurement. the last two were found by checking an instrument against itself — asking the stale-index check about the file it actually reads, and asking the trap about the branch nobody had run. that is the half that generalises, because measurement only ever checks the thing you already doubted.

which is why every gate added here is verified in both directions — silent on the real data, and made to fail on a fault planted on purpose. a check that has only ever passed has not been shown to be a check.
ask the index for a relationship, not for a person

nearly every genealogical search is a search for somebody you can already name. you type hendrik stefanus booijzen, born about 1827, and the index tells you whether it holds him. that works, and it is how most of this archive was built. but it has a hard ceiling: it can only ever confirm what you already suspected. if the person you need was never written down by your family, you cannot type their name, and so you cannot find them.

the search forms will also take a relationship. leave the forename blank, leave the district blank, and ask instead for any child whose mother's surname was kolbe. the index then answers a question nobody in the family was in a position to ask.
¦what you ask for what it can return ceiling
¦a persongivenname + surname + date the record of someone you named you must already know the name. everyone your family forgot stays forgotten.

¦a relationshipmothersurname, fathergivenname, spousesurname anyone standing in that relation, including people you could not have named noisy, and every hit needs separating from the namesakes by hand.

both results on this page's hardest day came out of that difference. three person-searches for elizabetha van der merwe returned nothing, and the third of them — her son's own baptism — was the best test this archive could devise. one relationship-search on the barrys returned two children on neither parent's death notice. the difference was not effort or luck. it was which question the form was asked.

the same logic runs underneath three other things this archive did. reading a marriage register's remarks column for the master's estate number is a relationship search done on paper — it indexes from a living remarrying widower to a file about a dead first wife. reading both parents' death notices rather than one gave a ninth child. reading a whole surname out of a probate collection, instead of searching it for a person, gave twenty-nine.

the cost is honesty about noise. a relationship search returns the right family mixed with strangers, and it returns the same event indexed twice to two different villages. the two barry names above are recorded as a lead and not as children, because an index line that fits a gap is not the same as a register that fills it.
what "verified" on the tree does and does not mean

many people in the source tree carry a tick and a star. those are myheritage interface marks — confirmed smart matches and direct-ancestor flags. they are not source citations, and this archive does not treat them as evidence. a smart match means another user's tree agrees; it does not mean a register does.
where this archive says documented, there is a named record behind it, listed on sources.

the family's own testimony is quoted in full, because it is the family's and because paraphrasing it would smooth away exactly the details that make it testable. a long passage on kitchener's clearance policy also sits in the source tree, copied there from a published history of the war; that passage is summarised and not reproduced, and its presence is reported as evidence of what the family believed rather than as evidence of what happened to them. the rebels →
the page must not be able to say less than the archive knows

on 17 september 2026 this archive was asked to look for a fault a sibling archive had just had: evidence kept in files keyed to a person, and a build script that never read them, so a person documented several times over got a page saying nothing had been read about them. the same fault was live here, by a different route, and had been for at least three days.

seventeen people had a page that said “this person is recorded in the archive’s index but is not yet discussed on any page.” among them the 1820 settler, whose name the built site carries 155 times; john barry, 158; george mountjoy, 140; petrus jacobus booysen, 110; johanna catharina mountjoy, 89.

the gatherer that collects every mention of a person dropped any name that was a strict prefix of a longer person’s name. the rule was written for a good reason — to stop john barry collecting every mention of john barry booyzen — and it was implemented as “delete the shorter man” rather than “let the longer name go first”.
so the moment anybody added george augustus kolbe of wakkerstroom, george augustus kolbe stopped existing as far as the build was concerned.
why it is worth a section

the data was never wrong. every record, every document, every citation was intact and on disk the whole time. what failed was the machinery between the evidence and the page, and it failed silently and in the safe-sounding direction — the page did not print a falsehood about a document, it printed a falsehood about the archive.
that is the worst kind for a site like this one, whose whole claim is that it says what it has read and what it has not.

the rule that comes out of it. a page may say “nothing is known” only when nothing is known — never because a build step lost it. so the check that now runs on every build does not look for the bug that was found; it looks for the shape of it: a person the index calls undiscussed whose name the built pages plainly carry. any future gatherer that eats a person trips it, however it eats them. it was verified the only way a gate can be — by putting the bug back and confirming the build refused.
two thousand four hundred and twenty-eight mentions came back. the correction →
an index is only honest if something checks it against what it indexes

three days after the last fault, the same shape again, one layer further out. /documents/ builds its own table of contents by matching <h2 id>, so a heading written without one is left out of the contents and has no anchor for anything to link to. thirty-five had accumulated.

among them: the 1842 will of a bond street tailor; the sworn falsehood in shoreditch in 1819; the oldest document in this archive; the grave at burgersdorp; the two 1845 documents that corrected the family tree twice over. full write-ups of documents, every one, and not one of them listed or linkable.

nothing was broken. the page rendered perfectly, every section was there to a reader scrolling past, and the link checker was satisfied — no link pointed at a missing anchor, because there were no links to point at them at all. that is the whole difficulty. the fault was an absence, and an absence is invisible from inside the thing that has it. it is the same lesson as the seventeen silent people above, and as the three letters that were out in the world with no work-list row watching for a reply.

the rule this archive now works to: wherever the build derives one thing from another — a contents list from headings, a dossier from pages, a work list from the letters on disk — something must count the two against each other and refuse when they disagree. a derived index that nothing checks will drift, and it will look right the entire time it is doing it.

the gate. checkregisters.py check 13 refuses the build when a page that builds a contents list from its headings carries a heading with no id. verified in both directions: with all thirty-six ids in place it passes with nothing failing; with two taken out again it names both headings and exits 1.

same method, same author: the defranceski (istria), the falco (arienzo, campania), the lerena (rosario, the cape, brisbane). the marriage of catherine mary sophia booyzen to nuno fernando lerena at mayfair in 1949 is the hinge between this archive and the lerena one.

everything documented in this archive traces to one of the records below. where a claim is inferred or is family testimony, the page carrying it says so.
myheritage — defranceski family site (23andme), the family tree "defranceski, lerena, taylor, barry, blazevic, booyzen", 15,643 people. read 9 september 2026 from david defranceski's account.

the tree is private and its profile pages are not publicly linkable. everything taken from it is reproduced here with its own citation where it carries one, and marked as uncited where it does not. myheritage interface marks — confirmed smart matches, direct-ancestor stars — are not treated as sources. method →
the services this archive searches, and what each one is for

a sources page that lists documents and never names the places they were looked for is half a page. these are the hosts this archive's own data links to — a gate counts them, and until today five of them appeared in the research and nowhere here.
familysearch.org — free, account required. the cape and free state dutch reformed registers, south african civil marriage and death registration, and the images behind most of what is read here.

findmypast.com.au and findmypast.co.uk — paid. the british and irish half: london parish registers, war office series, irish roman catholic parish registers. a one-month subscription runs to 16 october 2026.

nationalarchives.gov.za — free index, the file ordered from the depot. two databases since the 2026 migration and only one is complete: narssa says in writing that the new full-text search will not display all the records, so a nil from it is not a nil.

www.national.archsrch.gov.za — the old naairs search manager, which is the complete one. it answered 503 on 27 september and again on 7 october, and naairs.htm is now 404. linked to in this archive's data and currently dead.

billiongraves.com — partly free, partly paid, and the split matters: the search, the transcription with full dates and the per-stone gps are free, and the full-resolution photograph is behind a paid account. a transcription taken from here cannot be checked against the stone without paying.
archive.org — free. where sibree's register and the 1829 mirror of literature were read.

printed works read here, and what each one carries

books, not manuscripts — but every one of them was read from the page image and not from a transcript, and the pages that matter are published on the documents. six are out of copyright and were taken whole; three are lending-restricted and were read a page at a time through the internet archive's search-inside, which needs no account and is not a way round the restriction.
¦work what it carries, and where

¦the evangelical magazine and missionary chronicle, 1833 — pp. 410–412 “extracts from the journal of mr. george augustus kolbe, from 8th october, 1831, to 3rd september, 1832”, and the close of his letter of 1 september 1832 over his own signature. eleven months at philippolis: the school roll, the vaccinations, the new chapel, the temperance society. page 410 is published here. out of copyright; the volume was taken whole.

¦the evangelical magazine and missionary chronicle, 1831 his letter dated philippolis, 30 april 1831, to the foreign secretary. it dates his own arrival — “when i arrived, in april, 1828, with my colleague, in the bushman country” — after “nearly three years among the bushmen”, and carries his account of the people he worked among.

¦the evangelical magazine and missionary chronicle, 1830 james clark, writing from the bushman station, near caledon river, 31 december 1828: “brother kolbe and myself removed to this station, and arrived here in the beginning of may last.” also the station's origin — landdrost stockenstrom and the lieutenant-governor asked for it, and farmers subscribed cattle.

the transvaal probate collection is digitised, so these are readable rather than orderable — each should carry a sterfkennis naming the deceased's parents, occupation and children. between them they would settle what the men of this family did for a living in johannesburg, which is the last untested line of the family testimony.

reading them is rate-limited rather than blocked: familysearch began refusing requests partway through this work and recovers after a rest. the references are recorded here so the job resumes rather than restarts.

and on the afternoon of 13 september that stopped being true. the sentence above describes a limiter that opens a window, closes it after twenty or thirty calls, and reopens after about ten minutes. that is how it behaved all week. it is worth writing down that it can do something worse.

after two searches that afternoon the refusals did not lift. waits of four, twenty-five, thirty and forty seconds all returned 403, and the block then spread off the search service and onto the site: loading an ordinary results page in a browser produced a document with a body of zero characters — not a refusal page, not an error, nothing at all. nearly an hour of rests did not clear it.

two practical things follow. the first is that polling probably makes it worse, and checking every few minutes to see whether it has lifted is the opposite of the right move. the second is the one that matters to anybody reading a result on this site: a search that has to be abandoned halfway is a different kind of negative from one that ran. where that happened, the row on what has been searched is marked blocked and not nothing, because the index was never actually asked.

13 september 2026: the remaining six are blocked, and it is not an indexing problem. the collection is held on 762 films, 007805260 to 007831001. every film up to and including 007830062 serves its images. film 007830063 and every film after it returns 403 — twenty-eight tested, twenty-eight refused — and those are exactly the films whose indexed records run to 1946 and later.

five of the six sit behind that line: 3734/46, 1095/48, 5155/51, 769/52 and 10/57. no amount of browsing reaches them. the sixth, 52653 of 1923, is in the open half — but it is not name-indexed, and the films are not ordered by estate number. image 100 of three films in the same numeric neighbourhood gave a 1920 sterfkennis, a 1938 death notice, and a chinese clan genealogy. there is nothing to interpolate along.
so this queue no longer belongs on a screen. the originals are at the transvaal archives depot, pretoria, which is where these six now go. what was searched →

and one thing learned about the route in. the whole indexed surname can be pulled from one collection at a time — booyzen, exact, collection 2520237 returns 150 people — which is how the 1942 daschner file was found without knowing it existed. it also settles a negative: the 1946 to 1957 estates in this table are not in that index at all. they exist on film and were never keyed, so the remaining six have to be reached by browsing images rather than by searching names, and that is a different and slower job. what was searched →

and one head-on contradiction
wikitree gives petrus jacobus booysen a different father.

its profile booysen-267 is unmistakably our man — born before 21 september 1788, died 1 september 1876, the same two dates this archive carries. it makes his parents jan (boijens) booysen and magdalena de beer. this archive makes them gerthardus lodewikus booijsen and magdalena de beer, and not on the strength of a tree: the names are in line 3 of his 1876 rustenburg sterfkennis, no. 678, which this archive has read and imaged. same mother, same son, two different husbands.

the reason this is not simply a tree being wrong is that this archive has already met that jan. question 0 records a near-miss it deliberately declined to adopt — kab ncd 2/1: 49, a notarial will of 1793 for "jan booysen, married to the late magdalena de beer" — and set it aside as "wrong husband's name". another researcher, working independently, has put that same jan in that same position.
then the book itself was read, and it went the other way

withdrawn, 14 september 2026. what stood here for a day was a section headed "following it up the tree settles it — and the archive was right". it argued that jan booysen's wife and this archive's magdelena elisabeth de beer were two different women, fifty years apart, and that the tree had merged them. reading the source settled it the other way. the reasoning is kept on corrections rather than quietly deleted.

a member of g2g, pieter van zyl, answered within a day and named the book as freely downloadable: de villiers, geslacht-register der oude kaapsche familien (1893) — the original of which genealogies of old cape families is the revised edition, so the two references this archive was chasing turned out to be one book. it was downloaded and read rather than taken on trust.

page 34, de beer. zacharias de beer, baptised 5 march 1719, married anna pretorius on 12 may 1743. he is the fifth child of the progenitor matthijs andries de beer — so the code is b5, not the b6 wikitree carries. his daughters include c2 magdalena, baptised 16 october 1745, with no onward reference, and c6 magdalena, baptised 16 october 1754, "zie booijsen". the cross-reference to this family is on the second one, and 1754 is the birth year this archive has always carried for its own magdelena elisabeth — a figure its own page admitted was "off the family tree with no source stated". it is now sourced. they are one woman, not two.
and then page 78 names her husband, and it is not ours.

the booijsen section gives jan, baptised 29 january 1741, burgher at drakenstein, married 21 january 1770 to magdalena de beer and remarried 15 december 1793. his seventh child is "petrus jacobus, gedoopt 21 september 1788, gehuwd met anna maria van der merwe", and that man's first child is "david schalk, gedoopt 4 januari 1807".

four fields out of five agree, which is what makes the fifth serious. this is certainly the same man: there is exactly one "petrus jacobus, gedoopt 21 september 1788" in the whole book, and exactly one david schalk of 4 january 1807. and the word lodewikus does not occur anywhere in the volume. the only gerhardus-lodewijk name in the booijsen pages is a cousin baptised in 1770, eighteen years old when petrus jacobus was born.

so the archive's generation seven now rests on one line of one document, against a published genealogy built from the baptism registers. the 1876 sterfkennis names "gerthardus lödewikus booijsen"; it was written about a man of eighty-eight, and the field it is in asks a grieving family for the names of parents who had died some seventy years earlier. that is exactly the field that goes wrong on a death notice. it has not been overturned and nothing has been rewritten — but it is no longer the only evidence in the room. question 0 → · what was withdrawn →

nothing has been changed on the strength of it. a document this archive has read outranks a tree, and the 1876 notice stands. but the disagreement is now recorded, it has a published book and an exact page to be settled against, and the 1793 will has stopped being a curiosity. question 0 → · what was searched →
a library is not an archive, and this archive did not know that mattered
for three weeks this project has treated “the cape town holdings” as one place. it is at least two, and the second one has been invisible to every index in use here.

the western cape archives, 72 roeland street, holds public records — estates, wills, inventories, the master's series. that is where nearly every errand on this site points, and it is what naairs indexes.

the national library of south africa, 5 queen victoria street, holds manuscripts: private papers somebody gave to a library. separate building, separate reader's ticket, separate request. msb751, the ga kolbe collection, is there — four photocopied pages including a letter from london of 23 august 1830 — and this archive found it by accident, while searching a national index for something else entirely.
a family's papers do not sit where its records sit. the records are where the state kept them; the papers are wherever a descendant happened to give them.

which raises a question this site cannot answer and should ask out loud: how many other manuscript collections mention these families in libraries nobody here has thought to search? msb751 was donated in 1985 by a dr jean griffiths of somerset west, who is not a name in this archive and may have had more.
seven kinds of shut door, and the differences matter

whether a host answers is a mechanical question, and the table below it answers that. this is the other one: why a source is out of reach. seven of them are, for seven different reasons, and treating them as one thing — “not available online” — would throw away everything useful about them.

¦the savoy german lutheran registerfamilysearch film 008004264 digitised and withheld. a padlock on every one of 537 images. added 16 september 2026, and the most answerable of the seven. the register that would finish the kolbe family is photographed, catalogued, counted and indexed — and locked by contract to a familysearch center or affiliate library terminal, because the custodian is the national archives. nothing is missing and nothing is broken. the fix is a bus fare rather than a letter, which is not true of any of the other six. what is on the film →

put together they are an argument, and it is not the obvious one. almost nothing on this list is anybody refusing anything. two are technical boundaries nobody thought to publish, one is a physical property of old paper, one is a library defending itself from robots, one is a price, and one is a server having an afternoon. the single biggest obstacle to this archive is not access. it is that the edges of collections are undocumented — and an undocumented edge is indistinguishable, from a distance, from an empty archive. this site has made that mistake four times in a week and caught it four times, which is not a ratio anybody should rely on.

the check was wrong before it was right, and the way it was wrong is worth keeping. its first run called three live government domains dead, because it asked for an address record and a department can be perfectly alive with nothing but mail. dsac.gov.za — where every letter to pretoria has gone, cited twenty-five times on this site — has no website at all. on the strength of that first answer this archive was one edit from publishing that the pietermaritzburg addresses were dead. they accept mail. the check now asks for the mx before it says dark.

and on 20 september it was wrong the same way a second time, which is worse, because the lesson had already been written above. an end-to-end audit found this table asserting that www.familysearch.org was down — cited 7,275 times on this site — along with the national archives at kew, the university of edinburgh and google’s font cdn. all four answer an ordinary request perfectly well. familysearch returns 403, which is a bot check and which this check already knows how to record as guarded; it never saw the code, because the connection was refused before http to a user-agent that says thebooyzenarchive.

the fix is not to dress up as a browser. this archive identifies itself and will go on doing so. the fix is to stop calling a silence a death. there is now a state called unverified — no answer at all — and it is kept apart from dark, which means does not resolve in dns and is the only state here that means gone. a nil return is worthless without a control, and a refused connection is a nil return with no control. the rule was on /method/ the whole time.

it is deliberately not part of the build. a network probe inside a build fails when a government website is having an afternoon, which has nothing to do with the change being built — and a check that fails for the wrong reason is a check people learn to ignore. it runs on demand and writes what it finds here. one published address was wrong →

a search that returns nothing is only worth anything if the search itself is written down. every query below was actually run, on the date given, and its result is recorded whether or not it helped. and a second, flat register sits beside the sets since 7 october 2026, for a machine rather than a reader. record atlas imports each archive's searched.json, and it reads a list of objects under searched, rows or entries. this file keys its work under sets, and each row inside is a list — a question, an answer, a note and a verdict. so the importer read 0 rows from this archive while reading 1,525 from the other seven, and every search recorded here since the project began has been invisible to the shared map. the sets are what the page is built from and what a person reads; the searched array is the same work stated in the fields the atlas keys on — source, url, film, pages, outcome. the duplication is a known cost and is recorded as one: the two can drift, and the proper fix is to retrofit the sets, which is a deliberate job and not a thing to do in passing. from 9 november 2026 the flat register is no longer only written by hand. rows marked "derived": "sets" are made from sets by tools/searched_flat.py, using the source each set was run against, which site/src/data/searched-map.json states; a set that names no single source contributes nothing and says so there. do not edit a derived row: change the set or the map and run python3 tools/searched_flat.py --write. the build fails if they differ, or if a new set has no entry in the map.

¦and the other half of the same catalogue line a letter from his father in london, 23 august 1830found “letter, 1830 aug. 23, from johan kolbe, london, to his son, george augustus kolbe on his ordination.” the two men wrote to each other and the letter survives. this archive has spent a fortnight trying to connect the tailor of conduit street to the settler of colesberg through directories, censuses and an obituary, and has been beaten by a quota, a bot check and an empty shelf. a letter from london in 1830 is very likely to carry an address at its head — which is the exact question the brunswick square muddle turns on. it is a photocopy, and the catalogue does not say where the original is.

¦the tool's own first answer it called three live domains dead, and this archive nearly published itfound getaddrinfo asks for an address record, and a government domain can be perfectly alive with nothing but mx. dsac.gov.za — the department every pretoria letter has gone to, cited twenty-five times here — has no website and takes mail. so do dact.kzntl.gov.za and kzndac.gov.za. the tool reported all three as “does not resolve”, and the next edit would have said in public that the pietermaritzburg addresses were dead. they accept mail. the check now asks for the mx before it says dark, and reports “mail only”, which is the true answer and a more useful one.

¦what that does to the pietermaritzburg advice weakens it, and the note has been changedpartly the draft letter has been sitting unsent since 14 september on the argument that kzntl.gov.za is a retired domain and the address on the national archives' 2015 record is “almost certainly dead”. the domain takes mail, and so does the newer one. that does not prove a mailbox is read behind either — a domain accepting mail and a person reading it are different facts — but the reason given for not sending was stronger than the evidence for it. telephoning first is still the better plan; it is no longer the only defensible one.

¦nationalarchives.gov.za, written with a dot corrected — and it was in the row complaining about a wrong addressfound the naairs note of 13 september records that the catalogue is a frameset, and ends “written down because the wrong address cost this archive a day”. the host in it was national.archives.gov.za. the live domain has no dot. corrected wherever it appeared.

¦the london directories, by every free route left google books quota zero · hathitrust behind bot protection · archive.org has nonenothing whether john godloff kolbe was at brunswick square or at 34 conduit street needs a london trade directory of the 1810s to 1840s. the books api returns 429 with a daily quota of zero for anonymous callers. hathitrust answers with a cloudflare bot check, and this archive will not go around one. archive.org's earliest post office london directory is 1920. the volumes are on the paid genealogy services and at the guildhall library and the london metropolitan archives, and nowhere free. it is a door question now, and the door is in london — which is where wo 97 is, so the two travel together.

¦mountjoy in the newspaper transcriptions — the surname had never been swept “a saddler, who was discharged from the 21st light dragoons”found the friend of the free state, 25 november 1869. john montgomery, founder of burgersdorp, recalling his arrival at cradock in january 1822, when the village held about six people, and naming them: “messrs. solomon and s.m. de beer, the rev. mr. evans, mr. p. gie, james mountjoy (a saddler, who was discharged from the 21st light dragoons), the two messrs. ziervogel, mr. heilberg, fieldcornet b.j. vorster, and gert van deventer. after some trouble i obtained lodgings for the night from mr. mountjoy.” there is no room in a village of six for two saddlers of one name.

¦what that does to question 12, marked blocking since it was written it stops being unanswerable and becomes an errand at kewfound his death notice answers “names of the parents of the deceased” with not known. his 1817 marriage register rules a line through the column that should say where he came from — and that blank was there while he stood in the room. now both are explained: he did not arrive as a settler and no passenger list holds him, because he arrived in uniform. the 21st light dragoons were the cavalry of the cape garrison from the 1806 expedition. the colony had no way to know where he was from; the army did. wo 97 at the national archives, kew — chelsea discharge papers, arranged by regiment before 1855 — gives a soldier's parish and county of birth, his age at enlistment and his trade. with wo 12, the musters. the question's own note said “the way in is a cape arrival record, not an english birth record”. it was right, and the record has a name.

¦the same memoirist, twice in one week two walls, neither found by searching for the personfound john montgomery's “forty-five years ago” put george augustus kolbe at a bushman mission school at koolskop, on the ground where colesberg was later laid out. this one puts james mountjoy in the 21st light dragoons. both came out of reading a surname sweep to the bottom rather than skimming it, and both were sitting in the reminiscences of one old man who wrote down who he met.

¦booyzen, booijsen, booysen and daschner in the same index 5, 1, 180 and nought — and almost all of it somebody elsepartly daschner returns nothing at all in the whole collection. of the booyzens: the 1830 gazette notice of christina booyzen already held here; an 1859 intestate estate at middelveld, district bloemfontein for jan lodewyk booijsen, who married about 1819 christina magdalena de buijs, widow of cornelius faber, and whose estate had become mixed with faber's; and an 1862 report of a booyzen trek-farmer near the orange river who seized a party of bushmen accused of a shooting — “six men, seven women and seven children”. none of it connects. the 1862 numbers are set down because the paper recorded them.

¦barry paired with burgersdorp, barkly, indwe and kolbe the engine will not pair — it returns every barry it hasvoid unlike naairs, this index has no and that can be sent; a two-word query is scored, not filtered, and the results are twentieth-century death notices from durban. the negative is void rather than informative, and is recorded as void so that nobody — including this archive in a fortnight — reads it as “barry was searched”.

¦naairs, for the education-series sweep and francis mccabe's estate down. “the connection to the search manager server is inactive.”blocked three items on the work list run through naairs and all three are parked: the od sweep for the remaining surnames and farms, the rest of the two school files, and the landdrost's own estate at bloemfontein. not a negative about anything — an outage, recorded as an outage.

¦a gate for the atlas, which was the one register without one written, and it failed the build eighteen times on its first runfound the marico entry carried “in the field-cornet's papers” for weeks because nothing on the site pointed at it — no page cited the line, so no page could contradict it. tools/checkatlas.py now refuses a build where a place pinned approximate carries no “why”, and warns where a place with events is discussed nowhere on the site. first run: 18 failures, every one a farm pinned near its district with no note saying so. all eighteen now say what the pin rests on, and several of them say the pin is weak. the check was written to catch one old mistake and caught eighteen live ones.

¦a replacement address for the sandf documentation centre there isn't one — the published address is the dead onenothing sandfdoc@mweb.co.za bounced with 550 relay access denied on 9 september. it is the only address the documentation centre publishes, on its own directory entries and on every guide that lists it. what is left is the telephone (012) 339-4600, the schweikert building at 20 visagie street, and archive@dod.mil.za, which did not bounce and has not answered. a published address that bounces is worse than no address: everyone is writing into it and nobody knows.

¦the baptism finder — which registers exist for paarl (drakenstein), graaff-reinet and stellenbosch every register in the collection begins in 1843nothing 54 registers for paarl (drakenstein), 48 for graaff-reinet, 55 for stellenbosch — and sorted earliest first, the first row in every town is 1843–1844. this is the post-1842 ng kerk archive series and it does not reach the eighteenth century at all. the 21 september 1788 baptism cannot be got from this collection, and neither can anything else this archive wants from before 1843. it explains, retrospectively, why weeks of familysearch work on this family has produced nothing older than the 1840s. a fact about the filming project, not about the registers — the originals exist, at cape town.

¦the baptism database — mountjoy six, and four of them are a sibling group with exact birth datesfound maria elizabeth, born 12 june 1858 · johanna catharina, born 28 january 1860 · georg herkules johannes, born 16 january 1862, baptised 27 april 1862 · elsje petronella frederika, born 10 june 1864, baptised 17 july 1864. roughly two years apart. the names are the interesting part — georg herkules johannes and elsje petronella frederika are thoroughly cape dutch name-strings on an english surname, baptised in the dutch reformed church. this archive already holds a hercules johannes mountjoy born 16 july 1866 — same forenames, same day of the month, four years later.

¦is the 1860 johanna catharina the woman who died at indwe a candidate, and the field that would decide it is the paid onepartly this archive holds “johanna catharina mountjoy of indwe” with no birth date at all — she joined the indwe congregation on 23 july 1907 from barkly oost and the register records her dead there in june 1911. a woman born 28 january 1860 would be fifty-one. not entered: this family already contains one johanna catharina mountjoy, born 1819 and dead 1863, so the name repeats within it. what would decide it is the congregation the 1860 baptism was registered in, and the congregation is behind the paywall.

¦where exactly the paywall falls free gives dates; paid gives parentagepartly free on a baptism record: names, surname, date of birth, baptism date. “sign in to view”: baptism place, source, image, entry number, father's names and surname, mother's names and surname, parents. for a project that already has most of its dates and is short of parents, that is the wrong half — which is exactly why it is worth knowing before paying rather than after. nothing bought, no account made.

¦mooc 8/18.11 — the 1781 inventory of gerrit booijsen it names eleven enslaved peoplefound silvia, lena, sara, janna, dorinda, fortuijn, meij and februarij van de caab; dijk and farla van madagascar; achilles van mallabaar. eight born at the cape, two taken from madagascar, one from the malabar coast. the names are the ones given to them — fortuijn is fortune, februarij and meij are the months they were landed or bought in, achilles is the classical joke a slave-owner made. this project has run for weeks, reaches back to a marriage of 1733, and until today the word slavery appeared nowhere on it — because estate inventories had never been opened.

¦is it the right gerrit almost certainly, and published as almost certainlypartly de villiers has b3 gerrit booijsen married johanna du rand in 1733, father of c4 jan, a burgher at drakenstein — and the inventory is at drakenstein. a man who married in 1733 and died in 1781 is seventy-odd. the only other gerrit in the printed genealogy, b3c4d1, was not baptised until 1771. what settles it is the inventory, which names the heirs. the identification is the uncertain part; the eleven names are not.

¦the letter to the national archives in pretoria, 12 september — six transvaal estate files answered. “all the estate files you are requesting are bound files.”partly ms mavis xaba, archivist assistant, reading room, narssa: “unfortunately, we are therefore unable to scan these files and provide complete digital copies by email.” that is not a refusal, it is a physical fact about the record — the paper is sewn into volumes and will not lie on a scanner. it explains a great deal about what has and has not been filmed, and it retires an assumption this archive has been making for weeks: that the obstacle was willingness or staff time. she put a private researcher who specialises in estate files on copy. engaging her is the user's decision and the user's money, and this archive does not spend either.

¦is there any marriage of a gerhardus lodewicus to a magdalena de beer? a cape genealogist went looking and found nonenothing pieter van zyl: “i searched for a marriage between a gerhardus lodewicus and magdalena de beer but could not find one.” the pairing on line 3 of the 1876 sterfkennis exists in no marriage record anybody has been able to produce. the mother on that line agrees with the book exactly; the father does not.

¦van zyl's guess from memory — that a child of petrus jacobus carried the name he is right, and the child is nine lines lower on the same sheetfound line 3 of notice 678: parents, “gerthardus lödewikus booijsen” and “magdalena de beer”. line 12 of notice 678: eight children, all of age, the fifth being “jan gerthardus lodewikus booijsen”. the name in the parents' box is the back half of a son's name, in one clerk's hand, on one page — and the half that was dropped is jan, which is the name the book gives the father. a grandson named for his grandfather is the ordinary thing in this family, and this archive has a page proving it.

¦who was doing the remembering hendrik stefanus, the seventh child, who signed itfound h. s. booijsen countersigned the form beside the veldkornet, four lines below his own name in the children's list. born about 1828. his grandfather jan married in 1770 and remarried in 1793, and van zyl puts his death more than forty years before 1876. he was writing the name of a man he had almost certainly never met, about a father who was eighty-eight.

¦is the pedigree spine being moved to jan no, and this is deliberatepartly everything against gerthardus lodewikus is secondary. de villiers is a printed genealogy of 1893; pama's revision agreeing with it is one book agreeing with its own earlier edition, not two sources agreeing. against it stands a primary document signed by a son. this archive does not let a book overrule a page because the book is tidier. jan booijsen is entered as inferred, not documented, and the chart still shows gerthardus lodewikus at the top, marked open.

¦what would actually end it the baptism register entry of 21 september 1788partly de villiers is not a source, he is an index to one. his entry for petrus jacobus was compiled from the dutch reformed doopregister, and that entry names the father in a contemporary hand, written within days of the birth, by somebody with no reason to be confused. graaff-reinet, drakenstein and stellenbosch for september 1788, in that order — b3c4 jan was a burgher at drakenstein and the family is at graaff-reinet by 1812. first item on the errands page.

¦two babies, fourteen days apart he 21 september 1788, she 5 october 1788found volume 1 page 78 for him, volume 2 for her. the same author writing consistently with himself, which is worth exactly that and no more — but it is the first date of any kind this archive has had for her.

¦count the name across all three volumes once in part 1, fifteen times in part 2found part 1 holds the entire booijsen genealogy, and the string “david schalk” occurs in it exactly once — “david schalk, gedoopt 4 januari 1807”, which is our man, the child born the year after a van der merwe married into the line. of the fifteen in part 2, thirteen are inside the van der merwe section, generation after generation: 1738, 1739, 1761, 1787, 1790, 1791, 1797, 1800, 1804. david schalk is a van der merwe name and this archive can now say so with a count behind it.

¦adriana christina viljoen — who she was probably his first cousinpartly volume 3, villion thans viljoen: “(e) 12 hercules albertus, gedoopt 30 maart 1777, burger te graaff-reinet, gehuwd 26 februari 1797 met magdalena booijsen”, whose seventh child is “adriana christina, gedoopt 19 augustus 1810”. magdalena booijsen is b3c4d6 — the sister of petrus jacobus. eighteen in 1828, right district, right name. not proved: de villiers gives her no husband, and the 3 november 1828 cradock date is itself only on wikitree. the cradock marriage register would close it.

¦the booijsen–viljoen marriages of 1797 a brother and a sister married a sister and a brother, three months apartfound magdalena booijsen (b3c4d6) married hercules albertus viljoen on 26 february 1797. her brother jan jonathan booijsen (b3c4d5) married his sister judith cornelia theresia viljoen on 28 may 1797. two households became one twice over in a single year, and thirty-one years later a son of the third sibling married a daughter of the first.

¦b3c4d5e6, resolved last week from a gravestone, explained this week she has her mother's three names entirefound jan jonathan booijsen and judith cornelia theresia viljoen's sixth child is “judith cornelia theresia, gedoopt 16 augustus 1807”. the same mechanism as david schalk, in the same generation, in the house next door: a distinctive name enters this surname by marriage and is handed straight down.

¦mountjoy, downing, werdmuller, sleer in de villiers not there at allnothing zero occurrences of mountjoy, montjoy, downing, werdmuller or sleer across all three volumes. de villiers recorded the old cape families — the dutch, german and french of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. the british and the 1820 settlers are simply out of scope, which is a fact about the book and not about the families, and is the reason half this archive will never be found in it.

¦google books, to chase the london tailor into a directory blocked — quota zero without a keyblocked books.googleapis.com returns http 429, “quota_limit_value: 0”, for anonymous callers. item 9 — whether john godloff kolbe of the 1844 obituary was at brunswick square or at conduit street — is not closed and needs a different route. one thing did come out of it: a list of 234 london master tailors who met at the freemasons' tavern on 22 december 1799 over the combination act, printed in the times of 27 january 1800, includes “kolbe, john, 18, broad-street, soho”. right trade, right city, right age, and soho was the german quarter. not claimed, because a john kolbe in london is not yet this john kolbe.

¦who was mccabe — the surname the free state estate index files the commandant's widow under francis mccabe, landdrost of bloemfonteinfound the friend, 29 february 1872, with an obituary under it: son of dr mccabe, a staff-assistant surgeon attached to the british army on the cape frontier, born at one of the military posts in what is now british kaffraria on 29 september 1817; “married his second wife about ten months since — the widow of the late commandant j.g.e. kolbe, of kafirberg, near this town”; died suddenly of heart disease on 23 february 1872, aged 54. this archive has been saying for days that it did not know who mccabe was. he was the town's own magistrate.

¦how long the second marriage lasted about fifteen monthsfound married about april 1871, widowed 23 february 1872. she had been widowed on 3 april 1868 with twelve children, and she outlived the second husband by twenty-four years. his obituary counts both families: “four sons and two daughters, besides a large family of step-children”. for about eleven months there were eighteen children attached to one household.

¦how he died a cart into a sluit, on the anniversary of the state's independencefound he had spent 23 february superintending the burghers' annual target shooting for the government prize. at 5:15 he set off by spring-cart with four horses, adjutant van rensburg of the free state artillery and a servant, for the diamond fields, meaning to sleep at his own farm uitvlugt on the modder river. at half past seven, in deceptive moonlight, one hour's ride short of the farm of mr g.f. enslin, the cart went into a sluit washed out by the rains. g.f. enslin is already in this archive — he placed the 1863 notice saying maria elizabeth kolbe had died intestate. here he is a landmark on a road at night.

¦any of the twelve children, by name one — “john kolbe, jun.”found free state criminal court, reported in the friend in the second half of 1869: a horse thief pleaded guilty to driving off, in october 1868, from the farm springfield, ward upper modder-river, district bloemfontein, a black mare and foal belonging to “anna jacoba van der merwe, widow of late j.g.e. kolbe”, a blue schimmel mare and foal belonging to “john kolbe, jun.”, and a chestnut riding horse belonging to “jephts, a man of color, now residing at leeuwberg”. six months after the death, a son is holding stock in his own right beside his mother. and a man who would otherwise be in no document at all is named in the same sentence, with property of his own.

¦where the farm actually was about two hours' ride from bloemfonteinfound the friend, 13 january 1870, an auction advertisement dated bloemfontein 30 november 1869: “the farm, wildebeestkooi, adjoining the farm leeuberg, the property of the late j.g.e. kolbe, about two hours ride from the town of bloemfontein.” this archive pinned leeuwberg at fauresmith two days ago, 130 km away, and published the pin with its own objection attached. the objection was right. withdrawn to /corrections/ and the pin moved. kafferberg, kaalspruit, leeuberg, wildebeestkooi and springfield are one neighbourhood.

¦what the settler did before colesberg existed he kept a mission school for bushmen on the ground the town was laid out onpartly the friend, first half of 1869, “forty-five years ago, by john montgomery, founder of burghersdorp”, describing a journey from cradock about 1824: “i continued my journey towards the orange river, by koolskop, where the father of the late lamented commandant kolbe conducted a bushmen mission school, and which is now colesberg.” colesberg was laid out in 1830. recorded as an inference: montgomery is recalling forty-five years back and names the man only as somebody's father. it is also specific, and from a man who founded a town in the same district.

¦a fourth public office for the commandant foreman of the jury, bloemfontein, 1866found a forgery trial before mr van soelen — the same official who spoke at kolbe's graveside two years later. “the jury, through their foreman, mr. j.g.b. kolbe, of kafferberg, brought in a verdict of not guilty.” the initials are printed j.g.b. for j.g.e., in his own town's paper, in his own lifetime.

¦a grandson “little jannie”, ten years old, killed by lightning in 1884 — father uncertainpartly “the eldest son of mr. john kolbe, ‘little jannie’, a promising youth ten years old, was struck dead by the electric fluid on his father's farm five hours to the northward of bloemfontein.” the natal witness index carries the same death and names the father george. two papers, two fathers. if the john of 1884 is the john kolbe junior of 1868, this is the commandant's grandson, and this archive is not going to decide that on a preference.

¦kolbe-booysen — the compound the name page called a tree oddity it is a household in port elizabeth, and it is in print twicefound eastern province herald, 16 october 1944: “sawtelle – kolby-booysen. the engagement has been announced between levina (finnie), only daughter of mr and mrs d. kolbe-booysen, of port elizabeth, to raymond patrick, only son of mrs d. sawtelle, of cambridge, england.” and 19 april 1945: “kolbe-booysen – kruger… hilda, only daughter of lieut. and mrs f. kruger of heidelburg, transvaal, to william (s.a.a.f.), son of mr and mrs d. kolbe-booysen, of port elizabeth.” d is david — david kolbe booyzen, married maria jacoba smit 1921. a town and two children. and the headline spells it kolby and the body kolbe, four words apart.

¦the rest of the forty-three mostly somebody else, and set down as suchnothing a kolbe girl of eleven drowned in a dam in the hantam district in 1874, saving a hottentot girl who also drowned; rev. f.w. kolbe of the paarl on a subscription list; dr kolbe the editor of the s.a. catholic magazine, ill in the transkei in 1899; a watch-repair suit at grahamstown in 1872; a kolbe who swam three miles up a river after failing to save a drowning australian in 1900; and two cape town society marriages of 1890. none of them connects to anything here and none is being adopted because the surname is rare enough to tempt.

¦booyzen and marico, transvaal depot ten documents — seven claims and three nobody had asked forfound the other three are tab source od, the education files of the south african republic, and all three are about a school: a subsidy application, a book order and a set of quarterly returns, each headed “h de vries, jgl booyzen, kwaggafontein, distrik marico, pk kafferskraal”. the first carries a remarks field pointing at an earlier file, or13059/97. the remarks field is the thread.

¦pull the thread — kwaggafontein in the transvaal depot 72 documents; 48 of them this schoolfound from 4 october 1897, when g.e. ter haar of kafferskraal asked the government for a teacher, to april 1900, when the teacher asked for his cheque to be sent to the landdrost and the war ended the file. in between: the school commission finds a teacher (n. de vries); a telegram — “wagon leaves thursday to fetch teacher de vries, is everything in order?”; inspection reports by inspector t.c. stoffberg; a dispute over when the teacher moved into his house; a subsidy chased; school furniture bought; holidays; and two pupils leaving.

¦which of the forty-eight carry the surname eight, and always in the same placefound jgl booyzen is named on the subsidy application, two book orders, all four quarterly returns, the explanation of an adverse balance of £61-6-0, and a letter of may 1899 telling the department that in his opinion £8 too little subsidy had been paid, with reasons. he is on none of the holiday notices, form requests or railway certificates, which the teacher sent alone. that is the shape of a school commission's treasurer, not a teacher and not a parent.

¦which jgl booyzen not answered, and not guessedpartly the elder jan gerthardus lodewikus, born about 1818, died at vaalbank on 25 may 1885 and cannot be this man. his namesake born 4 december 1855 would be forty-two in 1898 and is a man of whom this archive has said for months that nothing is known of what became of him. marico adjoins lichtenburg; this family is documented in marico from 1892. it is also one of the commonest name-strings in the surname. recorded open.

¦the spelling, in one office, over ten months booyzen, booysen, booijzen — the same manfound january 1898 booyzen; 12 february booysen; 9 may booysen; 1 july booyzen; 20 october booijzen; 15 december booysen. one man, one farm, one government department, one register series, one year. nothing in this archive has shown the point so cleanly: the z is not a branch and the ij is not a generation, it is whichever clerk had the pen.

¦booysen and onderwyzer, transvaal depot sixteen — and one of them is on this family's own farmfound most are other booysens running other farm schools across the republic: wonderboom, hartsenbergfontein, kareeboomputten, zeekoefontein. but or19199/98 and or19484/98 read “ds. booysen (onderwyzer jp louw) vaalbank district lichtenburg postmerk rietkuil” — vaalbank is the farm where jan gerthardus lodewikus booijsen died in 1885 and his daughter in 1920. he sends the school's power of attorney and eighteen pence in stamps to the government bookkeeper, and co-signs the fourth-quarter returns.

¦and the best of the three vaalbank files or2037/99, 6 february 1899 — school materials for orphansfound “ds. booijsen, louw (onderwijzer), vaalbank, distrik lichtenburg, pk rietkuil. vraagt inlichtingen over het verschaffen van leermiddelen aan weezen, naar aanleiding van een geval ten hunnen.” asks how school materials may be provided to orphans, arising from a case among them. it is the only document in this archive in which a booysen writes to a government about a child who is not his own.

¦is ds. a pair of initials or the dutch ds. for dominee cannot be read from an index linepartly david schalk is this family's most used name-string, and ds. on this farm in 1898 would put a named relative on it. but six weeks earlier the same school wrote “jp louw ds van roojen” in exactly the same slot, and ds. van rooijen is far more likely a minister. one abbreviation, two readings, and this archive will not choose between them to make the better story true. the file settles it in a sentence; it has gone on the errands page.

¦the atlas line that said “in the field-cornet's papers” wrong, and corrected in placefound the papers are the education department's. a field-cornet appears in the bundle exactly once, valuing the teacher's dwelling in may 1898, in a document sent by somebody else. the line had been written from a memory of the record rather than from the record, and it survived because nothing on the site cited it. an event with no citation is an event nobody can check.

¦the seven towns, which needed no argument philippolis · bethulie · uitenhage · piet retief · hoopstad · steynsburg · queenstownfound all seven came out of two days' work and none was on the map. philippolis is where the 1868 obituary says the settler's children grew up — a fourth independent source for what this archive had inferred from baptism places. bethulie is where frederik fortunatus was born in 1839 and where he brought his own youngest daughter to be baptised forty-two years later. uitenhage is where the eldest son was born in 1822, two years after the landing.

¦leeuwberg, where the commandant died pinned at fauresmith, on one land filepartly a free state land file of 1903 reads “leeuwberg no 465 dist. faurismith extent about 1 200 morgen”. that is a farm of the right name in the right province thirty-five years after he died there, and nothing more. farm names repeat. the pin carries the caveat on the map.

¦kaalspruit, where he lived and lies pinned at bloemfontein, on a pair of namespartly his own advertisement of 9 march 1864 is signed from “kafferberg, kaalspruit”. a free state soil-conservation district is registered as “kaalspruit – kafferrivier (bloemfontein)” — the same two names paired, in the district whose bank he directed and whose paper he advertised in. a name pair is not a survey beacon and the pin says so.

¦the part that does not fit, said out loud fauresmith and bloemfontein are 130 kilometres apartpartly the obituary says he died at leeuwberg and that he “settled on the farm where he died and now lies buried on kaalspruit”. those cannot both be true of two farms that far apart. either one of this archive's two identifications is wrong, or the obituary is loose. both pins are marked approximate and the contradiction is printed with them rather than smoothed over by choosing one.

¦the friend, 10 april 1868 — five days before the grahamstown journal the grahamstown version is a reprint, and it drops a linefound the friend is the free state paper and printed it first. its wording: “of the eight sons and four daughters he has left behind him, one daughter alone is married, the youngest being but an infant.” the grahamstown reprint says only “of four daughters”. so the twelve children are eight sons and four daughters, which this archive did not know an hour ago. the transcriber also notes that the obituary “continues for a further half column, but is very difficult to read” — so there is more, and it is not transcribed.

¦two transcriptions of one sentence, disagreeing on the farm kaalspruit against “[randspruit]”partly grahamstown: “settled on the farm where he died and now lies on kaalspruit”. the friend: “now lies buried on [randspruit]”, the brackets the transcriber's own admission of doubt. one of the two is wrong and this archive could not say which.

¦and the man settles it himself, four years earlier “j.g.e. kolbe, kafferberg, kaalspruit, 9 march 1864”found a lost-property advertisement in the friend, signed with his own address as the paper printed it. kaalspruit is right and the bracketed reading is wrong. the advertisement does a second job: it concerns “a promissory note, date 9th march 1864, drawn by george augustus kolbe in favor of j.g.e. kolbe, payable 4 months after date for £154 stg”, lost on the market square at bloemfontein. the settler's eldest son and his twin-born brother, in one document, over a debt.

¦the friend, 23 october 1863 — an estate notice, printed twice a sister's death, dated at lastfound “derwyl maria elizabeth kolbe zonder testament na te laten is overleden en de nagebleven echtgenoot g.f. enslin … als executeur is aangesteld.” mary elizabeth kolbe died intestate and her husband george frederick enslin was appointed executor of her estate. this archive had “bef. 1867”, inferred from a baptism. it is now before 23 october 1863, from a notice her own husband placed in the paper.

¦a note on how the address is printed here as the paper printed it, and not used as a labelpartly the 1864 advertisement gives his address with a place-name that is a racial slur in south african english. this archive quotes the advertisement as it stands, because that is what quoting a document means, and does not carry the word anywhere else — the farm is indexed as kaalspruit.

¦then the stone, which this archive has had all along “born in london 23 february 1803 and died at burghersdorp 2_ november 1867”found the burgersdorp monument is on the kolbe page, photographed, and its caption quoted the inscription as far as “also his relict margaret downing…” and stopped there. the next two lines carry an exact birth, where this archive had “c. 1804”, and settle the death at 1867. a transcription that stops before the end of an inscription is not a transcription. the day of death is a 2 and a digit that will not resolve at any magnification, and is not guessed.

¦and the newspaper, put in its place “about three months since” was nearly fivefound yesterday this archive set the obituary of 15 april 1868 against its own 1867 and published the discrepancy rather than resolving it — which was right, because it could not then resolve it. the stone resolves it. what the obituary got right was the place: burgersdorp, which this archive did not have.

¦naairs · werdmuller · 266 documents, never searched before the settler's fourth daughter has three filesfound kab mooc 7/1/332 no. 205 — “kolbe, augusta louisa. wife of coenraad johannes otto werdmuller van elgg. will”, made 1868, filed 1873. kab mooc 6/9/145 no. 9981 — her death notice, 1873. kab mooc 13/1/299 no. 93 — her liquidation and distribution account, 1874, which means there was something to distribute. the will is the first document read here that ties her to that man by anything but a newspaper.

¦the date that settles yesterday's open question she died 1873. he remarried 7 july 1874.found a year and a month — which is what a widower does. yesterday this archive published the werdmuller descent as “a chain with a gap in it”, the gap being whether charles andrew belonged to the first marriage or the second.

¦and a document that puts father and son in one line gsc 2/1/1/41 no. 60, 1882 — “c.a. werdmuller and company”found “illiquid case. charles andrew werdmuller and coenraad johannes otto werdmuller trading as ca werdmuller and company versus … acknowledgement of debt.” father and son in business together in the year the father died. a son of the 1874 marriage would have been seven in 1882 and nine when charles andrew married in 1884. he can only be a child of the first marriage, and the first wife is the settler's daughter.

¦the loophole that is left, named rather than ignored an earlier wife, before augusta louisapartly c.j.o. werdmuller is in the cape supreme court from 1854, so he was an adult two decades before she died. if there was a wife before her, charles andrew could be hers. his 1882 death notice — kab mooc 6/9/187 no. 4160 — lists his children and would close it. it is now the most wanted page on the cape errand, because it decides whether a victoria cross married a great-granddaughter of the 1820 settler.

the entity audit — sweeping for other things that travel through data
an arrow entity printed at the reader on the home page · searched 14 sep 2026 · where it is used →

¦sweep the 642 built pages for a double-escaped entity nothing leftfound the bug the reader caught: three way-in cards on the home page passed their arrow as a data string — the arrow written as an html entity, ampersand r-a-r-r semicolon — and a string prop is escaped on output, so the page printed those five characters where an arrow belonged. arrows written straight into markup were never affected. having fixed the three, this sweep asks the built site whether the same fault is anywhere else. it is not.

¦ask the same of the source rather than the output — every entity sitting inside a quoted prop or data value in site/src no entity anywhere else in prop or data positionfound the source is asked as well as the output, because a page can exist without having been rebuilt. 429 em dashes, 306 arrows, 244 middots, 85 right single quotes, 74 en dashes and 69 right double quotes are in use across the site as entities, and every one of them is in markup, where escaping never touches it.

¦every file in site/src/data, for an entity written into data nonefound people.js, places.json, searched.json, corrections.json and the rest are clean, which is the root of it — the home page's three cards were the only place an entity had been written into something that would later be escaped.

¦then: a check in tools/drift.py, so it cannot come back the build now fails on a double-escaped entityfound the check reads the built pages, not the source, so it catches the symptom whatever the cause — an escaped entity reaching a reader is a bug no matter which prop or which component put it there. it is absolute, with no exception for a page that means to quote one; this page wanted to and spells the arrow out in words instead, because a check with an exception is a check that will be excepted. tested by planting one in the built home page: the build failed and named both the entity and the page. the reader found this one before the build did, which is the wrong way round, and that is what the check is for.

¦q.surname=kolbe · q.anyplace=wakkerstroom · south africa frederik fortunatus downing kolbefound born 1891 at wakkerstroom, died there 2 november 1918, transvaal probate 1918. he carries both of this family's kolbe names at once. frederik fortunatus is the settler's son, whom this archive already calls “the source of the fortunatus name across three families”. downing is margaret downing, whom george augustus kolbe married at st leonard's shoreditch in 1819 — a london surname with no business in the eastern transvaal except through that marriage. one man, born seventy-two years after the wedding, carrying both. the convergence is no longer a convergence; the wakkerstroom kolbes are this family's kolbes.
