¦findmypast, as a tool — recorded for whoever comes next three frictions worth knowingfound one: the results url takes keywordsplace, and a place passed as “placename” is silently ignored — 20,309 results against 12 for the same search. two: the newspaper results url cannot be reached by parameters at all; /search-newspapers/results?keywords= only works once the form has been clicked, and a direct navigation bounces to the landing page. three: result rows resist programmatic clicking, so opening a transcript is a manual step. none of this is a reason not to use it; all of it is a reason to budget more time than the searching itself takes.

¦newspapers: keywords=tolosberg, all 108 million pages 0 resultsnothing “we can't find any matching articles for tolosberg.” the name appears nowhere in the british and irish press. that is a scoped negative with real weight: it explains why the place is in no battle list and no gazetteer, and it means the capture of forty-two boers with two guns on 25 april 1901 was never reported in britain under that name. the place is real — a prisoner register and a medal roll both carry it — and the british papers never heard of it.

¦newspapers: keywords=booysen · keywords=daschner 3,262 and 42, none usablenothing the booysen spelling returns 3,262 against booyzen's 7, and daschner 42 — all of them modern, british or unrelated. recorded as a limit of the medium rather than of the search: british papers did not print the names of individual boer prisoners. the scheepers charge sheet is the exception because it was a trial. anyone expecting this family to appear in the british press should expect war reporting and nothing else.

¦lastname=kolbe · eventyear=1841 · keywordsplace=conduit street, london the household, four years before he diedfound 1841 england census, ho107, piece 734, book 1, folio 11, page 15, schedule 38 — st george hanover square, sub-district may fair, street conduit street. “john g kolbe, male, age 76, birth year 1765, birth county as transcribed: foreign.” two things follow. the archive corrected the family tree's “lamb's conduit street” to 34 conduit street from his death record; the census puts him in conduit street four years earlier, independently. and “foreign” is the first document here to say in its own words that he was not english — the german origin had been an inference off a german church burial. three women share the schedule: marianne, 35, charlotte, 30, and amelia a., 25, none of whom this archive had. no mary: george augustus's mother, named at his 1803 baptism, is not in the house.

¦1851 census · lastname=barry · firstname=john · b.1796 ±2 · yorkshire one man in the whole countyfound ho107 piece 2374, folio 563, page 12, schedule 46: “john barry, head, married, male, age 55, birth year 1796, birth town whitby, occupation ship owner, full address ship yards, ruswarp, whitby.” he is the only john barry born about 1796 in the 1851 yorkshire census. the 1838 licence gives a man of the same birth year whose residence parish was bilsdale midcable — residence, not birth — so a man born at whitby, living at bilsdale when he married margaret jackson in 1838, and back at ruswarp by 1851 is one life, not two.

¦1841 and 1851 censuses · lastname=barry · keywordsplace=bilsdale 0 and 0nothing no barry of any forename is indexed at bilsdale in either census. the bilsdale connection rests entirely on the residence parish given on the 1838 marriage licence, which is consistent with a man who lived there briefly and is not evidence of a family seated there. recorded because “a yorkshire farmer of bilsdale” is how the family tree describes him, and the censuses do not support the farm or the seat.

¦england & wales deaths · john barry · whitby district 1858 and 1860 — and that closes question 6found two john barry deaths are registered in the whitby district, in 1858 and in 1860. set against the 1851 census, where the county's only john barry of that age is a whitby ship owner alive at ruswarp, the conclusion is plain: the yorkshire john barry born 1796 died in yorkshire, at least five years after the cape man died at de bruins poort in 1853. question 6 asked this archive to break one profile holding two men. it is broken — not by finding the cape man, but by following the yorkshire man past the date the cape man died. caveat, and it is a real one: the death index gives no age, so neither whitby death is tied to him by anything but district and period.

¦1851 census · kolbe · conduit street, then all london gone, and only a governess leftnothing zero kolbes at conduit street in 1851 — he had died in 1845 and the household had broken up. in the whole of london in 1851 there is one kolbe: “j kolbe”, female, unmarried, 25, born london 1826, occupation governess, a visitor at 4 camberwell new road alfred place, lambeth. too young by a decade to be marianne, charlotte or amelia. the three women of schedule 38 are not in the 1851 london census under their own surname.

¦kolbe · london · 1836–1856 amelia married, and four other kolbes surfacepartly amelia ann kolbe married at st pancras in 1854 — indexed twice, in england & wales marriages 1837–2005 and england marriages 1538–1973. that is the amelia a. of the 1841 conduit street schedule, aged 25 there and marrying thirteen years later. four others, none tied to this family and all recorded so the next person does not have to find them again: emanuel christopher kolbe, born 1766, buried at bermondsey st mary magdalen 1836 — one year younger than johan gottlieb and worth testing as a brother; george kolbe, died 1848, westminster st margaret; elizabeth kolbe, died 1852, strand; and jane day kolbe, in the london gazette in 1852 and married in 1853.

¦a lead that does not need a subscription j. g. kolbe in the london gazette, 1836partly the search returns “kolbe, j. g., 1836, london gazette 1665–2018”. the gazette prints bankruptcies, dissolutions of partnership, and naturalisations — any of which would say what a german tailor in mayfair was doing in 1836, nine years before he died. the london gazette is free at thegazette.co.uk and fully searchable, so this one should not be spent on a trial. written down here because it was found on one and is worth following on none.

¦the state of it before today one query, 9 seppartly findmypast has been used exactly once in this project: a search for mountjoy born about 1782, which returned 12,984 results and was abandoned as untractable. that is the whole of it. every british and irish wall in this archive — john barry of bilsdale, john augustus barry born at sea to a mother “born neagle”, james montjoy the saddler, the kolbes in london, the downings in shoreditch — had never been put to it.

¦search syntax, established keywordsplace, not placenamefound recorded because it cost time. the results url takes firstname, lastname, yearofbirth, yearofdeath, eventyear, keywords and keywordsplace. a place passed as “placename” is silently ignored — the same search returned 20,309 results with it and 12 with keywordsplace. anyone repeating this work should check the result count changes when they add a place.

¦lastname=barry · firstname=john · keywordsplace=bilsdale, yorkshire the yorkshire man, documentedfound yorkshire, archbishop of york marriage licences index 1613–1839, record gbprs/or/york/m/00137233/1, page 21, sequence 3: “john barry, age 42, birth year 1796, residence parish bilsdale midcable, yorkshire”, licence dated 2 october 1838, intended marriage at helmsley, to margaret jackson, 35, of the parish of beadlam, yorkshire. question 6 says one profile holds two men — a yorkshire farmer of bilsdale and a man who died at de bruins poort in the cape — and until now the yorkshire half was an assertion off a tree. it is now a record, with a parish, an age, a date and a wife. it does not by itself prove the two are different men, since a man of 42 marrying in 1838 could have had an earlier family; what it does is give the archive a second john barry it can actually hold.

¦firstname=john augustus · lastname=barry · keywords=neagle two hits, both americannothing westfield, hampden, massachusetts, 1861. not this family. broadening to lastname=barry with keywords=neagle gave 193, overwhelmingly directories and north america. the mother's surname from the 1915 death notice is not, on this evidence, a way into the irish records by keyword alone.

¦lastname=barry · firstname=john · yearofbirth=1796 ±3 · keywordsplace=yorkshire two yorkshire men, not onepartly 358 hits resolve into at least two john barrys born 1795–96 in the north riding, and neither is obviously ours. a bilsdale man: the 1838 marriage licence to margaret jackson. a whitby man: baptised at whitby st mary the virgin 1795, a marriage licence in 1839, the 1841 census at whitby, the 1851 census at ruswarp, whitby — and an entry in britain, merchant seamen 1835–1857. the seaman is tempting, because john augustus barry's death notice says he was born at sea in 1819; but a man in the whitby census in 1851 is a poor fit for a death at de bruins poort in 1853, and nothing here names a son. a third john barry born 1796 married at stokesley in 1852. recorded so the next person knows the north riding holds several and that the name alone will not separate them.

¦newspapers: keywords=booyzen, 107,989,139 pages 7 articles, 3 of one storypartly the results url is /search-newspapers/results?keywords= — reached only by clicking the form; url parameters alone bounce back to the landing page. of seven articles, three are the same charge sheet from the trial of scheepers (sunderland daily echo 25 jan 1902 p3; edinburgh evening dispatch 23 jan 1902 p4; and a third under “operations in the northern transvaal”). the charge, reconstructed across three ocr readings: “barbarous act, contrary to customs of war — pieter booyzen, john van der berg, portlock rubidge and albert van der burgh, prisoners of war, placed in firing [line]”, at aberdeen, 21 may 1901. that is commandant gideon scheepers, tried and shot in january 1902, and this pieter booyzen is a man held by a commando, not riding with one — a cape context, three weeks after our three were taken at tolosberg. not adopted, and noted only because aberdeen is a district this family appears in. the remaining four articles are noise: a johannesburg suburb spelt booyzens, a mining share, and a bradford northern rugby player.

¦keywords=booyzen across all record sets a war grave in plymouthpartly 33 hits, of which 22 census and 7 military. one is worth writing down: jan booyzen, born 1898, died 1918, in lives of the first world war and the commonwealth war graves commission debt of honour, buried at plymouth (efford) cemetery, united kingdom. a twenty-year-old south african of this surname who died in britain in 1918 and lies there still. no connection to this family is claimed or tested.

¦full-text search, q.text=barry kolbe, south africa 0 resultsnothing the first hope was that full-text search — which reads unindexed images rather than volunteer indexes — could reach the two missing barry children. it cannot. south african full-text coverage does not include the dutch reformed church registers. that is a clean negative and it closes the last screen route to those two children.

¦full-text search, q.text=booyzen ~140 hits, 7 pages, 4 collectionsfound what the coverage does include, and what this archive has never once searched: voter records, south africa, voting records 1925–1931 · de list, cape province, military records 1901–1903 · land records, south africa, farm records 1895 and 1895–1955. the military one lands on the anglo-boer war years and the rebel question; the land ones land on question 11, the farm. all four are full-text searchable, which is a different kind of access from anything this archive has used.

¦rak 2508, “ewaton book 2” — the land-register index, images 14 and 15 four booyzen entries, with foliospartly an alphabetical index in three columns, surname · christian name · folio, read from the image and not from the ai transcript, which is unreliable. the booyzen block reads: “booyzen · catharine mary [s…] · 2492” and “jacobus nicolaas · 201”; “booijzen · matthys joh… · 1866”; “booijzen · jacobus nicholas · 2267”; “booyzen · jacobus nicolaas · 1931, 1939”. two of those names are in this archive. jacobus nicolaas booyzen is the eldest of the eight on the 1863 death notice, who “ended in the transvaal” with estate tab mhg 52653 and nothing else attached to him — and evaton is in the transvaal. the catharine mary reading is the family's signature female name and the hardest of the four to be sure of. nothing is adopted: a surname in a land index is not an identification, the folios have not been followed, and the ledgers those folios point into are a different volume from this index.

¦rak 2384, wonderboom south — the folios followed into a transfer register three booyzen transfers, one dated 1907partly image 219 of 261, image group 121082126. a deeds transfer register for wonderboom south, which is pretoria — the district where david schalk booysen was living at goedehoop when he remarried in november 1905. three rows carry the name. (1) “e. s. d. gey van pittius (gel. schulte)” to petrus jacobus booyzen, 1939, £25. (2) “boedel wyle p. j. booyzen” — the estate of the late p.j. booyzen — to magdalena johanna booyzen. (3) “m. j. booyzen (born bezuidenhout), wed.” to david schalk booyzen, 9 april 1907. the household reads petrus jacobus, david schalk, magdalena johanna — which is this archive's direct line name for name, and is exactly why it is being written down as a lead and not as a finding. not proved and not adopted. if the david schalk of april 1907 were this archive's david schalk booysen, born cradock 1848, it would carry him seventeen months past the last date held for him and give him land; but the transferor is a widow born bezuidenhout and this archive's man married a widow born stols, so the household may be a different branch entirely. the next step is the deed itself, not this ledger line.

¦“de list”, military records 1901–1903, image 51 of 69 — read from the image three booyzens, prisoners of warfound a printed anglo-boer war prisoner-of-war transport list, south africa government archives (pretoria), image group 008019246, volume no. 10469–32561. three consecutive entries: “18463 booyzen, stephanus francois, 28” · “18464 booyzen, petrus jacobus, 29” · “18465 booyzen, david schalk, 54”. all three on the same ship, the city of cambridge, sailing 3 june 1901, all three entered from pretoria, pretoria. consecutive prisoner numbers on one transport means taken together. this archive has asked for years whether the family fought and has only ever been able to answer for the cape, where the roll holds no booysen. this is the transvaal side, and it is a different question with a different answer.

¦so/pow film 008019246 — what the nine items actually are a much fuller register existsfound the de list that produced the three booyzens is item 3 of nine on the film “archives of the staff officer, prisoners of war, cape town, 1900–1903 (so/pow)”, 1,058 images. item 1, 292 images, is a far better record: “prisoners of war in cape peninsula” and “prisoners of war at cape town and natal”, ruled into pris. no. · surname · christian name · age · home address · town or district · field cornetcy or commando · where captured · date of capture · date of receipt · remarks. home address, commando and place of capture are exactly what the de list does not give and exactly what this archive needs. it is organised in batches by arrival — each batch headed “prisoners of war received at cape town from [dates], nos. n to m” — and alphabetical by surname within each batch.

¦bisecting item 1 to nos. 18463–18465 a different number seriesnothing bisected from image 7 (nos. 10646+) through 63 (15084–15644) and 106 (~17014) to images 139 and 140, which cover 18403–18894. the three numbers do not belong to our men there: 18463, 18464 and 18465 in this register are erasmus hermanus, pieter and johannes christoffel de beer. so the de list's numbers are a separate series and cannot be used to locate anyone in the fuller register, despite both volumes being catalogued “no. 10469-32561”. worth recording because the opposite assumption is the obvious one to make.

¦the b surnames in the may–june 1901 batch, checked five booysens, none ourspartly our three sailed on 3 june 1901, so the batch whose captures run late april to early june is where they should be. its booysens are 18511 jan johannes anthony of sweet klip, standerton, wolmaransstad commando, taken at weltpoort 26 may 1901; 18512 albertus benjamin of lydenburg, taken at boschveld 26 april 1901; 18513 piet van zyl, 23, staats artillery, taken at schraalhaans 1 june 1901; 18514 willem adrian; and 18515 gerhardt jacobus of jackalskraal, winburg, vet river commando. not one of them is stephanus francois, petrus jacobus or david schalk. the three remain to be found by checking the b pages of the other batches — a bounded browse, and not done.

¦the b pages of the 5 april–27 may 1901 batch, walked all three found, with their commandofound image 126 of item 1: “18463 booysen, stefanus francois, 26 · 18464 booysen, petrus jacobus, 27 · 18465 booysen, david schalk, 53”, each with home address pretoria, town or district pretoria, field cornetcy or commando pretoria, where captured tolosberg, date of capture 25 april 1901. two other booysens bracket them and belong elsewhere — 18462 adrian jacobus of fauresmith, edenburg commando, taken at springhaan nek in december 1900, and 18466 gert of bloemfontein, taken at kaffirskraal in october 1900. the register separates those two as cleanly as it groups ours.

¦tolosberg, looked up a war record for the manfound not in any gazetteer reachable by search, not in the standard battle lists, not in a day-by-day 1901 war diary. it is in the medal-roll database at angloboerwar.com, kept by dr david biggins — and the entry is about this man by this number: “booysen was one of 42 boers captured on 25 april 1901 at tolosberg in the waterval valley, eastern transvaal, together with 2 guns and much stock. he was sent to india as pow no 18463.” quoting a city coins auction catalogue of november 2020 describing his abo medal, the same entry makes him a zarp — the zar's police, based at pretoria — under commandant j. p. de la c. schroeder, in action at talana, modder spruit, colenso, platrand (wagon hill) where he was wounded in the right leg, spion kop and dalmanutha. strong secondary evidence: the medal and the application have not been seen here, and it is the prisoner number rather than the name that ties it to the register.

¦q.givenname=petrus jacobus · q.surname=booi* · 1786–1790 · south africa date filter ignoredblocked the decisive record — the baptism of 21 september 1788, which names the father and would settle de villiers against the 1876 sterfkennis — does not surface. the endpoint returns 19th and 20th century entries regardless of the birthlikedate range, and the same happened with anydate on graaff-reinet. this is consistent with what question 0 already says: the 18th-century cape registers are not name-indexed and have to be read page by page. not a negative about the register, a negative about the index.

¦q.surname=booij* · q.fathergivenname=jan · q.mothersurname=de beer de villiers corroborated twicepartly the mother filter did not bite and the wildcard dragged in dutch booijink and booijman families. but two entries land squarely on de villiers' page 78: petrus jacobus booijzen, born 1814, of gerrit booijzen and anna elisabeth theron; and anna susanna booijze, baptised 12 may 1805 at graaff-reinet, of jan jonathan booijze and judith cornelia etresia viljoen. the book gives jan's sons gerrit married to anna elisabeth theron in 1791 and jan jonathan married to judith cornelia theresia viljoen in 1797. two of jan's sons confirmed from records, independently of the book — which raises what the book says about the third son, petrus jacobus.

¦q.surname=barry · q.fathergivenname=john augustus · south africa nine children, a whole householdfound the query question 13 named as untried. it does not answer which two of the eleven are missing — these are grandchildren, not children — but it hands this archive a family it did not have at all. john augustus barry ii, who was a name on two death notices with no wife and no issue, married alida jacoba van ellinckhuizen and had nine children baptised at burgersdorp and then dordrecht, 1871 to 1889. the eldest is a third catherine mary sophia. the seventh is anton rector kolbe barry — the kolbe name in a fourth generation, sixty-two years after the settler landed. a fourth john augustus appears at elliot by 1908, the same village where henry james booyzen married in 1912.

¦the two 1848 barry index entries, opened and compared one man, not twofound henry jaonas barry (baptism indexed 13 nov 1868) and hennery james berry (baptism indexed 13 nov 1848) share a birth date of 13 july 1848, share parents john barry and margret willemina kolbe, sit in the same collection, and are both attached in the familysearch tree to one person: james henry barry, 1848–1939, l6j6-jhx. the film's own title closes the question — “graaff-reinet. baptism records 1846–1851” cannot contain an 1868 baptism. gained: an exact birth and baptism for james henry barry, and the correct place, graaff-reinet, against the cape town and tulbagh the index gives. lost: the tenth-child candidate. image located, apid:th-909-70517-31299-17, and not yet read.

¦film 008119684, image 930 — the entry itself, read entry 603, and a name's originfound “603 · het kind is n. henry james · get. 13 july 1848 · gedoopt 13 novr 1848 · v. john barry · m. margret willemina kolber · gt: petrus jacobus joubert, catharine sophia maria kolber.” the year is 1848 in the clerk's hand, the forename order is henry james rather than james henry, and the godmother — whom this archive held as plain “catharine kolbe” — carries catherine maria sophia eleven years before her sister gave it to the daughter this archive had been treating as the head of that chain. the namesakes page called it a barry name. it is a kolbe name.

¦q.mothersurname=olivier · q.fathergivenname=hendrik stef* — the three untraced daughters, again thirty hits, none oursnothing the relationship search that worked on the kolbes fails here, and the reason is worth writing down: olivier is common enough, and “hendrik stefanus” frequent enough as a forename pair, that the engine returns strydoms, le rouxs and rossouws from jamestown to oudtshoorn and not one member of this household. a method is not a key; it works where the names are rare. anna johanna maria, elesabettha maria cornelya and magdalena johanna booijsen remain exactly where they were.

¦film 008119684, image 876 — john augustus barry ii's font, 1847 three kolbes at the fontfound entry 80: “het kind n. john august · get. 13 maart 1847 · gedoopt 12 april 1847 · v. john berry · m. margaretwina kolbe · gt: john kolbe, margaret kolbe, augusta kolbe” — the third witness the least certain of the three. read with entry 603 of the year after, where the godmother is catharine sophia maria kolbe, the pattern is plain: at both fonts every witness is a kolbe, and the forenames this archive has been calling barry names are the names of the people standing at them.

¦q.surname=b*rry · q.mothersurname=kolb* and col* — every spelling the index uses seven children, and four known ones missingnothing the mother is indexed as kolbe, kolber, kolbee, colbe, colby and colbee, and her forenames run margret willemina, margret lowisa, margaretha louisa willemina, margarita elizabeth willemina and margerite elizabeth wellemina. sweeping all of them returns seven baptisms — 1847, 1848, 1850, 1853, 1859, 1861, 1863 — and not one name this archive did not already hold. the important part is what is absent: hendrik nicholaas, richard peter, margaret mary and kathleen mary are all named on their parents' death notices and none of the four is in the index. so the index cannot find four children this archive knows existed, which settles that it will not find the two it does not. this route is closed, and closed for a demonstrable reason rather than a discouraging one. what is left is the registers themselves — graaff-reinet, burgersdorp and dordrecht — read across the gaps at 1851-1852, 1854-1858 and after 1864.

¦the register that would settle it, located and measured one book, 534 imagesblocked the two missing barry children, if they were born in the gap, are in a single volume: burgersdorp. baptism records 1852–1866, image group 008039088, 534 images — it covers 1854 to 1858 entire, and the years on either side. landmarks for bisecting it: 1853 is at image 54 (entry for william fredrik barry, 23 october), and 1866 is at image 528. that is roughly 36 images a year, which puts the 1854–1858 gap at about images 70 to 250. there is no name index at the back — 528 onward are ordinary 1866 entries. not yet read: this is a sequential browse of some 150 images and it was not attempted in the session that located it, deliberately, because the viewer's image-number box does not reliably move the single-image view (the grid view does jump, and is the way in). written down so the job resumes rather than restarts.

¦familyhistory.bdm.qld.gov.au · subjectfamilyname=booyzen · births, marriages and deaths nothing at allnothing the spelling this archive uses does not occur once in queensland's register between 1829 and 1996. neither does booysens, nor slier, nor schoeman.

¦· subjectfamilyname=booysen two, and neither is oursnothing betty beatrice booysen, who died in 1977, was born an appleby of english parents. jasper van graan booysen, who died in 1994, is the son of hendrik hermanes booysen and dorothea catharina van graan — an afrikaans household, and a real one, but no hendrik hermanes and no van graan appears anywhere in this archive. a shared surname and a shared country of origin are not a join.

¦· mountjoy, kolbe, daschner, pretorius, olivier, engelbrecht, enslin fifty-nine rows, all other familiesnothing the queensland kolbes are a german catholic family who married wiemers and thurners at toowoomba. the queensland daschners descend from josef daschner and fany wagner, bavarians — not from joseph heinrich daschner of stutterheim. most olivier hits are the word used as a given name, in the barkus family. the pretorius rows are afrikaans and unconnected: ben johannes pretorius married edith watts treasure at brisbane in 1918, and neither name is in this archive.

¦what the null actually closes one standing question, answeredfound queensland's index covers births to 1926, marriages to 1951 and deaths to 1996. across that whole span no member of this family registered a birth, a marriage or a death in queensland. the family's arrival in brisbane is as recent as this archive says it is, and there was no earlier australian branch to find.

¦boijens-9 and de_beer-638 — following the contradiction one generation up contradiction explainedfound jan booysen married magdalena de beer on 21 january 1770 and married again on 15 december 1793, so his wife was dead by then; this archive's magdelena elisabeth de beer died in 1843. fifty years apart, which is the objection question 0 raised against the 1793 will when it declined to adopt it — the reasoning was right, and the will is now positively his. the tree's own de beer profile explains the rest: codes b6c2 and b6c6, baptisms in 1745 and 1754, and a sibling list holding both a magdalena and a magdalena elizabeth. two women merged into one profile. gained: a candidate for our woman's parents, zaccharias de beer and anna pretorius, and a second printed reference, de villiers and pama vol 1 p. 78.

¦does the letter carry an address at its head? no — “london” and nothing finernothing this was the question the enquiry most hoped for. an 1844 obituary puts the family at brunswick-square; the rate books, the gazette, the census and the burial register put him in soho and then conduit street. the letter does not settle it. recorded as plainly as the finds, because a document that arrives and does not answer the question is still a result.

¦is “lms missionary” from the papers or from the donor? from the papers, in the father's own handfound “mr miles had called at our house & informed me that you had been fully accepted by the [l.m.s.] as one of their missionaries”, and “dr philip was exceedingly glad to hear of your being accepted”. john philip was the lms superintendent at the cape and had carried the previous letter. independent of john montgomery's memoir, which was written down forty-five years after the fact. two witnesses to the mission, forty-five years apart.
¦what are the other pages? the four pages are the letterfound there is no second item in the collection. the catalogue's “photocopy, 4 pages” is the letter and nothing else.

¦where is the original, and who was dr griffiths? the background file holds nothing furthernothing “unfortunately the background file does not give any further information on the donation or any other donations by dr. griffiths.” the whereabouts of the original is not recorded and cannot be pursued from that end. a clean negative from the only place that could have answered it.

¦“kind love from your sisters & brother” the line that dates the obituaryfound sisters plural, brother singular, august 1830. of the eight sons the 1844 obituary counts, exactly two were alive — george augustus at the cape and henry in london with dropsy. henry died 13 april 1832. from that day george augustus was “the last remaining of eight sons”, and the grahamstown journal did not say so until december 1844. the obituary is corroborated and the date it became true is now known.

¦henry, from his father's pen dropsy, and “resigned to the catastrophe”found this archive had john henry kolbe's font, his 1819 old bailey deposition, his 1819 marriage, his 1824 bankruptcy and his 1832 burial. it now has his illness and his father's grief, twenty months before the end.

¦elizabeth kolbe, who married john milne in 1817 she is betsey and she lives in edinburghfound “milne with elizabeth & family had transferred their residence to edinburgh… betsey likes the situation very well.” four days ago she was a line in the westminster marriage index. a nickname is something no register ever gives.

¦charlotte kolbe an inference no longerfound on 17 september this archive marked marianne, charlotte and amelia of the 1841 conduit street household as inferred daughters, because they matched no baptism and the 1841 census records no relationships. “charlotte sends you an evangelical magazine.” her record moves from inf to doc. marianne and amelia are still inferred.

¦what else is in it a suit of black clothes, two kings and a baboonfound “a suit of black clothes, hope they may be wide enough for you, as i understand that you are stout as long” — clerical black for a newly accepted missionary — with a sash, a waistcoat and last year's newspapers. the death of george iv on 26 june and william iv “a king after the people's heart”. the french revolution of july 1830 as three-week-old news. and a request that his son ask the society whether a baboon story in a magazine called the mirror is true.

¦an unasked-for second document a dsab entry by dr karel schoeman — not yet readnothing two pages written for the dictionary of south african biography, found in the background file, by dr karel schoeman of the national library, with a list of bronne (sources). it is a secondary work, but schoeman was a serious historian and the source list is the useful part. this archive has not read it.

¦can the marriage of miss mary field to mr bellew, a surgeon, be found? no — and the negative is controlled six waysnothing the letter of 23 august 1830 says “the eldest, miss mary, that was, has married a mr bellew, a surgeon”, so the marriage is before that date. findmypast, using the spouselastname filter with a nonsense-value control returning 0: field × bellew returns one record in the whole life events collection and it is 1854 at stepney — twenty-four years too late. exact spellings bellew, bellow, ballew, belew, bellewe and bellows, each against 1823–1835: all zero. widened to 1814–1844: still zero. the variants engine is worse than useless — it collapses bellew into bell, boyle and balow and returns 1,724 rows. either the marriage is outside findmypast’s london coverage, or a seventy-year-old man misspelled a surname he had heard spoken. the five friends named in that letter remain the only people in it this archive cannot reach.

¦the story from the mirror — can it be found after all? yes — and it is by james hoggfound the mirror of literature, amusement, and instruction, volume xiv (1829), pp. 313–318: “spirit of the public journals — a singular letter from southern africa. communicated by mr. hogg, the ettrick shepherd.” fiction, printed as a settler’s letter home, by the author of the private memoirs and confessions of a justified sinner. chief karoo offers oxen and “a choice virgin to boot” for the wife; “he foretold i should repent it”; captain johnstone and nine british soldiers; the wife carried across the river by “a band of pongos, (ourang-outangs)”; found as their queen. five earlier searches failed because they hunted a surname that does not exist — the narrator is anonymous and it is his son who is called william. the tailor was right: “here we look upon the story as a fictious & romance”.
the dsab draft on george augustus kolbe — and the eleven sources it names
a secondary work checked against the archive line by line, and its reading list worked as far as a desk can work it · searched 20 sep 2026 · where it is used →

¦who wrote the dsab typescript? karel schoeman — and the library said so in the covering emailfound melanie geustyn, senior librarian, national library of south africa, with the background file in front of her: “the author, ks, would be dr. karel schoeman who worked here at the national library.” her “would be” is a librarian’s hedge and the right one — the typescript carries initials and a date, not a signature — but she reads them with the institution’s own knowledge behind her. this archive reasoned its way to the same answer from the inside and published it as an inference it would not assert, having not read the sentence the attachments were attached to. logged as a correction.

¦does the background file say anything more about the donation, or about dr jean griffiths? no — and that is an answer, not a silencenothing “unfortunately the background file does not give any further information on the donation or any other donations by dr. griffiths.” a librarian went to the off-site vaults, pulled the accession file and looked. where the original of the photocopy is remains unknown, and so does whether the catalogue’s “lms missionary” came from the papers or from the donor — that second question was asked and has not been answered.

¦does the dsab entry agree with this archive where both have the same fact? yes — on nine points, from nine different documentsfound the 1802 birth; j.g.e. kolbe 1822–68 at leeuberg as a commandant; margaret downing 1803–1867; the 1819 london marriage at a very young age; the apothecary’s trade on the settler roll; the farm wurthemberg; ten children; philippolis from march 1831 (this archive has a daughter born there that year). every one of those this archive got from a register, a stone, an obituary or an advertisement, and the entry cites none of them. that is what makes the single disagreement worth reporting.

¦is the entry right that the settler’s father was a german apothecary? no — he was a tailor, and the archive can prove it seven waysnothing 121 westminster rate book entries, the printed roll of 234 master tailors of 1799, the master tailors’ list of april 1834, three london gazette dissolutions all reading tailors, the 1841 census occupation column, the westminster burial register, and john henry kolbe’s deposition on oath at the old bailey in 1819. the trade is the son’s, moved one generation up. the entry is accurate wherever its author had a record; the one thing he had no record for is the one thing he got wrong.

¦does the entry’s “knapdaar” contradict the obituary’s “wirtemberg”? no — the entry says they are the same farmfound “die plaas wurthemberg (soms ook aangegee as knapdaar)”. the heading alone looked like a conflict and the body resolves it. what this archive gains is a second name to search in the deeds records and naairs.

¦was msb 751 written “on his ordination”, as the catalogue says? no — the ordination was 25 may 1833nothing two years and nine months after the letter. the letter reports acceptance as a missionary, which is a different step, and the entry supplies a third — mission assistant on 8 february 1828. the archive had repeated a finding aid as though it were the document. logged as a correction.

¦“extract from the journal of messrs melvill and kolbe”, transactions of the missionary society (1829) — is it online? found — and the reason the first search failed is the interesting partfound the printed version is filed under the other man’s name. full citation: “extracts of the journal of messrs melvill and kolbe, addressed to the rev. richard miles, superintendent of the society’s missions in africa, philippolis, 25 nov. 1828”, council for world missions (lms) archives — which is source 4 on the dsab’s own list, two lines above source 6, and the entry never says they are the same document. “an edited version, dated 18 nov. 1828, appears in melvill (1829).” legassick quotes it: the travellers met refugee groups with “no other means of subsistence than the wild animals found in these parts” — the first words of george augustus kolbe’s this archive has read, and they are about famine. and the journey is printed in full in a book still sold: karel schoeman (ed.), early white travellers in the transgariep, 1819–1840 (protea book house, 2003), p. 30. the google books api refuses this archive entirely — http 429 to every query — and the same searches through the ordinary books interface returned all of this in four minutes.

¦sibree, a register of missionaries, 4th ed. (lms, 1923) — is it online? not found under that title on the internet archivenothing it would give his lms service dates in a single printed line, which is exactly what is wanted to test 8 february 1828, 25 may 1833 and 19 june 1837. searched, not found, and left on the work list.

¦is there any published corroboration of the bethanie claim of 1834, independent of this entry? no — it looked like two witnesses and it is onenothing an encyclopaedia article states that the berlin missionary society founded bethanien for the korana in september 1834 on the advice of the lms’s g.a. kolbe at philippolis — and its footnote cites schoeman’s own 1985 book, die huis van die armes. the draft entry and the article rest on the same man’s research. this archive nearly published it as independent corroboration and it is not. a claim repeated in two places can still be a single witness.

¦are the griqua council’s own papers for 1836 in print? yes — and the entry could not cite themfound karel schoeman (ed.), griqua records: the philippolis captaincy, 1825–1861, van riebeeck society ii/25 — 162 official and semi-official documents including the philippolis law book and the correspondence between the captaincy’s officials and the missionaries. published after this typescript was typed — this row said two years until 11 october 2026, when the catalogue record was read and gave 1996, which is four. it is the obvious place to test the 1836 accusation, the hendricks agitation and the acquittal. available as a purchasable ebook from hipsa; no free digitisation found.

¦is a portrait of george augustus kolbe known to exist? the entry names twofound a likeness of him as a young man, in 1992 with c.j. du plessis of ruigtevlei, district bethulie, reproduced in burger olivier’s so onthou ons die oewerbewoners van ou “grootrivier” (1973); and a charles bell watercolour of a church service at philippolis in 1834 with kolbe in the pulpit, in the africana museum, johannesburg, reproduced in the journal of andrew smith, ed. lye (1975). this archive holds no likeness of anybody born before 1850. neither has been seen.

¦can the charles bell picture of kolbe be found? yes — and in a country the entry does not mentionfound university of edinburgh, centre for the study of world christianity, cswc 60 — five photographs, 1834–1840, photograph copies of sketches by c. bell of african congregations. item 3 is “mr. kolbe… at philippolis in 1834”. the dsab sends the reader to the africana museum in johannesburg for the original watercolour and says nothing of scotland; edinburgh’s catalogue says nothing of johannesburg. the other four sitters include jean-pierre pellissier, who is source 9 on the dsab’s own list.

¦does edinburgh describe him correctly? no — it calls him “a moravian missionary?”nothing with the question mark. he was london missionary society, on the nlsa’s catalogue of msb 751 and on his own father’s letter of 23 august 1830 — “fully accepted by the [l.m.s.] as one of their missionaries”. this is the first time this archive has been in a position to correct an institution rather than be corrected by one, and the letter that does it can ask for a copy of the photograph at the same time.

¦is the “mr miles” of the 1830 letter the richard miles of the 1828 journal? very probably — and it is an inference, not a documentpartly richard miles, formerly pastor of brigg in lincolnshire and appointed to demerara, was sent to cape town to act as dr philip’s substitute while philip was in england. philip was in england from 1826; miles was acting superintendent at the cape in 1828, which is why kolbe addressed his journal to him there; by 1830 philip was back and miles was in london, calling at a tailor’s house in soho. the letter says only “mr miles” and gives no forename, so the office, the continent and the dates carry it and nothing else does. published as an inference and marked as one.
msb 751 read again, from the file rather than from a preview
the same four pages at full resolution, two days later — nothing wrong, a good deal missing · searched 20 sep 2026 · where it is used →

¦does the full-resolution reading contradict anything already published? no — not one wordfound the heading “london august 23. 1830”, the opening “dear george”, the l.m.s. acceptance, mr miles calling at the house, dr philip carrying the earlier letter, henry and the dropsy and “resigned to the catastrophe”, milne and betsey removed to edinburgh, charlotte’s evangelical magazine, the suit of black clothes, george iv and william iv, the french revolution of july 1830, and — the line the whole argument rests on — “kind love from your sisters & brother”. all confirmed from the file.

¦was dr philip only the courier? no — he is in the room, and he is pleasedfound “dr philip was exceedingly glad to hear of you being accepted by the l.m.s. as you may well imagine, he has promised to write to you a letter by the first opportunity.” this archive had him as a man carrying an envelope. he is in london in august 1830, he has heard the news, and he undertakes to write to george himself. that letter, if it was written, is another document with george augustus kolbe’s name on it, and the place to look is the cwm archive at soas that holds his journal.

¦who is the “john” the clothes are for? very probably the commandant, aged eightpartly “i have enclosed also a jacket & waistcoat for john & a further jacket also for him, tell him his old father has sent it him, & to make haste to fill them out.” clothes for a growing child. george augustus’s eldest son was john gerson eliezar kolbe, born 7 july 1822 — eight years old in august 1830, and the man who died a commandant at leeuwberg in 1868. if that is him, this is the earliest document in this archive that mentions him. “his old father” is the difficulty and is not glossed over: the writer is the boy’s grandfather. marked as an inference.

¦does the letter name anybody outside the family? yes — five people, and none of them is anywhere else herefound mr & mrs stanhope; mr warner and mrs warner; mrs field and her daughters, of whom “the eldest, miss mary, that was, has married a mr bellew, a surgeon, whom i do not know whether you may recollect”. this archive has had the soho household entirely through official paper — rate books, a census, the gazette, a burial register. these are the first people in it who simply knew them. a surgeon named bellew marrying a miss mary field about 1829–30 is searchable.

¦what is the story from the mirror that he asks his son to check? two pages, and the strangest thing in the letterpartly a scottish colonist, “either williams, or williamson”, settled close to the xhosa; orang-outangs raid his fruit; he shoots a young one that proves to be a chief’s son; weeks later mrs w. is carried off; he suspects a xhosa chief who had offered oxen and “2 or 3 of his finest caffre women” for her and been refused, whose messenger had said “you will repent of your obstinacy”; he raises a company of soldiers under capt johnson and is on the point of war when a witness is produced who saw an orang-outang carrying a woman across the river; the chief then furnishes his own men to help, and after nearly two years she is found living among the animals as their queen. the father does not believe it — “here we look upon the story as a fictious & romance” — and writes to the one man he knows who is actually there to ask “whether that report may be founded in truth, or falsehood”. the number of the mirror has not been found.

¦do the margins give the street address after all? no — and they are the only lines not readnothing pages two and four carry notes written across the fold about how to direct the box, naming the revd mr murray and dr philip. they are partly illegible at this resolution and are not guessed at. everything else in four pages has been read. brunswick square against conduit street remains open.
sibree’s register of lms missionaries — found free, and it is the best source on him yet
source 5 on schoeman’s list, written up here this morning as “not found” · searched 20 sep 2026 · where it is used →

¦is sibree’s register (lms, 1923) online? yes — free, 225 pages, and this archive said it was notfound a complete pdf at missiology.org.uk. this archive searched the internet archive, found nothing under that title, and published “not found”. that was a negative about one shelf reported as a negative about the world — the same fault this archive names on /method/ as the reason a nil return is worthless without a control. the google books api refuses this machine outright (http 429 to every query); the ordinary web search found it in one attempt.

¦does it hold george augustus kolbe? yes — entry 278, and it is his whole mission lifefound “was previously connected with the graaff reinet missionary society, and laboured among the slaves around graaff reinet. was accepted provisionally by mr. miles, feb. 8, 1829, which action was confirmed by the directors, july 29, 1829. first laboured with mr. clark, at the bushman station, caledon river. thence proceeded to philippolis, arriving there, march 13, 1831. on may 26, 1833, he was ordained by the french missionaries, messrs. lemue, pellisier, and arbousset. his connection was dissolved by the directors, june 19, 1837.” index: service 1829–1837.

¦who was the “mr miles” who called at the tailor’s house in 1830? the man who accepted him — not a messengerfound “accepted provisionally by mr. miles, feb. 8, 1829, which action was confirmed by the directors, july 29, 1829.” richard miles was acting superintendent of the lms at cape town from 1825, sent to stand in for dr philip while philip was in britain. and it explains the father’s adverb: provisionally by miles, confirmed by the directors, and a father told his son had been “fully accepted”. the letter is using the society’s own vocabulary correctly, because the officer concerned was in the room.

¦does sibree agree with the dsab draft? on three points exactly, and not on three otherspartly agree: the graaff-reinet society and the slaves, almost word for word; clark and the bushman station; the dissolution on 19 june 1837 to the day. differ: acceptance 8 february 1829, not 1828; philippolis 13 march 1831, which is finer than schoeman’s “march 1831” and agrees with it; ordination 26 may 1833 not the 25th, and by lemue, pellissier and arbousset — three men, with no casalis. pellissier is source 9 on schoeman’s own list. both are printed works and neither is the manuscript; this archive gives both and prefers neither in print.

¦was f.w. kolbe of the rhenish mission related to this family? no — and the lms’s own register is the one that is wrongnothing sibree, entry 522: “kolbe, frederick william. born, nov. 3, 1821, in south africa. son of rev. g. a. kolbe (no. 278).” died at cape town 25 december 1899 aged 78; author of an english–herero dictionary. schoeman: “f.w. kolbe (1821–99) van die rynse sendinggenootskap was nie aan hierdie familie verwant nie.” same man, same society, same years. and he cannot be adopted on sibree’s word: 3 november 1821 agrees with his age at death, and the settler’s known eldest was born 7 july 1822, which agrees with his age at death. eight months apart. sibree also gives a sister, charlotte kolbe born 25 december 1829, who married rev. william sykes at paarl in 1860. not adopted, not dismissed, and on the work list. resolved the same afternoon. three independent works against sibree: the new catholic encyclopedia on his son monsignor f.c. kolbe — “the son of a westphalian (german) protestant missionary who had married the daughter of a member of the london missionary society”; s2a3, which names him friedrich wilhelm kolbe, rhenish missionary and herero scholar, married at cape town in 1849 and at okahandja by april 1850; and dsab vol. 5 (1987), which has its own entry on him and was in print five years before schoeman wrote, which is why the draft marks him with an asterisk. sibree has two kolbes in south africa, entries 278 and 522, and a compiler joined them. charlotte kolbe born 25 december 1829 goes with him.
the nautilus roll, and the story from the mirror
two more of schoeman’s eleven sources worked — one delivered, one did not · searched 20 sep 2026 · where it is used →

¦what does the settler roll actually say? “kolbe, george augustus 20. chemist. w margaret 19.”found from nash’s settler handbook, page 98, published in full at 1820settlers.com. he was sixteen — born 7 december 1802 and sailing from gravesend on 3 december 1819, four days before his seventeenth birthday. she was sixteen. about three years added to each.

¦is the roll consistent with the marriage allegation? no — and that is the interesting partfound at shoreditch on 20 january 1819 both swore to being “of the age of twenty-one years and upwards”, because a minor could not marry by licence without a parent’s consent. eleven months later he is twenty and she is nineteen. nobody twenty-one and upwards in january is twenty in december. they were not maintaining a fiction; they were telling each document what it needed.

¦what became of owen’s party? it collapsed in 1821, and it explains the gapfound fifty-two people, no. 3 on the colonial department list, joint-stock and recruited in london by thomas owen of 9 carey street, horseferry road, westminster, correspondence handled by his father the rev j owen of fulham. located at spanish reed place near the kap river. owen — “this querulous man”, per special commissioner hayward — refused to draw rations for his people; his brother w.s. owen replaced him; owen left early in 1821 and the party dispersed. the settler was eighteen, with no leader, no rations and no location, and the next record of him is the graaff-reinet mission about three years later.

¦is there an original roll to go back to? three cape archives references, and no ship’s returnfound co 6137/1,4 (the list under owen’s direction), co 8543 (hayward’s notes) and co 3917 (the memorial of independent settlers aboard the nautilus). a memorial is a petition and a petition is signed — that one could carry his signature at seventeen. nash records that no agent of transports’ return has ever been traced for the nautilus, so these three are the whole basis of the roll.

¦can the story from the mirror be found? no — searched and not foundnothing two of the father’s four pages go on it and he asks his son to say whether it is true. searched google books and the open web on the story’s own terms — “ourang outang” and “orang outang” with carried off, wife, colonist, caffre, mirror, 1829 and 1830 — and google books returned no matches at all. recorded so nobody repeats these terms. next: the runs of the mirror on project gutenberg and the internet archive, searched volume by volume rather than by phrase, and the names williams or williamson with capt johnson.

¦two familysearch search behaviours worth writing down a parent filter that ranks rather than filters, and one that silently vanishespartly first: q.mothergivenname + q.mothersurname does not restrict the result set — it returns 3,499 rows and puts the eleven real ones on top. past the first page the matches stop and unrelated transvaal probates begin. reading a count as a result set would be wrong in both directions. second: adding q.givenname to that same query drops the mother parameters altogether — 263 rows of every frederik fortunatus kolbe in south africa, mother ignored. and q.fathersurname=kolbe with the same mother terms returns 0. same shape as the findmypast finding in september: filters here annihilate each other silently, and a zero is a statement about the query before it is a statement about the family.

¦does a signed-out familysearch session return an honest zero? no. it returns “no results found” and a count of 0blocked this archive has warned about this since 21 september on a peer's report, and today it happened here, controlled, by accident. the identical search url — kolbe, mother anna jacoba van der merwe, south africa — returned 3,499 results in the morning and 0 forty minutes later, on the same machine, in the same minute of the same afternoon. the only thing that changed was the browser context: the pane restarted with an empty cookie jar. the page does carry a banner — create a free account or sign in to see all available results — so it is not a pure fabrication; but the result count says 0 and the body says no results found, and a reader skimming for a number gets a false negative. the documented remedy was tried first and did not work. the estate's rule is before asking a person to fix something, open a second tab; a fresh tab in the same pane is signed out too, because the loss is the pane's and not the tab's.

¦what this costs, and what it does not nothing already found is in doubtpartly every familysearch result recorded today was taken from the signed-in session and is unaffected. what is blocked is the rest: the arks for five of the commandant's children were not captured before the session dropped, so those five are still not entered as people, and the three estate files found this afternoon cannot be opened. no zero recorded today came from the signed-out session — the only zeros here are the cape baptism searches for johan casimir and peter benjamin, both run while signed in and both controlled against fifteen and five positive results in the same collection.

¦which endpoint answered, and when recorded because a date is not enough when one service has two doorsfound all of the above ran on the new database, nationalarchives.gov.za/search-the-collections?search_api_views_fulltext_op=and&search_api_views_fulltext=<term>&items_per_page=60, on the afternoon of 27 september 2026. the old database, national.archsrch.gov.za/sm300cv/smws/sm300dl, answered 503 in the same session, and naairs.htm is now 404. why the endpoint and not only the day: a dated nil is not atomic. on a day when a service moves, two searches an hour apart can hit two different corpora and a day-level record cannot tell them apart — the luwinski session found exactly that inside its own 16 september, which contains an outage, the discovery of a new address, and searches on it. across six archives in this estate, 1,369 of 1,381 negatives name what was searched, 1,316 carry a date, and exactly one carries a time. naming the database is enough right up until one database has two endpoints serving different corpora.

¦does the well-known barry family of swellendam connect to this one? no — and the instrument that says so is the largest this archive has ever appliedfound this was a named lead, untested, and it is now answered. a researcher, wendy, wrote to david on 11 june 2008 with a complete descendant report of the english barrys — 1,604 numbered principals over eleven generations, 1659 to 1999, the product of twelve years' work in archives, libraries and letters to “most of the barry names in all the south african telephone books”. it is the family of joseph barry (1796–1865) of hitchin, hertfordshire, who built the swellendam trading house. it contains not one name this archive holds. kolbe 0, mountjoy 0, booyzen 0, booysen 0, downing 0, daschner 0, fortunatus 0, burgersdorp 0, barkly 0, indwe 0, grahamstown 0. the control is the point: the tree is not simply an english one that never reached the cape — it says south africa 200 times, cape 236 and swellendam 129. it is in the right country and the right century and this family is not in it.

¦then which barrys are these? she names a third group, and says she had not traced itpartly her first paragraph sorts the south african barrys into three: the irish, who came “out to south africa in the early 1800” and are her own; the english, whom she traced because the two intermarry so often “that the trees overlap”; and — in her words — “the other barry family that came to south africa in the late 1700 from london”, which she was only then “going to have a bash at”. this archive's barrys are almost certainly the third group, and the fit is close: its earliest is a john barry who died at de bruins poort in 1853 with no birth, no arrival and no burial found, and his son john augustus barry i, born 1819 “at sea”. not adopted — three groups is a working researcher's sorting, not a census, and a family can always be a fourth thing. but it is the first time anybody has told this archive where not to look, and that is worth as much as a name.

¦she had two finished trees. which one did she send? the english one only — and the irish one is the one this family's lore points atpartly checked rather than assumed, and it changes the ask. the attachment is a single report, “descendants of thomas barry” of stockton, coventry — ireland appears 0 times in 399,920 characters, cork, dublin, limerick and waterford 0 each, and “irish” twice, both in her covering note. so the irish tree, which she descends from and had also completed, is not in this email. and it is the interesting one. this archive's barry page carries the family's own words about john barry: “as an irishman, john barry was reputed to be anti english…” the one tree that would test the family's own story about its barrys is the one she did not attach, and she finished it before 2008. that is now a specific thing to ask a specific person for, rather than a wall.

¦what the letter is, and what it is not a compiled tree from a named researcher — a lead list, not a witnesspartly the same rule this archive applies to geni and to the 2012 barry report applies here. wendy's report is a compilation: it cites no document per person, and its dates come from “archives internet and libraries” and from hundreds of conversations. its value is as a negative and as a direction, and neither of those needs it to be a witness. where it would become one is person by person, against registers — and nothing in it needs to be, because nobody in it is claimed as kin.

¦basutoland records, page 436 — read as an image a sworn witness puts the settler at bethulie in june 1831found deposition of frans johannes cornelis cronje, smithfield, 14 september 1858, before j. j. sauer, landdrost of the caledon river district. hunting up from colesberg in june 1831 with the three venters, his brother stephanus and hendrik weber, commandant of the district: “we then met with the missionaries kolbe and klerk with some bushmen at bethulie.” “klerk” is almost certainly james clark, the man sibree pairs him with at the bushman station, written down by a dutch deponent as he heard it — and that pairing is what identifies the kolbe. the earliest independent sighting of the settler this archive has.

¦and it does not fit the chronology said plainly rather than smoothedpartly sibree has him at philippolis from 13 march 1831; schoeman's chronology says march 1831 as well. a june 1831 sighting at bethulie puts him back at his old station three months after leaving it, or puts a year's slip into a deposition sworn twenty-seven years after the fact. nothing here decides which, and the archive does not get to pick the one that reads better. the deposition also has a purpose: these were taken to argue the land had been empty, so «no other native tribes besides a few bushmen» is interested testimony and is read as such.

¦reading the page instead of the transcript two words changedfound the ocr gives “barend teater” and “bethulle”; the type says barend venter and bethulie. neither alters the finding and both would have gone into this archive as fact. the leaf was found the way the last one was — the scan's _djvu.xml, one page object per leaf — which is now simply how this archive reads a free book.

¦theal, the republics and native territories 1854–1872 no kolbe at all, and the controls are loudnothing the standard history of exactly this commandant's state and exactly his years: 516 mentions of moshesh, 105 of bloemfontein, 255 of «commandant» — and not one kolbe. nor in theal's fragment of basuto history. a commandant of bloemfontein who died in office in 1868 is not in the authoritative history of the republic he served, which is worth knowing both as a fact about the books and as a measure of how far this family sat from the people who wrote them.

¦holden, history of the colony of natal (1855) the other kolbe, confirmed from a third directionfound a blue book report on damaraland signed “f. n. kolbe, in the service of the rhenish missionary society” — the initial is an ocr slip for f. w. this is the man the whole day was spent separating from this family, and here he is in 1855 doing exactly what dictionary of south african biography i, 433 says he came to do in 1844: rhenish mission, damaraland. three independent sources now agree about him, and none of them puts him anywhere near the settler.

¦booyzen, barry, mountjoy, daschner · across all five nothing, except two more barrys who are not thesenothing theal names advocate j. d. barry, recorder of the high court in griqualand west. that is the third cape legal barry this archive has met today and, like sir jacob and james michael, he is written down only so nobody joins him on. no booyzen, no mountjoy, no daschner in any of the five.
the society's own magazine printed him, and it is free
rows 121 and 138 — eleven months of his journal, and the date that was in dispute · searched 11 oct 2026 · where it is used →

¦archive.org · the evangelical magazine and missionary chronicle, by volume 1828 to 1837, unrestricted, all ten takenfound the serial this archive wanted was never the only one. row 121 went after the quarterly chronicle of transactions and established it is not on the internet archive. the lms's monthly is, under evangelicalmagaz…, one volume a year, freely downloadable, and it covers every year he was in the field. thirty megabytes of it read in one pass. the run is not complete — 1838 onward thins — but 1828 through 1837 is there.

¦evangelical magazine and missionary chronicle, 1833, pp. 410–412 “extracts from the journal of mr. george augustus kolbe”found 8 october 1831 to 3 september 1832, at philippolis, day by day. attendances, admissions, the school roll climbing from ninety to 335, a chief writing to a veld-cornet about colonists beating his people, twenty-six people vaccinated on 18 january 1832, a thanksgiving for deliverance from small-pox, the church discipline set out in his own hand, the new church opened on 1 april 1832 — built by the district, stone walls twelve feet high, five hundred seats and a hundred left in the street. row 138 says the sum of his own words here is one sentence at second hand. it is now eleven months.

¦the same journal, 21 july 1832 the obituary corroborated sixteen years earlyfound “the veld-cornet joubert … and two other farmers, arrived here this afternoon, for the purpose of obtaining medical advice, and also to attend the religious services of the station.” the grahamstown journal said in 1844 that he had been “for many years engaged in rendering them medical advice and assistance whenever called upon”, and this archive had only the obituary's word for it. here is the thing itself, in his own journal, with the farmers named by office and riding in for it.

¦evangelical magazine and missionary chronicle, 1831 — his letter of 30 april 1831 he dates his own arrival, and it closes the conflictfound “as i resided for nearly three years among the bushmen previous to my removal to this station …” and then, plainly: “when i arrived, in april, 1828, with my colleague, in the bushman country.” this archive has carried sibree's 8 february 1829 against the dsab's 8 february 1828 since september. both can now stand: 1828 is when he went, 1829 is when the society formally took him on. sibree was never dating an arrival. nearly three years from april 1828 also lands exactly on sibree's own «arriving at philippolis, march 13, 1831» — the two halves of that entry were always consistent and nobody had the middle.

¦evangelical magazine and missionary chronicle, 1830 — james clark's letter of 31 december 1828 the colleague says it from the other sidefound “brother kolbe and myself removed to this station, and arrived here in the beginning of may last” — written at the bushman station, near caledon river, in december 1828, so «may last» is may 1828. the letter also gives the station's origin: landdrost stockenstrom of graaff-reinet and the lieutenant-governor asked clark to begin it, farmers in the district subscribed cattle, and the bushmen had been driven off their fountains by boers crossing the boundary. two men, writing three years apart and neither for posterity, put him there in april or may 1828. and the station is the boesmanskool that became bethulie.

¦the 1828 and 1829 volumes · the caledon journey of november 1828 not there, and that is row 121's answer narrowednothing neither volume names him once. the dsab says the melvill and kolbe journal was printed “in the transactions of the missionary society for 1829”, and this establishes that it was not in the society's monthly — so the citation means the quarterly chronicle of transactions, the separate serial row 121 has already shown is not on the internet archive. the journey is still unfound and the place to look is now one place smaller.

¦the same letter, on the people he worked among recorded whole, not in the half that reads wellpartly he writes that the bushmen's raids “proceeded from a recollection of former injuries, excited by the intrusion of the colonists into their country”, and that “truly, the oppression of the bushmen has been great; they have been looked upon, by many, little above the level of the brute creation; and having been subjected to a temporary slavery, they have smarted under the lash of the oppressor.” he also calls them, on arrival, “a wild and uncivilized race — a band of robbers, and haters of men”, says not one had been brought to the faith, and that “temporal advantages are all they desire.” both halves are set down. quoting only the sentence that sounds right now would be choosing his words for him, which is the one thing an archive holding a man's own journal must not do.

¦the letters received tables, 1831 to 1836 a spine of dates nobody has to guess atfound the magazine lists every letter the society received, by missionary and station. g. a. kolbe, philippolis: 30 april 1831 · 4 october 1831 · september 1832 · 10 october 1833 · 20 october 1835. that is a documentary timeline of his correspondence with london, and each date is a letter that exists somewhere in the cwm archive at soas — which is row 135's enquiry, now able to ask for things by date.
a kolbe in westminster paying for the mission at philippolis
one sighting, one year, and what would settle it · searched 11 oct 2026 · where it is used →

¦evangelical magazine and missionary chronicle, 1836 · the subscription lists “miss a. kolbe”, orange street chapel auxiliarypartly in the juvenile branch of the orange street chapel auxiliary, with a bare “miss kolbe” in a collector's list on the same page. orange street chapel is off leicester square in westminster — this family's parish — and a few minutes from conduit street, where amelia ann kolbe was living at the 1841 census. the society is the one her brother served, and 1836 is a year he was at philippolis. a surname, an initial, a parish and a society is the whole of it. no address, no age, no relationship is printed, and this archive has already spent today keeping four kolbes of one name apart. recorded as a lead against her record and nothing is altered.

¦the other nine volumes, for the same thing one year onlynothing the subscription lists of 1828–1835 and 1837 carry no kolbe at all. a single sighting in a single year is weaker than a run would be, and is written down as a single sighting. it also means the lists were read and not merely the one that answered.

¦what would settle it the auxiliary's own papers, at the address already being written topartly the magazine prints a total, not an address. the orange street chapel records, or the lms auxiliary returns in the council for world mission archive, would carry the subscriber's own hand — and cwm at soas is exactly where row 135's letter is going. this costs nothing to add to an enquiry already written.
findmypast has no south african records except a war
row 78 — the subscription's last days, and the plan for them was impossible · searched 12 oct 2026 · where it is used →

¦findmypast.co.uk · the record-set catalogue, searched by place name twelve sets for south africa and every one is militaryfound the boundary, and it retires an errand rather than answering it. row 78 named the two things worth the remaining days: 1819–20 passenger lists, and the 1903 certificates. the certificates were answered in september. the passenger lists cannot be answered on this tool at all, and now there is a tested reason rather than a failed search. searching the catalogue of all 2,977 record sets by place: “south africa” returns 12, every one of them anglo-boer war — nominal rolls, rolls of honour, soldiers' wills, war memorials, and the australian, new zealand and glasgow contingents. “natal” returns nothing at all. “cape” returns two, and both are cape breton in nova scotia. “transvaal” returns the same nine boer war sets again. there is no south african civil registration here, no parish register, no passenger or arrival list, and nothing whatever before 1899. the four searches are a control on each other: the mechanism plainly works, because it returns twelve relevant sets for one name and zero for another.

¦findmypast.co.uk · travel & migration, barry, keyword «cape of good hope» 178 hits, and the cape ones are a naval yard in the 1790sfound the one item row 78 had left. 178 results, and the genuinely cape-located ones are edward barry in the british royal navy ships' musters at the naval yard at the cape of good hope, 1797–1800 — a british set that happens to record cape postings, not a cape set. the rest drift to tasmania and great britain on a loose keyword. bounded to 1819 ±2, travel & migration returns 16 barrys and every one is australian — new south wales settlers and convicts. nothing at the cape in the year john augustus barry i was born «at sea».

¦wo 127 · south africa, local armed forces nominal rolls, 1899–1902 — 53,416 records a source this archive had never opened, and the register proves itfound the one south african thing findmypast does hold, and it is a good one. a transcription of tna wo 127 by kevin asplin: name, rank, regimental number, unit, and often dates of enrolment and discharge. this archive's register holds zero rows from any boer war source, so despite row 86 re-running the four surnames in september, this set had never reached it. searched all four surnames with variants on 12 october.

¦wo 127 · kolbe, with variants nil, and the control is in the resultnothing three hits and not one is a kolbe — j m kilby, thomas kilby, a f kyser. the variant matcher plainly fired, which is what makes this a negative worth recording rather than an empty page: no kolbe served in any unit on this roll.

¦wo 127 · mountjoy, with variants george mountjoy, private 664, district mounted riflesfound one exact mountjoy in 53,416 records, and the surname is rare enough for that to mean something. pte. 664, district mounted rifles — a locally raised cape colony unit, organised by district, and this family's mountjoys were at cradock, dordrecht and barkly east, which is that recruiting ground. it cannot yet be given to a man. the transcript carries no age and no district, and this archive holds three georges who could be of age in 1900: george mountjoy of barkly east, who has no dates at all; george herkules johannes mountjoy, born 16 january 1862; and george mountjoy of kokstad, born about 1862. the 1889 george was a boy of eleven and the 1823 george was seventy-seven. three candidates, no discriminator, nothing claimed.

¦wo 127 · booyzen / booysen, with variants nicholas george peter booysen, trooper, nesbitt's horsefound eight hits, four of them real and probably one man: booysen, n. booysen, nicholas booysen and nicholas george peter booysen — trooper, nesbitt's horse, 26 january to 18 september 1900, remarked “discharged, services no longer required”. nesbitt's horse was raised in the eastern cape. no man of this name is in this archive — its nicholas-bearing booysens are a hendrik stephanus nicolaas of 1882, a hendrik stefanus nicolaas of 1862 and a jacobus nicholas before 1842. not claimed.

¦wo 127 · barry 34 hits and the index cannot choose among themnothing too common a surname for an index with no age and no district. 34 results, including a j h barry who could be james henry and a george barry who could be several people. nothing attributable, and that is the finding: this set identifies a rare surname and defeats a common one.

¦the side of the war these rolls describe the same districts, the other sidefound worth setting down before anybody is adopted off these rolls. wo 127 lists men who served the british in locally raised colonial units. the men this archive already holds from that war went the other way: fred j. barry, plaasboer of ivanhoe, tried as a cape rebel in june 1901, and the two kolbes taken prisoner and shipped to cape town on wo 108/368. so this source describes neighbours, and possibly relatives, who chose the opposite side in the same districts in the same months. that is a reason to be slower about identification, not faster.
what the zeros are worth

a zero with a stated scope is evidence. there is no estate file for hercules johannes mountjoy in the cape archives, and because the estates on either side of him run unbroken from 1938 to 1948, that absence means something: an estate too small to report.

a zero without a scope is not. the camp database returns nothing for this family — but it is built largely from camp death lists, so it records who died far better than who was interned and walked out. that claim is unsupported, not disproved, and the page says so.

and a zero from the wrong index is worth less than nothing, because it can mislead for years. the farm list result above is void: the register is an orange free state land roll and was never going to hold a cape farm. it took a control search to notice.
the searches that found something are on the other pages. these are the ones that make those worth believing.
