the people register follows twelve lines, and one of them is called testimony taken back
did a mistake in the archive's own working — a bug, a bad build, or a word used loosely.

found it is a confidence label sitting in the line field. one person — a living booyzen, held on testimony — carried l: "testimony", and testimony is this archive's own word for s: "lore", three fields away in the same record. so the reader was offered “testimony (1)” in the line filter on /people/, between daschner (15) and lerena (1), as though this archive followed a family of that name. nobody was misdescribed and nothing was claimed about her — the line field only groups — but the register's own list of the families it follows was wrong, and that list is read as a statement. it was found sideways, while counting the l values to answer a different question entirely: what the record atlas should be told this archive's families are. a field whose values are never counted can hold anything. the line is now booyzen, which is her surname and was always the answer. →
the frederik fortunatus hofmeyr kolbe in the dsab's printed index is probably a misreading taken back
did a document read wrongly, or a conclusion drawn past what the document says.

found it is a biographical entry, and it names his parents. row 173 met the name in a user tree, found the same string in the dictionary of south african biography's index, and wrote that it was probably a misreading — reasonable caution about an index line nobody had opened. the entry is at volume v, page 419: born and died at wakkerstroom, 27 september 1919 and 18 june 1969, an agricultural extension officer, the son of frederick fortunatus kolbe and his wife anna margaretha catharina moolman. the dates match the tree to the day and the dictionary adds the two names the tree did not have. the caution was right and the guess inside it was wrong, and the difference is that the index was treated as a thing to explain away rather than a thing to open. still nothing is joined: a published entry about a man at this archive's kolbe place is a lead, not a descent. →
a gate added yesterday was grading a build from a fortnight ago method

found two faults, one of them in the new gate. check:pin had been refusing the build since the kit was repinned on 9 october. ci was green on that very commit — which settles it: ci installs from the pin, so the pin was fine and the thirteen-day-old local node_modules was not. npm ci fixed it and left the lockfile byte-identical. then the install revealed the second fault. the new check:nav was wired --dist dist, hardcoded, where every other --dist script honours archive_out. this archive’s build.sh exists so that sessions can build into private directories without clobbering each other — so the gate was reading site/dist: 807 pages from 27 september, 352 people, and neither of the two added yesterday — and reporting “conforms” on a 843-page build it had never opened. the kit tool names the variable in its own error message: “build first, or point archive_out at the build you made.” the wiring ignored it. one line, fixed in this archive’s own package.json and proved in both directions.
“25 records and genuinely filtered — every one has a kolbe parent” taken back

found fifteen of the twenty-five. the other ten are kolobe, kolkobet, colbert and culbert — sesotho and other surnames reached by familysearch's fuzzy name matching, which is the index working as designed. the filter is real and the name is fuzzy, and those are different claims. q.fathersurname does restrict to records having a parent of that surname; it does not restrict to the spelling you typed. how it happened, which is the part worth keeping: the result rows were scraped with a /kolbe/i test that returned fifteen, and the page's own total of twenty-five was then reported as though all twenty-five had been looked at. counting the hits and quoting the corpus are two different measurements and only one of them was made. caught within the hour by going back to read all twenty-five rather than the matching ones — which is also what turned up an eleventh child for the commandant. →
three pages carried the john barry conflation as unresolved for three weeks after it was resolved taken back

found the work was done on 14 september and only the person's own entry was told. the yorkshire john barry was separated from the cape one and followed past the date the cape one died — the 1851 census has him a ship owner at ruswarp, whitby, the only man of that age and name in the county, with whitby deaths registered in 1858 and 1860; and the bilsdale burial he was supposed to have is absent from 5,934 indexed bilsdale burials. work list row 83 was closed the same week. meanwhile three places went on saying the opposite. /tree/ carried a panel ending “until they are separated nothing above it can be trusted”; /disputed/ graded the dispute fatal with the instruction “separate them”, on a page that has a resolved status and uses it elsewhere; and the ancestor chart labelled him “john barry, 1796–1853”, which is the conflated pair — 1796 is the whitby man's birth year and the cape man has none. the text lived in three places and the truth in a fourth: a hardcoded panel in tree.astro, a wall node in pedigree.json, a row in disputed.astro, and the finding itself in people.js. correcting one corrects nothing. all four now agree, and the person's birth field says plainly that 1796 belonged to the other man. this one reached readers, unlike the latent contradiction corrected earlier today: /tree/ and /disputed/ are both linked from the main menu. →
mhg 1095/48 reported as still needing to be ordered from pretoria taken back

found it was read a month ago and its images are on this site. the death notice of george downing mountjoy booyzen is transcribed at /documents/ with three images, and it is the document that corrected his death date to 11 december 1947 — 21 february 1948 being the day the notice was signed. the mistake was method, not reading. today's sweep tested every item on the held pretoria order against familysearch, found this man indexed only as the spouse on his wife's 1944 file, and concluded from that alone that his own estate “stays on the order”. searching one outside index is not the same question as asking what this archive already holds, and only the second question was skipped. this is the third instance today and the second after the rule was written. a correction filed this morning named the same habit; row 212 was then given a rule saying each item is to be checked against this archive before it is opened; the rule was applied to the six mountjoy estates and not to the pretoria order an hour later. the source register was also carrying it both ways and would have caught me: the estates table chipped the file blocked while the read table vouched for the same document with its image published. both corrected. a gate was considered and refused — only two references in the whole register are vouched by the read section, so a check would be measuring a population of two. →
“not one of the ten is joined to this house yet”, written of the mountjoy estates on 27 september taken back

found two of the ten were already drawn as children of that house, and had been for seventeen days. estate kab mooc 6/9/5047: 58379 was read and published on 10 september, and its distribution account names the heirs of james jonathan mountjoy of barkly east. annie louisa nepgen, born mountjoy and louisa elizabeth diesel, born mountjoy are two of them, and both appear on this site’s own /households/ page as his daughters. the naairs sweep of 27 september then listed the same two women among ten estates it called unattached. the sentence was not stale, it was wrong when it was written — the search result was written up without being checked against this archive. that is the third instance of one habit. work list row 212 did it again on 8 october, listing an estate image to open that question 12 already records as read; and a letter of 20 september asked a paid researcher for a death notice “for the parents” of a woman whose parents were already held here. the failure is never the searching. it is writing down what a result list says without asking what this archive already holds. →
james montjoy's death notice cited as image 338 of film 007844936 taken back

found it is at image 339, and 338 is another family's death notice. both frames were opened on 9 october: image 338 is the death notice of christoffel hendrik olivier, trader, aged 56 years 4 months and 10 days, who died at his own house in the town of graaff-reinet on 15 june 1840 — his parents, not he, are the cornelis hermanus olivier and agnieta elizabeth van wyk on line 3, and this draft said otherwise for ten minutes before line 1 was read. image 340 is willem jacobus van der merwe of bouwbosch fontein. no connection to this archive's oliviers is claimed or looked for; the name is here only to prove the frame is not montjoy's. the james montjoy notice, stamped 4393, is at 339, which is where the familysearch record ark 1:1:qp4z-wk68 lands. the reading of the document was never in doubt — every fact this archive published off it is confirmed: saddler, born in “europe”, parents not known, a house and erf at cradock worth £90, died in the village of cradock in september 1827, and four children named james, george, johanna and jacoba, all minors. what was wrong was the way back to the page. a citation off by one sends the next reader to a stranger's family, and this one was published in three places — /sources/, question 12, and /documents/, which also sets out the arithmetic that produced it. that arithmetic is the lesson and it is being kept: the reference numbers do not ascend by exactly one per image, because an estate running to two or three frames breaks the step, so interpolating from image 330 at reference 4386 predicts 4393 at image 337 and the narrowing stopped one frame short. an interpolated citation is a prediction and has to be re-read off the frame it landed on. →
william frederick thomas barry was born on 29 september 1861 taken back

found that is his baptism date, and the register records no birth date for him at all. entry 79 of the graaff-reinet baptism register is headed “gedoopt 29 sept. 1861” — baptised. the entries on either side carry a birth date and his does not: 78 is geb. 24 april 1861, 80 is geb. 16 aug. 1861, and 79 is a name with no geb. this archive took the one date on the entry and filed it as a birth, which is the commonest error there is in a baptism register and the easiest to make when an index labels its single date event date. what is actually known is that he was baptised on 29 september 1861 and born at some point before it. and a second thing goes with it: this archive reasoned from “born 29 september 1861 at graaff-reinet” that the household had returned to graaff-reinet between burgersdorp and dordrecht. the godparents are the mother's sister and her husband. a child is christened where its godparents are; a baptism place is where the font was, not where the family slept. →
the commandant's eldest, found by asking for a father instead of a name found

found catharina wilhelmina kolbe was an inference built from a year, a town and a surname. she is now documented, and she is the eldest of the twelve. her 1909 civil death registration gives father jan gersem eliezer kolbe, stock farmer, mother anna jacoba, and — in the field that asks a twice-married woman to name the other husband — pienaar, which ties her to the bloemfontein bride of 8 october 1860. born 1844 in the cape colony, a year after her parents married; dead at veelroem, district ladybrand, of heart disease and dropsy. her son registered it and signed jan g. e. anderson, his grandfather’s three names entire, four lines below where that grandfather is named. the commandant gains a trade — stock farmer, from a document rather than an obituary. and the method is the part worth keeping. she is indexed under anderson, a surname this archive never held, so no search for her could have found her. searching the index for her father did. q.fathersurname=kolbe returns 25 filtered records in that collection — but only as the sole name term; paired with a surname it merely re-ranks, and a count that moves proves the field was read, not that it filtered.
a knot untied in september, still tied on three pages in october taken back

found the john barry conflation was resolved on 14 september — the yorkshire ship owner separated out and followed past the date the cape man died — and only his own entry was told. /tree/ went on ending its panel “until they are separated nothing above it can be trusted”; /disputed/ went on grading it fatal — separate them, on a page that has a resolved status and uses it for four other disputes; and the ancestor chart went on labelling him 1796–1853, which is the conflated pair, 1796 being the whitby man's year. the sentence lived in three places and the finding in a fourth — a hardcoded panel, a wall node in pedigree.json, a row in disputed.astro, and the person in people.js. all four now agree, and the wall is stated as what it actually is: not a contradiction but an absence — no birth, no arrival, no burial, and a son registered in 1903 as an irishman born in ireland.
a collection that ends in 1961, and two references from 1969 method

found the held pretoria order tested item by item against the film. one comes off it: mhg 40293 is filmed, free and read, and its reference needed no completing — so the favour row 193 was holding open can be closed without asking anybody for anything. the other four stay, and two of them could have been ruled out in a sentence: collection 2520237 ends in 1961, so the two /69 references are outside it by eight years. row 202 had guessed “likely free too” from a neighbouring success in 1918. a collection's date range is the first thing to read, not the last. and the search method itself was nearly wrong. familysearch does not fold booyzen and booysen — 249 records against 2,417, two different populations — and the first pass of this sweep searched one spelling only. two negatives were written before that was checked. separately, three source entries contradicted their own rows — 2428/40, 2945/44 and 1928/42 each carried a blanket “located; most are unread and on hold against cost” while their own rows said read and linked to a transcription. three of the four read rows in that table. corrected to say the file is filmed and the image published here. and the damage was latent, which is worth saying rather than overstating. that held line is rendered by sourceblock on pages that cite an id, not by /sources/ itself; it reaches a reader on 10 pages for other entries, and on none for these three, because no page cites them yet. nobody was told the wrong thing. the next page to cite one would have been.
the ten mountjoy estates were two families, and the question that would join them is blank on every form found

found the last six opened, and row 201 closes. two of the ten were always this archive’s own — barkly east daughters it had published a month ago. at least three belong to a different mountjoy house in the transkei, whose head is now documented: george mountjoy of kokstad, born in the orange free state about 1862, dead at tongaat in 1943 at eighty-one, married to mary fischer in the king williamstown district, nine children named on his death notice. his daughter minnie is the wilhelmina louisa burger of the list; his son alfred married the aletta johanna hattingh of it. elizabeth maria demmer fits neither house — born at dordrecht about january 1862, which makes her fifteen months older than the barkly east mother and so no daughter of hers. and the one line that could join or separate these families is refused every time it is asked. “names unknown.” “do not know, both deceased.” “not known.” a hundred and two years apart, three informants in this surname were asked who the dead person’s parents were, and none of them could say. ten estates have become three orders.
a daughter who died too early to be counted, and a list that was never held up against the archive found

found four of the ten mountjoy estates opened. the find is wilhelmina ernestina brummer, born mountjoy, dead at twenty at barkly east in june 1898, whose death notice names father john james mountjoy and mother maria louisa bertha — three forenames that match this archive’s maria louisa bertha kumm exactly, a birth in the town that couple married in, a death in theirs. she is entered as a person and refused as their daughter, because the 1938 distribution of her supposed father’s estate pays two grandchildren their dead mother’s share and pays no brummer anything. a daughter who died forty years before her father is invisible to his estate; that is why her own notice is worth having, and also why it cannot be checked against it. the other finding is about this archive, not the mountjoys. on 27 september it wrote that not one of the ten was joined to this house — seventeen days after it had itself published two of them as daughters of exactly that house. the search was fine; the write-up was never held against what was already held. third instance of one habit, and now on /corrections/.
the biggest single gap, and the parents were never in the index found

found tab mhg 40293 is read from the film. the death notice of frederik fortunatus downing kolbe, dead at twenty-seven in the influenza of 1918, names vader george augustus kolbe and moeder martha sofia kolbe, geboren klopper — a parentage this archive had only from a brother’s death registration and a sister’s estate file. the index attached to the same record says there are no other people in the group. the parents are on the image and were never indexed. and the mother’s name is what decides it: two men called george augustus kolbe lie in one cemetery at wakkerstroom, born two years apart, and only one of them married a klopper. it also takes a file off a paid order — the reference needed no completing, and the index’s “villieria, pretoria” is a farm portion in the district of wakkerstroom, where this archive already had him.
the estates were never behind a counter — both probate series are filmed and free found

found row 201 wanted ten cape mountjoy estates ordered as one enquiry. they do not need ordering: the cape probate series is name-indexed and imaged on familysearch — 116 mountjoy records, including one of the ten with her birthplace and exact death date, and james mountjoy the saddler, question 12's man. so is the transvaal series, and its volumes are titled probate estate case files, not an index — the image opened is a sterfkennis. tab mhg 40293, the file this archive calls its biggest single gap and that david is holding off on cost, has an ark and a picture, and the index puts the death at villieria, pretoria rather than wakkerstroom. no image is read yet and nothing is adopted from an index.
the publishing debt closed, and a gate that had been telling the truth for three weeks method

found rows 183, 184, 185 and 189 are done. sources: 0 of 42 → 46 of 46 accounted for, unlocked by this morning's refactor — the kit reads held only on a dict row, and these rows were lists, so the archive could not have declared a holding however it tried. hosts: the row said three undeclared, it was six, and three of them i added myself this fortnight while leaving the sources page alone — the row's thesis demonstrated on its author. pages: 0 bespoke, and one of the two exemptions was justified by a blocker removed this morning, so it is rewritten with a reason that is true. lines: measured, and two of the row's claims are out of date — luwinski uses branchrivers now, and this archive has no families page at all.
seventeen pages declare their sources, and twenty-five record why they do not method

found row 186 finished. the instinct was a sourceblock on all 42 pages and that would have been worse than the gap — /errands/ lists what this archive has not got, /searched/ rows are already citations, /sources/ cannot rest on itself. 17 declare, 88 items, every id resolving; 25 are exempt with a reason each. automated assignment was tried and measured first: 34 of the 46 sources carry an archival reference and those references appear on almost no narrative page, because the pages argue from names and the register lists numbers. the gate enforces that every page has been thought about, not that every page declares.
sources given ids, and four pages now say what they rest on method

found 0 of 41 pages declared their sources, and the cause was that the sources had no names. sources.json was four tables of html cells; every row now carries an id derived from its own first cell, not its position, 46 of them with no collisions, and the rendered page is byte-identical to before. /kolbe/, /barry/, /women/ and /direct-line/ now carry 29 declared ids, all resolving. and a gate now reads data-missing — the attribute sourceblock leaves when it silently drops an id it cannot resolve, which nothing had ever looked at.
the 1861 font read: a sister at the font, not a family on the move found

found entry 79 of the graaff-reinet baptism register, read at the page. the place was never an index artefact — the volume is the parish book. the godparents are catharine maria sophia kolbe, the mother's own sister, standing with a joubert, which is what a married couple does at a font. so the baptism 250 kilometres from burgersdorp needs no migration to explain it, and this archive's four-stage barry journey was over-read from a place field. a third godparent is ralph peter thomas and the child is william frederick thomas. and the date on the entry is gedoopt — a baptism, not the birth this archive filed it as.
the colesberg marriage was always there, indexed under berry found

found entry 735, 23 february 1846 — the date this archive adopted eleven days ago from a book and marked inferred. it is documented now. the clerk wrote john berry and the man signed john barry, three lines apart, which is why no search for barry in twenty-seven years found it; the search that worked used his wife's surname and not his. new from the page: their residence at stormberg spruit, the minister thomas reid, and a consent column reading “de weduwe kolbe, moeder” with nothing on the groom's side where the entries on either side each name two fathers.
ireland searched for john augustus barry, and the instrument's edge found before the answer found

found seven days of subscription left and the planned campaign already done, so it went on the question his 1903 death registration opened: born about june 1819, irishman born in ireland, mother born neagle. no john barry of a nagle mother is baptised anywhere in ireland in that window — 47 records, johns at 1811, 1845, 1860, 1876, and the window demonstrably covered. the more useful finding is the boundary: of findmypast's irish sets only the catholic baptisms and civil births from 1864 index a mother's surname, so the search could only ever have found a catholic child. and 45 of the 47 are county cork.
pama's barry migration tested against fonts already held, and it fails twice found

found no service, no order, no letter — a book's claim checked against registers this archive had already read. pama said the children were born at burgersdorp up to nicolaas, then at dordrecht. the fonts say graaff-reinet 1847, 1848, 1850, burgersdorp from 1852, graaff-reinet again in 1861, dordrecht in 1864 — and the 1847 entry was read at the image, with three kolbes standing as witnesses. pama's pivot child has no font at all, so that half of the claim is tested only by itself. a reading that would make him right about the wrong generation is recorded: the sentence fits the sons' household, burgersdorp 1873–1883 then dordrecht, almost exactly.
john augustus barry i and margaretha kolbe married about 1850 at burghersdorp taken back
did a conclusion that does not follow — the documents read correctly and the inference drawn wrongly, or a control that tested the wrong thing.

found their eldest son was born in 1847, and this archive drew him under that marriage. the 1850 rested on one word — “probably” — written by their son r. p. barry on his father's death notice in 1915, sixty-five years after the event. the same son had written “unknown” on his mother's notice three months earlier, which this archive quoted elsewhere as a sign of how little he knew, and then used his guess as a date anyway. meanwhile people.js said “married 1846” the whole time. two of this archive's own files disagreed, and the marriage page published the wrong one. what it is now: 23 february 1846 at colesberg, marked inf because the exact date and place come from pama, reported in a letter of november 1999 that had been in david's files for twenty-seven years. the book is not what makes it safe — this archive does not let a book overrule a page. 1850 is refuted by arithmetic on the archive's own data, and 1846 was already here. how it was caught matters more than the date. not by a gate, not by an audit, but by a stranger's letter arriving at a page nobody had re-read. there is a gate now — child-before-wedding refuses a household whose marriage postdates a child drawn under it, and it fired on this row and on james henry barry, born 1848, before the fix. →
a 1999 letter corrects a marriage this site has been publishing wrong found

found three more barry letters out of david's files, one of them this family entirely. pama, via a correspondent in november 1999: john barry married margaretha wilhelmina elizabeth kolbe at colesberg on 23 february 1846. this site said 1850 — a son's “probably” on a 1915 death notice — while drawing that couple's eldest son, born 1847, underneath it. two of this archive's own files disagreed and neither noticed. there is a gate now, and it fired on two children before the fix. also gained: birth years for hendrik nicholaas (1857) and pieter richard (1866), and a burgersdorp-to-dordrecht move to test against fonts.
a 2008 letter in the inbox answers a lead this archive raised in september found

found david remembered a long email about the barrys. it is there: 11 june 2008, a complete descendant report of the english/swellendam barrys — 1,604 people, eleven generations, twelve years' work — and not one name this archive holds appears in it, though it names south africa 200 times and swellendam 129. the swellendam lead is answered and it is a no. its writer also sorts the south african barrys into three groups and names a third, “from london in the late 1700”, which she had not then traced and which this family probably belongs to. the letter sat unread here for eighteen years, which is a finding about method and not about the barrys. and she sent only one of her two trees. ireland appears nowhere in the 400,000 characters; the irish barrys — her own line, and the one this family's lore points at with “as an irishman, john barry…” — are untested, and she finished that tree too.
a civil marriage entry gives ages, occupations, fathers' names and witnesses — so the image would name the fathers taken back

found it does not, and this archive should never have said it would. the claim was written into the work list, into two people's records, into two marriage rows and into a timeline entry, and it was the whole reason for wanting the images. the free state civil marriage form of 1869–72 has no parents' columns. read at the page, its columns are: no., datum, volle naam en toenaam, ouderdom, staat, ambt of beroep, woning ten tijde des huwelijks, huwelijksgeboden of licentie, toestemming — then the parties' own signatures, the witnesses', and the minister's. consent is recorded by relationship and not by name: the 1872 entry says “moeder” and stops. where the error came from is the shape of other countries' civil marriage registers, which do carry fathers — an assumption about a record set, made without opening one, and then repeated confidently enough that it survived being written down five times. what it cost and what it did not. no conclusion rested on it, so nothing has to be unpicked; but it stood as the justification for a piece of work, and a reason to do something is a claim like any other. what the images gave instead is better than what was expected: a condition, an occupation, and a farm that puts three of these people in one household. →
williem johannes kolbe of panfontein was born on 9 july 1847 in the district of philippolis taken back

found the register says 2 august 1847, and fauresmith. the 9 july came from the afrikaans wikipedia article, which cites p. j. nienaber, afrikaanse biografiese woordeboek (1947), p. 139 — a page this archive has never seen, reached at two removes. the baptism entry (familysearch 1:1:q2hl-bycg, free state dutch reformed registers, entry 18) gives born 2 august 1847, baptised fauresmith 12 march 1848, of a father the register abbreviates to “john kolbe” and of anna jacoba van der merwe. a register written seven months after the birth beats a dictionary written a century later, and the archive now carries 2 august. what is not corrected is the pedigree — nienaber's parents are exactly the register's, which is the dictionary being vindicated on the thing that mattered and wrong on a date. the discrepancy is left visible rather than tidied: four weeks is too small to be a different man and too large to be a slip of the pen, and somebody may one day know why. a note on the attribution below this entry. the register's abbreviation of the commandant — john kolbe — is also, letter for letter, the whole held name of a different man in this archive: the settler's son john kolbe, who has nothing to do with it. the attribution tool matched him, correctly by its own rule and wrongly in fact, and he is refused in corrections-who-deny.json. a quotation is not a mention, and a tool that cannot tell the difference needs a human to say so once. →
two collaborative trees disagree about frederik fortunatus kolbe of bloemspruit's birth year, so neither settles anything taken back

found true, and the reasoning under it was wrong. this archive wrote on 20 september that the disagreement between geni's 1857 and the familysearch tree's 1859 showed the two were not independent witnesses. the opposite turns out to be the case: each tree is following a different document. 1859 is his gravestone; 1857 is the age of 73 on his civil death registration. the trees were the only honest parties in the room — they disagreed because their sources disagree. and geni's date is a splice: “22 october 1857” takes the day and month from the stone and the year from the death form, so it reproduces neither document while looking more precise than both. the rule that survives, sharpened: where trees differ, do not ask which tree is right — ask what each one is copying, because a compiled date can be a composite of two sources and match neither. and the first draft of this entry was filed against the wrong man. written with the bare name, it was attributed to frederik fortunatus kolbe (1839–1929), the settler's tenth child — a different man by twenty years, whose page would have carried a correction about somebody else's gravestone. the archive holds four men of this name and the tool prefers the longest, so the fix was to write the longer one. caught the same morning, by reading what the tool printed rather than that it exited 0. →
of three johan casimir kolbes in this archive's own register, not one is joined to this house taken back

found one of them was the settler's son, and the evidence was already published here. written on 21 september while resolving the casmier spelling, and correct in its reasoning: a shared surname is not a relationship, and the three men were index rows rather than witnesses. but the second row — johan casimir kolbe, married elizabeth geertruida pienaar — is him. his banns were called at colesberg on 1 may 1867, the town his father's death notice was signed in and his mother died in that year; their children include a george augustus and a margaret dewning. what went wrong is not the rule but the tense. not joined is a statement about what has been done; not joinable is a statement about the world. the sentence was written as the first and read ever afterwards as the second, and so the row was never worked. the fix is a habit, not a gate: when this archive refuses a lead for want of a link, it should say what would supply the link — here, the mother's name, which is exactly what found him six days later. →
a search set published twice, because a script saved one file and then crashed on the next taken back

found this archive published the same search set twice and nothing said so. a script appended the familysearch signed-out set to searched.json, saved it, and then died several lines later on a max() over a work-list column another session had typed as a string. the crash message was about the work list; the damage was in searched.json, already written. the corrected re-run appended the set again, and the page carried it twice through two commits. why it is a correction and not a typo: /searched/ is a record of what work was done, so a set printed twice says this archive searched the same ground twice on the same day. that is a claim about the work and it is false. the general fault, which will happen again: a script that writes several files is not atomic, so a failure in the last one leaves the earlier ones committed — and re-running it is not idempotent unless somebody made it so. caught by an assertion in the very next script, which expected two matches and found three; a gate now refuses two sets sharing a heading and a date. →

daschner and mountjoy swept at naairs for the first time, and there are now two databases found

commit e40087d says the regenerated dossiers changed order and nothing else — “345 are reordered and nothing else … zero have changed content” taken back

“findmypast is the wrong tool and that is worth writing down: it indexes württemberg almost entirely as a birthplace field in emigration records, not as german parish registers. kolbe + württemberg returns 0 there against a working control.” taken back

work list row 177, on the 2012 barry register report: “there is no casmier, casimir or kasimir anywhere in this archive.” taken back
did a search run over part of the ground and written up as though it covered all of it.

found he is in both of his parents' death notices. the settler's notice, signed m. kolbe — margaret, the widow — at colesberg in january 1845, names ten children and johan casimir kolbe is the fifth of them. margaret downing's own notice of 25 november 1867, signed by her son-in-law g. d. o. werdmuller, names him again — and that document is careful about the dead, entering mary elizabeth as “(dead), who was married to george f. enslin” and him plainly. so he was alive at about twenty-three. both transcriptions have been in notes/documents-transcribed.md since 10 september. he is also on the archive's own kolbe page, in the list of children, with the variant spelling “casiner” already recorded — and the same page's prose singles out casimir by name as one of the family's extraordinary forenames. what went wrong is the shape of the search. the archive's people list was searched and the archive was reported on. people.js is where a person's record lives; it is not where the archive's evidence lives, and this man had no record precisely because nobody had joined the notice to the list. a search of the index is not a search of the holdings, and the one place he was missing is the one place that was looked. the compiled report was right and this archive was wrong about its own documents — its “casmier” is a third spelling of a name in two primary sources. he now has a record. →
commit e212628: a build failure that afternoon “did not reproduce. green on the re-run — one failure is the weather.” taken back

found it was not the weather. it was a bug in build.sh that had been there all day, and the re-run passing is exactly what it looks like. the two build steps read cd site && npm run build >/dev/null && cd .., and set -e does not abort on a failing command inside an && list. proven with a three-line script: cd site && sh -c "exit 143" && cd .. falls through to the next line, leaves the working directory in site/, and the script exits 0. so when astro was reaped, the pass failed, cd .. never ran, the script carried on, and python failed to find site/tools/links.py — two steps downstream of the real event, with the trap faithfully reporting “not killed, exited 2 during: links.py”. the re-run passed because nothing killed it that time, not because there was nothing wrong. and the worse half: a killed build could have exited 0. the three-line proof does exactly that. if the reaped step had been followed by steps that happened to pass, build.sh would have printed “build complete” over a build that never finished. found only because the d'arcy session asked this archive to test its own stopper, which meant killing a live build on purpose — the first time a build here was killed deliberately rather than by the machine. the fix is a subshell, ( cd site && … ), which restores the directory by construction and propagates the failure, so set -e fires on the step that actually failed. verified by killing a build mid-flight: it now stops at “killed by signal 15 during: first pass”, with nothing surviving. the rule this breaks is my own, stated the same day: three identical failures is a fault and one is the weather. that is a decent heuristic for load and a bad one for a bug that only shows when something else goes wrong, because the trigger is intermittent and the fault is not. a failure that does not reproduce has not been explained; it has only been survived. →
the tailor was right, and the story he asked about is fiction by james hogg found

found in 1830 the father devoted two of his four pages to a magazine story — a settler near the xhosa, orang-outangs, a wife carried off — and asked his son whether it was true. five searches failed. it was found by downloading the volumes and reading them: the mirror of literature, vol. xiv (1829), pp. 313–318, “communicated by mr. hogg, the ettrick shepherd”. it is james hogg's fiction, printed as a settler's letter home. and the reason five searches failed is the tailor's one mistake: he gave the colonist's name as williams or williamson, and the narrator is anonymous — william is the son. a negative built on a detail remembered is a negative about the memory.

found the coverage is excellent and the nil is real. published within the hour on the strength of a count: 1,131 downing baptisms in england for 1800–1806 and almost none in london. that was the wrong control — counting one surname by county tests where the downings were, not whether the index reaches london. the right control is a common name: of 100 smith baptisms sampled in the same window, thirty-seven are london, middlesex or westminster; of 76 kolbe baptisms, six. the index covers london well. so the near-absence of london downings is not the index failing — there were very few downings in london. and the correction reverses the argument twice: the nil is a real negative, and a family with a london birth in 1803, no london baptism and no london kin in the registers is what a family newly arrived from the country looks like — which strengthens the welcombe marriage of 1802 instead of weakening it. the rule this archive already had and misapplied: a nil return is worthless until a control shows the search works, and the control has to test the thing you are doubting. →
the welcombe marriage of 10 may 1802 is a candidate for margaret downing’s parents, and a strengthened one taken back

found it is not. withdrawn the same day it was raised. published this morning as a candidate on a name match and a nine-month interval; called strengthened at lunchtime when a london baptism could not be found for her. the question nobody asked until evening was whether the welcombe couple stayed. they did. every downing record in that parish reads: 1802 john marriage, 1803 john baptism, 1806 william baptism, 1809 emmey baptism, 1810 elizabeth baptism. they baptised a child at welcombe the year after the wedding and went on doing it. margaret was born in london in february 1803. and the last line of the parish list explains the whole thread: a mary downing buried at welcombe in 1834, which is the year both trees give margaret’s mother. a previous researcher almost certainly found the one downing–pooley marriage in england and a mary downing burial in the year they wanted, in the same tiny parish, and joined them — the same search this archive ran today, stopping one question earlier. so “mary king pooley, 1768–1834” is probably not a record but a reconstruction, which also explains why this archive’s own copy of the tree calls her mary p king: two compilers, the same fragments, two guesses. →
www.familysearch.org is down, and so are the national archives at kew and the university of edinburgh taken back

found none of them. /sources/ published that table for five days, and familysearch is cited 7,276 times on this site. familysearch answers 403 — a bot check — and kew and edinburgh answer 200; all three were used from this desk on the day the table was found to be wrong. the cause: checkexternal.py identifies itself honestly as “thebooyzenarchive”, and firewalls refuse unfamiliar user-agents at the connection, before any http status exists — so the tool’s own sensible rule that 403 means guarded never ran, and a refused connection was written down as down. the fix is not to dress up as a browser. this archive identifies itself and will go on doing so. the fix is to stop calling a silence a death: there is now a state unverified, kept apart from dark, which means does not resolve in dns and is the only state here that means gone. after the fix: 27 up, 11 unverified, 5 mail-only, 4 dark, and no host claimed down. the rule was on /method/ the whole time — a nil return is worthless without a control, and a refused connection is a nil return with no control. →
the library named the author in the covering letter and this archive read past it found

found the national library sent the dictionary of south african biography entry on george augustus kolbe, and melanie geustyn's covering sentence named its author: karel schoeman, writing in february 1992 and heading it voorlopige teks — provisional text. this archive read the enclosure and not the letter. the entry was then tested line by line against what is held here: nine statements agree and two are wrong. it says the death notice records eight children; it names ten. and it says knapdaar is not a name this archive has held, when knapdaar is written on the death notice. the dsab was terminated after volume v in 1987, five years before this was written, so on the published record that typescript is the only form the entry has ever taken.
a preview is not a document, and the same four pages carried more taken back

found msb 751, the letter of 23 august 1830 from the london tailor to his son, had been written up from a preview. read again at full resolution from the downloaded pdfs, the same four pages gave dr philip in london, clothes sent out for “john”, a year of newspapers, and five named friends. and the catalogue is wrong about its own document: it calls this a letter written on the son's ordination, and the page reports him “fully accepted by the [l.m.s.] as one of their missionaries”, which is the acceptance and not the ordination. the timeline had been carrying the catalogue's wording since it was first entered and now carries the letter's.
sibree's register, found free, and mr miles turns out to be the man who accepted him found

found james sibree's a register of missionaries (lms, 1923) was located complete and free. it gives kolbe's whole mission life in one entry and settles a question this archive had left open: mr miles was the officer who accepted him, not a messenger carrying somebody else's decision. four of his own journals were catalogued the same day at soas — cwm/lms/05/05/100, /102, /106 and /108, the first being the tour north-east of philippolis with melvill in november 1828 — with the 1836–37 incoming correspondence in box 15.
seventeen people had a page saying they are “not yet discussed on any page” taken back

found among them george augustus kolbe, the 1820 settler, named 155 times in the built site; john barry, 158; george mountjoy, 140; petrus jacobus booysen, 110; johanna catharina mountjoy, 89. the data was fine and the build threw it away. dossiers.py dropped any name that was a strict prefix of a longer person’s name — a rule written to stop “john barry” swallowing “john barry booyzen”, which instead silenced the shorter man entirely. the fix keeps the shorter name and fences it with a negative lookahead, so it matches everywhere except where the longer name begins. 2,428 mentions came back. nothing refused the build while this was true, so a gate now does: checkregisters.py fails when a person the dossier calls undiscussed is named in the built pages. found because the estate asked this archive to look for a fault the mazza archive had just had. →
wo 12/1430 is the muster book to read for james mountjoy taken back

found it is the 20th and 21st dragoons for 1867–1868 — fifty years after he was discharged, and the re-raised regiment rather than the one that garrisoned the cape. the 21st light dragoons has a continuous wo 12 run of its own and the piece that covers his discharge is wo 12/1450, 1816–1817. the wrong reference had been written into a letter to kew; the letter was still unsent and now names the right piece and says an earlier version had it wrong. →
the 21st light dragoons left the cape in 1816 taken back

found september 1817. an extract of a letter from the cape dated 1 and 10 september 1817, printed in the sun, the star, the public ledger, the morning herald and the hampshire chronicle that november: “the 21st light dragoons have embarked for india”. the 1816 figure was written on 15 september with no source attached and stood in three files. it matters because he married in march 1817 — under 1816 he was already a civilian when he married, and under 1817 he had six months to choose between a wife at graaff-reinet and a transport to madras. →
the burgersdorp sweep of images 605–818 found five new people taken back

found three. johanna catharina mountjoy, born 28 january 1860, was already held in full — a daughter of george mountjoy who married william henry keys — and the sweep only confirmed her and gave her a reference. frederick fortunatus werdmuller was already held from a 1907 petition and a 1953 estate; what the sweep added was his birth and his mother, which is a real gain and not a new person. the duplicate person records were caught by the build's own name-collision check for the first and by reading the register for the second, before either reached a page. the rule it costs: a sweep that returns a name is checked against the archive before it is called a find. →
johan gottlieb kolbe was buried at the german church of the savoy, entry 55, grave 7 taken back
did a claim taken from the family tree and repeated before it was tested.

found taken from a family tree and repeated here. the westminster burials register, held by the city of westminster archives centre, has him died 18 november 1845 and buried 26 november 1845 at st john the baptist, great marlborough street, page 7. the date matches to the day and the seven matches; the church does not. the register also gives a death date and a birth year of 1764, neither of which this archive had. →
johan gottlieb kolbe had one wife, called mary taken back

found he had two, and both were called mary — which is why one of them could never be made to fit a run of baptisms from 1792 to 1819. the first died 2 august 1814 aged 46; the second died 15 august 1824 aged 36. both are in the german lutheran church register, tna rg 4/4631. →
r_177176049779 is this archive's reference for petrus jacobus booysen's 1812 birth taken back

found it was recorded once, from a findmypast search run without a subscription, and never opened. opened twice on a live full subscription, findmypast's own transcript page returns a 500 error. the reference does not resolve. it stays on the page as a struck citation rather than being quietly deleted. →
the german savoy registers are rg 4/4625, 4626, 4628 and 4631 for burials taken back

found rg 4/4630 belongs on that list too. the 1807 burial of charles samuel kolbe is entered in both 4631 and 4630, with the same death date and the same age to the day — a register and its duplicate. the archive's own note named five volumes and missed one. →
three booyzens listed together as deaths in concentration camps taken back

found only two of the three died in a camp. read on the university of cape town database's own pages rather than through two intermediaries: gert jacobus (johannesburg rc, aged 2, farm rietvallei, district marico) and gertruida magdalena (vereeniging rc, aged 19, farm rietvlei, district heidelberg) are each recorded “died in camp: yes”. jan gerhardus lodewicus, aged 2, is recorded “died in camp: no”, with no camp and no farm attached at all. listing the three together was this archive's compression, not the database's — and it is the same failure as reading an index line as though it were the record. gertruida's entry also carries the note “or irene rc”, so even her camp is uncertain. →
the national archives' catalogue given as “national.archives.gov.za/naairs.htm” taken back

found the live domain has no dot in it — nationalarchives.gov.za. the host as published has no address record and no mail record at all. it appeared in the note of 13 september that ends “written down because the wrong address cost this archive a day”, which is the row that exists to stop exactly this. found by a tool written to check whether the sources this site cites are still there; it looks for hosts named in prose as well as in links, because this archive writes its sources in sentences. →
“willem hermanus pieterzen — anna catharina slier's first husband” taken back

found he is the son. de villiers's volume 3 gives “hermanus pietersen, namen van ouders onbekend, gehuwd 5 april 1807 met anna catharina slier”, and their children as “1 willem hermanus, gedoopt 12 maart 1809; 2 johan christiaan, gedoopt 28 april 1810”. this archive built one man out of two documents that spell him differently — the 1817 marriage register's harmanus pieterze and the 1840 death notice's william pietersen — and a long name looked like a way to reconcile them. the husband is hermanus; willem hermanus is the boy baptised in 1809. this archive half knew, because its own note already called the 1851 godfather “his son”. the naming claim survives and improves: willem hermanus is willem for his mother's father, willem slier of hamburg, and hermanus for his own father. a second half-brother, johan christiaan, was invisible for as long as the two men were one. →
“luus with booyzen returns nothing” — published against the five unplaced silverton children taken back

found it returns a marriage. the marriage transcription database on gendatabase.com: “1928 · cornelius abraham luus × susanna frederik alettha booyzen”. the negative was true of naairs, which is the only index this archive had asked, and it was published as though it were true of the record. a marriage register is not an estate index. a sentence that says “returns nothing” has to name what was asked, and this one did not. whether this susanna is the “ousie” of the silverton pillar is a separate question and is not being assumed. →
leeuwberg pinned at fauresmith, on a 1903 land file naming a “leeuwberg no 465, dist. faurismith” taken back

found it is a different farm of the same name. the friend of the free state of 13 january 1870 advertises “the farm, wildebeestkooi, adjoining the farm leeuberg, the property of the late j.g.e. kolbe, about two hours ride from the town of bloemfontein”. fifteen or twenty kilometres, not a hundred and thirty. the pin stood for two days, and it was published with its own objection printed beside it — that fauresmith is 130 km from kaalspruit while the obituary says he died at one and lies at the other. the objection was the right one and it has answered against the pin. moved to bloemfontein, still approximate. the two-farm contradiction this archive could not reconcile was never a contradiction: leeuberg and kaalspruit are neighbours. →
“1898 — jgl booyzen of kwaggafontein, district marico, in the field-cornet's papers” taken back

found the papers are the education department's. the atlas has carried that line under marico since the entry was built. the three documents behind it are tab source od — the school files of the south african republic — and they are a subsidy application, book orders and quarterly returns for a farm school. a field-cornet does appear in the bundle, exactly once, valuing the teacher's dwelling in may 1898, and that is a different document sent by a different man. the line was written from a memory of the record rather than from the record. corrected in place, and the record is now eight documents instead of three. →
margaret downing “c. 1804, london” — and, for a day, a death date thrown into doubt by a newspaper taken back

found the stone had both answers and this archive had the stone. the burgersdorp monument has been on the kolbe page for weeks, photographed and captioned; the caption quoted it as far as “also his relict margaret downing…” and stopped. the next two lines read “born in london 23 february 1803 and died at burghersdorp 2_ november 1867.” her birth moves from a guessed year to a date. and the death was never in doubt: yesterday's grahamstown journal obituary said she died “about three months since” — january 1868 — and this archive published the discrepancy rather than resolving it. it was nearly five months, and a journalist rounding is a journalist rounding. the fault is the caption: a transcription that stops before the end of an inscription is not a transcription, and this one hid two facts in plain sight for weeks. →
pretoria answered, and a forum closed the oldest question found

found two replies in one morning. the national archives in pretoria, silent since the letter of 12 september, answered: all six estate files are bound, and bound files cannot be scanned and emailed. not a refusal — a physical fact about the record, and one that explains a great deal about what has and has not been filmed. ms mavis xaba put a private researcher who specialises in estate files on copy; engaging her is the user's call. she did not say any of the six references was wrong, including the one this archive could not find on microfilm at all. and on wikitree, riël smit answered the question this archive most wanted answered, in nine words: de villiers & pama (1981) still place petrus jacobus under jan. pieter van zyl had already searched for a marriage between a gerhardus lodewicus and a magdalena de beer and found none, and remembered — correctly — that a child of petrus jacobus carried the name. he is on line 12 of the same sheet: jan gerthardus lodewikus booijsen. the name in the parents' box is the back half of a son's name, and the half that was dropped is the father's. both letters went out the same morning: a short thanks to ms xaba asking only whether mhg 52653 is a valid reference, and a first approach to the private researcher — what she charges and how, her view on whether the work is worth doing at all, and an offer to start with one file. it is the first paid-research approach this project has made; everything before it has been a request to an institution.
“148 rows read of 184 — thirty-six documents were not reached, and this archive is not going to call 148 a complete enumeration” taken back

found the caution was right in spirit and wrong in fact, and the fact is worse. all ten pages had been walked. the thirty-six were not unreached — they were thrown away by this archive's own row filter, which required a description field longer than three characters and so silently dropped every row whose description column the index leaves short or blank. re-run without that condition the same query returns 194 rows, 184 of them unique: the exact count. this archive published a scope caveat that blamed the source for a hole it had dug itself — which is the same failure as the blank name column, one layer up: a filter that drops what it does not recognise looks exactly like an archive that does not hold it. the thirty-six turn out to include seven anglo-boer war compensation claims by booyzens in the marico district. →
martha angeline kolbe, sixty days old, was “buried at volksrust”, and volksrust held a concentration camp taken back

found both halves withdrawn, six hours after publishing. her stone is in wakkerstroom main cemetery. the index this archive read gives the burial as “volksrust, eastvaal district council, mpumalanga” — and that is a district municipality, not a town; wakkerstroom lies inside it. this archive read a modern administrative area as a place of burial, which is a failure of reading and not of the source. with the town goes the camp. the stone reads “ter gedachtenis van ons geliefde kleine”, in dutch, and the mason's town is cut across its base: newcastle, twenty-five miles away in natal. a family stone in a town churchyard, cut by a monumental mason in another colony, is not a camp burial. the care taken in the original entry — “records the burial place without claiming the camp” — was not enough, because naming the camp at all in an entry about a child who died in december 1901 makes the claim whatever the sentence says. →
the 1902 prisoner of war could not be assigned to either george augustus kolbe of wakkerstroom taken back

found now it can, and the withdrawal of the morning is replaced by an answer rather than a shrug. both men are buried in the same cemetery and both stones are read. the younger: “george augustus — geb. 29 julie 1863 — oorl. 28 sept. 1954”, which is the colesberg font date to the day. the elder: “george augustus kolbe — geb. 2 oktober 1861 — oorl. 8 november 1934”. the pow record says age 40, event 1902. a man born 2 october 1861 was forty from october 1901 to october 1902; a man born 29 july 1863 was thirty-nine for the whole of 1902. the prisoner is the elder man. this is recorded as a correction rather than quietly fixed, because the archive published a claim, withdrew it, and then reversed the withdrawal, all in one day, and a reader is owed the whole of that. →
george augustus kolbe of wakkerstroom, born colesberg 1863, was a prisoner of war in 1902 — “the fourth man of this family taken in that war” taken back

found withdrawn within the hour, and by the same record that produced it. the pow entry — wo 108/368, the master list of boer prisoners numbers 1 to 32561 — gives residence wakkerstroom, which is what the claim was built on, and this archive stopped reading there. it also gives age 40, nationality transvaaler, prison natal. the man baptised at colesberg on 11 october 1863 was thirty-nine in 1902. a second george augustus kolbe, born at burgersdorp in 1861 and dead at standerton in 1934, was forty or forty-one that year — and his own marriage entry to susanna margaretha swart gives his residence as wakkerstroom too. two men of one name in one town, which this archive had itself written down as a warning in the same hour, in the same run of searches, and then walked straight past. the prisoner is more probably the older man. nothing decides it but the age, and an index age is a weak thing; so the claim is withdrawn rather than reassigned. →
the wonderboom deeds register showed a transfer from m. j. booyzen, widow, to david schalk booyzen on 9 april 1907 taken back

found the transferor is right and the date is not. her gravestone at rebecca street, pretoria, reads “magdalena johanna booyzen (geb. bezuidenhout), geb. 8 mei 1870, oorl. 29 jan 1955” — so the ledger's “8/5/1870” beside her name is her birth date, which identifies her beyond doubt. but her husband petrus jacobus booyzen died on 25 march 1947, so she was not a widow in 1907 and cannot have transferred anything as one that year. the 9 april 1907 read off that row belongs to a different row: the ledger's columns were mis-aligned in the reading. what survives is the identification; what is withdrawn is the date, and with it the suggestion that david schalk booysen could be carried to 1907. →
both testable pow ages run one to two years high against this archive's dates taken back

found that described the de list, not the record. the fuller register gives stefanus francois as 26 — exact against a birth of about october 1874 — and david schalk as 53, within weeks of his fifty-third birthday on 9 june 1848. the de list's 28 and 54 are the outliers. the caveat was published on the strength of the weaker of two documents before the stronger had been found. →
the de list's prisoner numbers are a separate series and do not locate these men in the fuller register taken back

found they are the same series and they locate them exactly. the claim came from misreading a leading digit: image 139 of item 1 begins at 19431, not 18431, which the batch title on image 136 states outright — “nos. 19,431 to 20,705”. the de beer entries read as 18463–18465 were 19463–19465. in the correct batch, image 126, numbers 18463, 18464 and 18465 are stefanus francois, petrus jacobus and david schalk booysen. →
catherine maria sophia is a barry name taken back

found it is a kolbe name. the 1848 graaff-reinet baptism register, entry 603, names the godmother in full as catharine sophia maria kolber — eleven years before her sister named the daughter this archive had been treating as the head of the chain. the namesakes page called it “a barry name that outlives the barry surname by eighty years”; it outlives the kolbe surname instead, and the archive already held the woman, filed as plain “catharine kolbe”, without noticing she carried the name first. →
a relationship search had found one name the barry notices never gave taken back

found it found none. henry jaonas barry is james henry barry, who was already in this archive — the same baptism indexed twice, once as henry jaonas with the year read as 1868 and once as hennery james berry with it read as 1848. same birth date, same parents, and familysearch attaches both to one tree person. the register itself decides: “graaff-reinet. baptism records 1846–1851” cannot hold an 1868 entry. so the “baptised at twenty years old” that made him interesting was a mis-transcribed year, and “jaonas” was a mis-read “james” — which is what the archive's own register search implied when it found jonas nowhere among the barrys or kolbes. the eleven-against-nine gap is unchanged: two children are still missing, not one. →
magdelena elisabeth de beer was carried here under wikitree's codes, b6c2 and b6c6 taken back

found the codes are b5c2 and b5c6. de villiers 1893 page 34 puts zaccharias de beer — her father — as the fifth child of matthijs andries de beer, not the sixth, and pieter van zyl said so on g2g before the book was opened; reading page 34 confirmed it. the b6 is wikitree's, and this archive repeated it for a day without checking it in print. it matters more than a digit: a de villiers code is an address, and quoting the wrong one sends the next reader to the wrong family. where this archive quotes the wikitree profile it still says b6, because that is what the profile says — the error being reported is not the same as the error being made. →
the two magdalena de beers were two different women, and the tree had merged them taken back

found they are one woman. de villiers 1893, page 34, marks only the second — magdalena baptised 16 october 1754 — with “zie booijsen”, and 1754 is the birth year this archive has always carried for its own magdelena elisabeth. the argument published here for a day ran the other way: that jan booysen's wife was dead by december 1793 while ours died in 1843, so they could not be the same. the 1843 death date is the weak link, not the identity — this archive's own page said both her dates came off the family tree with no source stated. what actually followed from reading the book is the opposite of what was published: she married jan, and generation seven is now in question rather than confirmed. →
gravestones, a camp, and the wrong country's newspapers found

found the genealogical society's gravestone data, reached through naairs, gave two things. a kolbe of thirty-five dead in the concentration camp cemetery at volksrust between 1899 and 1901 — the first camp death to touch any surname in this archive, against a question that had been answered “searched, and not found” on a different name. and margaret downing kolbe, born 1899, buried in natal in 1979: george augustus kolbe married margaret downing at shoreditch in 1819, and eighty years later a girl was christened with the whole of it. then eggsa corrected something published this morning. searching the british press for this family returned almost nothing and that was written down as a limit of the medium. it is a limit of the country. eggsa holds transcribed cape colonial papers — the eastern province herald, the fort beaufort advocate, the queenstown free press — with booysen entries from the 1860s on, free and unread.
tolosberg, and a policeman who was at talana found

found the place name was in no gazetteer, no battle list and no war diary — and then it was in a medal-roll database, attached to this man by his prisoner number. tolosberg is in the waterval valley, eastern transvaal; forty-two boers were taken there on 25 april 1901 with two guns and much stock; and stephanus francois booysen, pow 18463, was sent to india. he was a zarp, one of the zar's police, who had been at talana in the first week of the war, wounded in the right leg at wagon hill, and present at spion kop and at dalmanutha. this archive has quoted the family's war testimony for the whole project with nothing to test it against. it has something now.
a better register found, and a number that does not travel method

found the de list is item 3 of nine on the staff officer for prisoners of war film. item 1 is the register worth having: home address, town, field cornetcy or commando, where captured and date of capture, for every man. bisected it by prisoner number to the right pages and found that the numbers do not carry across — 18463 to 18465 there are three men called de beer, so the de list numbering is its own series. checked the b surnames in the batch whose captures match our men's sailing date: five booysens, none of them ours. the route to their commando and their farm is now mapped and not yet walked.
three booyzens on a prisoner-of-war transport found

found the family fought. a printed pow transport list in the pretoria government archives carries three consecutive entries — 18463 stephanus francois booyzen, 28; 18464 petrus jacobus booyzen, 29; 18465 david schalk booyzen, 54 — all three shipped on the city of cambridge on 3 june 1901, all three from pretoria. consecutive numbers on one transport means taken together. this archive has spent months establishing that no booysen is on a cape rebel roll, which was the right answer to the wrong question: these men were transvaal burghers, and nobody here had thought to look for them as prisoners rather than as rebels.
the folios followed, into a pretoria transfer register method

found the land-index folios led to rak 2384, a deeds transfer register for wonderboom south — pretoria, the district where david schalk booysen was living when he remarried in 1905. three rows on one page carry the name, and the household reads petrus jacobus, david schalk, magdalena johanna: this archive's direct line, name for name. one row transfers land to a david schalk booyzen on 9 april 1907, which would be seventeen months later than anything else held for the man of that name. it is not proved and nothing has been adopted — the transferor is a widow born bezuidenhout and this archive's david schalk married a widow born stols. a name cluster is a reason to order the deed, not a reason to believe it.
full-text search, and a land register nobody here had opened found

found tried familysearch's full-text search — which reads the images themselves rather than a volunteer index — hoping it would reach the two missing barry children. it does not: south african full-text coverage excludes the church registers, which closes that route for good. but it covers four collections this archive has never searched, two of them land records. in rak 2508, an 1895 land-register index, the booyzen block runs to four entries with folio numbers, and one of the names is jacobus nicolaas — the eldest of the 1863 eight, who this archive knows only as a man who ended in the transvaal with an estate number. evaton is in the transvaal. nothing adopted; a surname in a land index is not an identification.
the book found, measured, and not read method

found having shown the index cannot reach the two missing barry children, the next question is which book can. it is one volume: burgersdorp baptism records 1852–1866, 534 images, covering the whole 1854–1858 gap. it was located, its scale measured by two landmarks — 1853 at image 54, 1866 at image 528 — and checked for a name index at the back, which it does not have. then it was left unread. a hundred and fifty images is a sequential browse rather than a search, and saying so with the film number and the page arithmetic written down is more useful than half-doing it.
the index cannot find four children it is known to have method

found swept the barry baptisms under every spelling the index gives the mother — kolbe, kolber, kolbee, colbe, colby, colbee — and it returns the same seven children and nothing new. that is not the finding. the finding is that hendrik nicholaas, richard peter, margaret mary and kathleen mary are all named on their parents' own death notices and none of the four appears in the index at all. an index that cannot produce four children known to exist will not produce the two that are unknown. the route is closed for a demonstrable reason, and what remains is the registers themselves, read across the gaps.
two fonts, a year apart, and every witness a kolbe found

found having read one barry baptism, the one before it was worth reading too. at the 1847 font the witnesses are john kolbe, margaret kolbe and augusta kolbe; at the 1848 font, catharine sophia maria kolbe. two children, two years, and not a barry witness between them. that is the same conclusion the namesake correction reached from one entry, arrived at a second time from another — the names this archive has called barry names belong to the people who stood at the fonts, and they were all kolbes. the olivier daughters, asked for the same way, returned thirty strangers: the method works where the names are rare, and olivier is not.
a godmother's full name, and a chain that started in the wrong family found

found the image flagged unread an hour earlier was read, and the entry gave up more than the date it was fetched for. entry 603 of the graaff-reinet register writes the child as henry james, settles the year at 1848 in the clerk's hand, and names the godmother in full: catharine sophia maria kolber. this archive already held her — as “catharine kolbe”, a line in a burgersdorp entry five years later — without noticing she carried catherine maria sophia eleven years before the barry daughter who has been standing at the head of that namesake chain since the page was written. it is not a barry name. it never was.

found yesterday's one new name is withdrawn. henry jaonas barry is james henry barry — one baptism indexed twice, the year read as 1868 on one entry and 1848 on the other, and the register's own title, graaff-reinet baptism records 1846–1851, rules out 1868 without needing the image. what survives is better than what was lost: an exact birth and baptism date for a man this archive carried as “about 1847”, the correct parish, and confirmation of the birth-spacing argument made against him. two barry children are still missing.
nine grandchildren, and the one record that would settle it is not indexed found

found familysearch came back and the queued queries ran. the decisive one failed in an informative way: the 1788 baptism that names petrus jacobus's father does not surface, because the date filters are ignored and the 18th-century cape registers are not name-indexed — a negative about the index, not the register. two other entries independently confirmed de villiers on two of jan booijsen's sons, which strengthens the book against the death notice. and the relationship search on the father, queued as question 13, returned a household: john augustus barry ii had a wife and nine children this archive had never seen, including the kolbe name carried into a fourth generation.

found a g2g answer named de villiers 1893 as downloadable, so it was downloaded and read rather than taken on trust — which is the whole point of this archive, and it cut against yesterday's conclusion. page 34 makes the two magdalena de beers one woman, withdrawing what was published here for a day. page 78 then makes petrus jacobus (1788) the seventh child of jan booijsen, agreeing with this archive on his baptism date, his wife and his son's baptism, and disagreeing only on his father. generation seven now rests on a single line of an 1876 death notice against a genealogy built from the registers. nothing rewritten; the question has changed shape.

found he had at least seven. his first wife's 1891 sterfkennis lists them all, of age: petrus jacobus, ocken johannes, anna johanna maria, elesabettha maria cornelya, alettha catrina johanna, magdalena johanna and hendrick stefanus nicolaas. the 1908 notice names four because by 1908 only four were left. →

found they were his first wife's. the zeerust marriage register, entry 13, dates the second marriage to 14 april 1892 and gives the bride's age as fifty-one and her condition as widow. by 1908 all four children were adults, two of them married women. the archive put them under the marriage it could name rather than the marriage that could have produced them. →

found born in ireland. the 1903 registration of his death, made by the son who was present, enters him as “irishman born in ireland”. the 1915 notice this archive had been using was sworn by another son twelve years later and says “at sea, exact whereabouts unknown”. the archive had the weaker document and had not looked for a better one. →

found g2g questions 2082757 and 2082786 are live — the mhg 10/57 sterfkennis, and which of two magdalena de beers married the booysen, with two printed page references to be checked against a death notice. the private message to the profile manager who has seen the 1957 file is composed in the form and unsent: wikitree ends that form with an anti-spam question, and answering it is the one thing this archive will not do on the user's behalf. the forum had no such check.
the tree was wrong, and it showed its working found

found two more wikitree profiles turned a flat contradiction into an explanation. jan booysen remarried on 15 december 1793, so his de beer wife was dead by then and ours died in 1843 — fifty years apart, exactly the objection this archive raised when it set the 1793 will aside. the will is now positively his. and the tree's own de beer profile carries two cape codes, two baptisms nine years apart, and a sibling list holding both a magdalena and a magdalena elizabeth: two women merged into one, which is what put the wrong father over our petrus jacobus. out of it, for the first time, a candidate for magdelena elisabeth de beer's own parents.
a question asked in public for the first time method

found every enquiry this archive has made so far has gone to an institution and waited. this one went to a forum of people who own the same books. g2g question 2082757 asks whether anyone has seen the sterfkennis in transvaal estate mhg 10/57 — the file on the familysearch films that refuse images, and the one a wikitree profile cites as a source. it arrives carrying the johannesburg cemetery entry rather than only asking. posted, then edited within the minute: the double-bracket profile syntax does not work in a g2g body and published as visible brackets.
wikitree, which this project had never once opened method

found asked whether it had ever been looked at, the honest answer was no — the word appeared nowhere in the project, though eleven myheritage trees, geni and the familysearch tree were all listed. thirteen booyzen profiles read. five are this family. it is a user tree and stays a lead rather than a source, but it cites documents, and one citation is the thing question 0 has wanted since the beginning: a page number into the published suid-afrikaanse geslagsregisters. it also gives petrus jacobus a different father — jan booysen, the same man as the 1793 will this archive declined to adopt — against line 3 of an 1876 death notice this archive has read. nothing was changed. the disagreement was written down.
