¦oct 1817 at st helena, guarding napoleon: the 66th regiment of about 1,000 men, a detachment of the 21st light dragoons of about 100, and two or three companies of royal artillery. star; oxford journal; belfast news-letter

¦14–17 nov 1817 extract of a letter from the cape of good hope, dated 1 and 10 september 1817: “the 21st light dragoons have embarked for india.” sun; star; public ledger; morning herald; hampshire chronicle
and this is the sentence the whole table was read for
james montjoy married anna catharina slier at graaff-reinet on 9 march 1817. his regiment sailed for india six months later.

a soldier who married in march 1817 and was keeping a house and a saddler’s trade at cradock by january 1822 was discharged at the cape before september 1817, and the thing he was choosing between was a wife at graaff-reinet and a transport to india. this archive has been trying to date his discharge from the cape end for weeks. the london end dates it in one line.
three windows, not one
he could have come out with the regiment in 1806 at about twenty-four, with the 1810 reinforcement, or with the draft of 140 men in october 1813.
all three are now dated, and the wo 97 attestation years for the regiment cluster at 1799–1801 and 1805 — which favours the first. the wo 97 sweep →
why a cavalryman would take his discharge

parliament said it out loud in march 1809: the 21st were at the cape “where they could have nothing to do”. eleven years of garrison duty, one review, and a colonel — banastre tarleton — who never saw them.
a trade and a marriage at graaff-reinet against another eleven years in madras is not a difficult choice.
a name that turns up twice
the regiment was reviewed at the cape by sir john cradock, governor, and pronounced in the highest state of discipline.
the town james mountjoy settled in is named after the man who reviewed his regiment. there is nothing in that but a coincidence of governors and place-names — and it is still worth writing down.

what this does not do. it does not name him, and it does not touch his parentage. wo 97 still holds no mountjoy of that regiment, and the reason still stands: the pre-1855 discharge papers hold only men discharged to a pension, and a man who took his papers at the cape to marry and make saddles is not one. what has changed is that his discharge now has a deadline, and the muster books — wo 12 at kew, which list every man by name, quarter by quarter — would show him leaving it. question 12 →
17 september · the errand is one piece, and the piece this archive had written down was the wrong one

the kew catalogue was searched again before the letter went. it gives the regiment a continuous run of muster books, and the run ends where the regiment does — disbanded in 1820, with nothing again until the 1860s.
¦piece covering what was happening
¦wo 12/1442–1445 1798–1804 home service. the wo 97 attestations cluster here.
¦wo 12/1446 1805–06 york, then portsmouth, then the cape
¦wo 12/1447 1807–09 back from south america; “nothing to do”
¦wo 12/1448 1810–12 the reinforcement; cradock’s review
¦wo 12/1449 1813–15 the draft of 140 men
¦wo 12/1450 1816–17 the marriage, and the embarkation for india. one piece covers both.
¦wo 12/1451–1452 1818–20 india, then disbandment
held at the national archives, kew, with no access conditions recorded. not name-indexed — they have to be read, and a man’s disappearance from a muster dates his discharge.
and the correction, which is the reason for going back at all
on 15 september this archive searched the same catalogue, concluded correctly that wo 97 would not hold him, and named the piece to read instead: wo 12/1430. that went into a letter drafted to kew.
wo 12/1430 is the 20th and 21st dragoons for 1867–1868. fifty years late, and the re-raised regiment rather than the one that garrisoned the cape.

the letter was never posted. it now names wo 12/1450, gives the newspaper evidence for the september 1817 departure, and tells them in as many words that an earlier version had the wrong piece. a letter that asks the wrong archivist for the wrong box gets one answer and burns a month, and the only thing that caught it was searching a catalogue twice. the corrections →
1868–1914 · leeuwberg, a commando, and a farmers’ president — the free state kolbes in the british press

commandant john gerson eliezar kolbe, the settler’s eldest child, died of typhus caught on commando on 3 april 1868, on the farm leeuwberg, leaving a widow and twelve children — eight sons and four daughters. this archive can put a hand on two of the twelve. the prisoner list and the newspapers between them now put kolbes back on that farm, in the field, and at the head of the free state’s farmers.
1901 · a kolbe still on leeuwberg
andries frederick kolbe, aged 45, taken prisoner and entered on the war office list as of leeuwberg, bloemfontein — wo 108/368 folio 431, sent to cape town and natal.

thirty-three years after the commandant died there, a kolbe is farming it. born about 1856, he would have been twelve when his father—or whoever it was—died at leeuwberg, and he is inside the age bracket of the eight sons.
no descent is documented and none is claimed. what is documented is a farm, a surname and a date.
1901 · a kolbe commando in the field

may 1901, colesberg. “kritzinger, with 200 men, has passed through this district. the hertzog, brand and kolbe commandos…” — london evening standard, globe and westminster gazette, 21 may; leominster news, 24 may.
september 1901. “kolbe’s attitude is doubtful. he is reported to have expressed a wish to surrender.” — derby daily telegraph and derby and chesterfield reporter, 5–6 september.

november 1901. “general kolbe captured. bloemfontein, wednesday. — hamilton’s column, operating in the district of reddersburg…” — birmingham mail, 21 november; warwick and warwickshire advertiser, 23 november.
colesberg, bethulie, reddersburg, bloemfontein. that is leeuwberg country, and 1901 is exactly when the commandant’s sons would have been commanding.
1914 · a kolbe at the head of the free state’s farmers

“a cordial welcome was given to the south african farmers at the general meeting, and at luncheon in the yard mr g. a. kolbe, president of the orange free state agricultural association and chairman of the orange free state delegation…” — western daily press, dundee courier, cork free press and exeter and plymouth gazette, 2 july 1914.

named in the delegate list of 26 june 1914 in the daily telegraph as “mr. g. a. kolbe (bethulie)”, beside mr e. w. hunt of pretoria and mr j. h. perks of koingha. on 22 july the daily malta chronicle has him sending a telegram of respectful greeting to queen wilhelmina on the delegation’s behalf.

and the war office list of 1901 holds a george augustus kolbe of sterkfontein, bethulie, aged 32, a free stater, sent to natal — wo 108/368 folio 581. same initials, same district, and thirteen years between them.
what this is and what it is not

it is four documents and a district. a man on the commandant’s farm in 1901; a commando under the commandant’s surname in the commandant’s own country in the same year; a general of that name taken at reddersburg in november; and a farmers’ president of bethulie in 1914 carrying the settler’s forenames and, very probably, a prisoner’s number thirteen years earlier.

it is not a pedigree. the document that would make it one is vab mhg m777, the 1896 estate of the commandant’s widow anna jacoba van der merwe, filed under her second husband’s name mccabe — which would name all twelve children. it is identified, it is unread, and it is in bloemfontein. the commandant →

one limit worth stating. findmypast’s newspaper archive is british and irish. its own coverage facet lists england, scotland, wales, both irelands, india, barbados, china, jamaica, australia and new zealand — and no south africa at all. everything above is the cape and the free state seen from fleet street, through reuter’s wire and a war correspondent. it is not a substitute for the south african papers, and the eggsa newspaper index remains the only route into those.
23 august 1830 · “your affectionate father, j g kolbe”

this archive has held a tailor of conduit street and a missionary of colesberg and not one document showing the two men in contact. a catalogue line said one existed. on 15 september it wrote to the national library of south africa; on 18 september melanie geustyn, senior librarian, sent four pages. this is the first document in this archive that johan gottlieb kolbe wrote himself.
london august 23d 1830

about a month ago i wrote to you by dr philip informing you that mr miles had called at our house & informed me that you had been fully accepted by the [l.m.s.] as one of their missionaries — to which i do congratulate you, now, accompanied with fervent prayers to god that he may vouchsafe to bless your ministry amongst the poor bushman & other heathens to whom it may please him to send you…
the question it was asked, and did not answer

the enquiry asked, above everything, whether the letter carries an address at its head. an 1844 obituary puts the family at brunswick-square; the rate books, the gazette, the census and the burial register put him in soho and then conduit street.
it says “london” and nothing finer. the one line that would have settled it is not there.
written down as plainly as the finds, because a document that arrives and does not answer the question is still a result.
and the question it answered completely

the enquiry also asked whether “lms missionary” in the catalogue came from the papers or from the donor — because the only other evidence was john montgomery’s memoir, written down forty-five years after the fact.

it is in the father’s own hand, in 1830. mr miles of the society called at the house; dr philip — john philip, the lms superintendent at the cape — carried the previous letter and “was exceedingly glad to hear of your being accepted”. two independent witnesses to the mission, forty-five years apart.
the longest passage in the letter is about another son.

henry had wrote to you himself & left his letter at the mission house to be forwarded to you with the first opportunity… he keeps up pretty well at present, but what effect the winter may have upon him if it should set in very cold, as it did last winter, is perhaps not doubtful, since it must prevent him from taking exercise by walking, & which is a great means of keeping down the dropsy, of which he bears still the symptoms… i trust also that you will join your prayers, that he may vouchsafe to prepare him to a fit state of meeting his god… he appears at present to be resigned to the catastrophe.

this is john henry kolbe, baptised at westminster on 29 july 1800. this archive has his font, his deposition in the old bailey in january 1819 (“my father is a tailor, and lives in church-street, soho”), his marriage to matilda ford three months later, his bankruptcy in 1824, and his burial in the german lutheran register on 22 april 1832. now it has his illness, and his father’s grief, twenty months before the end. the trial →
“kind love from your sisters & brother”
sisters plural. brother singular.
in august 1830, of the eight sons the 1844 obituary counts, exactly two were alive: george augustus at the cape, and henry in london with dropsy. henry died on 13 april 1832.

from that day george augustus was “the last remaining of eight sons” — and the grahamstown journal did not say so until december 1844. the obituary is corroborated, and the date it became true is now known to within a fortnight.
elizabeth, who is betsey, and lives in edinburgh

“milne with elizabeth & family had transferred their residence to edinburgh… he says that betsey likes the situation very well, & they think that they will settle there rather than in london; milne & betsey desire their best to you.”

four days ago this archive found, in the westminster marriage register, elizabeth kolbe married john milne in 1817 at st clement danes. that was a line in an index. this is her father calling her betsey and saying where she went.
charlotte stops being an inference
“charlotte sends you an evangelical magazine, with the account of the death of the rev. w. orme, late secretary to the l.m.s.”

on 17 september this archive wrote that marianne, charlotte and amelia of the 1841 conduit street household match no baptism in the family’s own register run, and that their place in the family was an inference from living in the house. charlotte’s is an inference no longer.

“a suit of black clothes, hope they may be wide enough for you, as i understand that you are stout as long” — clerical black, for a newly accepted missionary — with a sash and waistcoat, and a set of last year’s newspapers, some of which henry, who read them every week after his father had finished with them, seems to have lost.

“on the 26 june last we lost by death our king george 4th and have now a william the 4th, formerly duke of clarence… he appears to be a king after the people’s heart”, and in france “a new revolution has taken place” — charles x and the ordinances, three weeks old when he wrote.
a tall story, to be checked

he has read in the mirror of a scottish colonist near the caffres whose farm was raided by baboons. london thinks it “a fictitious romance”. “i should think that your society would have heard some thing about it, & therefore i should be glad to hear from you, whether that report may be founded in truth or falsehood.”
a tailor in conduit street asking his missionary son to fact-check a magazine.

what this cost and what it took. one letter, sent on 15 september to an address checked first against the host table on this site’s own source register. a holding reply the next morning saying the manuscript collections live in off-site vaults. the document itself on the third day, with a second one nobody asked for — a two-page entry written for the dictionary of south african biography by dr karel schoeman, with a list of sources, which this archive has not yet read. the background file holds nothing further on the donation or on dr griffiths, so where the original is remains unknown and unpursuable from that end.

it ends: “commending you to god’s holy keeping, & if it should not be his will to see each other again in this world, that i may have the happiness of seeing you shine as a great star before the throne of god & the lamb.” they did not see each other again. george augustus died at wirtemberg on 1 december 1844; his father died at 34 conduit street on 18 november 1845, not knowing it.
read again, from the file itself — and a preview is not a document

everything above was read in a mail client’s preview overlay, on a screen eight hundred pixels wide. on 20 september the two pdfs were opened properly. nothing already published turned out to be wrong. a good deal turned out to be missing, and the list above was written as though it were an inventory. it was a sample. corrections →
dr philip was in london, and he was pleased
“dr philip was exceedingly glad to hear of you being accepted by the l.m.s. as you may well imagine, he has promised to write to you a letter by the first opportunity…”

this archive had philip only as a courier — the man who carried the previous letter. he is in the room. the most powerful man in the society’s southern african work heard that a soho tailor’s son had been accepted, was exceedingly glad, and undertook to write to him personally. that letter, if it was written, is another document with george augustus kolbe’s name on it, and the place to look is the same cwm archive at soas that holds his journal.
a box, and clothes for a boy
the suit of black clothes was not the whole of it. the letter encloses a jacket and waistcoat “for john”, and a further jacket also for him —
“tell him his old father has sent it him, & to make haste to fill them out.”

clothes for a growing child. george augustus’s eldest son was john gerson eliezar kolbe, born 7 july 1822 — eight years old in august 1830, and the man who would die a commandant on the farm leeuwberg in 1868. if that is who “john” is, this letter is the earliest document in this archive that mentions him, and it mentions him growing out of a coat.

and in august 1830 he was the only john in that house. the settler named a later son john too — and that child was born in 1834 and died in 1835, four years after this letter was written. there is no other candidate.

“his old father” is the remaining difficulty, and it is not glossed over: the writer is the boy’s grandfather. it may be a german-speaker’s english for the old man of the family, or a word this archive cannot resolve at this resolution. the identification is an inference and is marked as one — but the household has only one john in it. inference
a year of newspapers, and who read them

“i have also enclosed a set of newspapers of last year, with the exception of the one of the 4th of decr last, which cannot be found, supposing that henry, who has them every week, after i have done with them, — has lost.”

the household read a paper weekly; the father first and then henry; a year of them was kept and packed for the cape; and one number had gone astray and the blame was placed, mildly, on a son who had four months to live when the sentence was written. it is the only description this archive has of what anybody in that house did with an ordinary evening.
and the house had friends, who have names
the archive has had this family entirely through official paper — rate books, a census, the gazette, a burial register. the letter carries the first names of people who simply knew them:

mr & mrs stanhope, who “desire their best regards to your family”. mr warner, who asked that his and mrs warner’s best regards be presented. mrs field and her daughters — and “the eldest, miss mary, that was, has married a mr bellew, a surgeon, whom i do not know whether you may recollect”.

a marriage in another family, reported across six thousand miles because the two households knew each other. none of these five people is anywhere else in this archive, and a surgeon named bellew marrying a miss mary field about 1829 or 1830 is a searchable thing.
“whether there is any truth in a story published in a work called the mirror”

this archive summarised this as a baboon story he wants fact-checked. it is two pages long, and it is the strangest thing in the letter. a scottish colonist — “i believe his name to have been either williams, or williamson” — settled close to the xhosa. orang-outangs raid his fruit; his servants drive them off and he shoots a young one, which turns out to be a chief’s son. weeks later mrs w. is carried off. he suspects a xhosa chief who had earlier offered oxen and “2 or 3 of his finest caffre women” in exchange for her and been refused, and whose messenger had said, shaking his head, “you will repent of your obstinacy”. he gets a company of soldiers under capt johnson and is on the point of war when a man is produced who saw a large orang-outang carrying a woman across the river. the chief then furnishes men of his own to help find her, and after nearly two years she is recovered, living among the animals as their queen, with the son also carried off.
the father’s own verdict, and it is the reason this belongs on the page:

“here we look upon the story as a fictious & romance, but it is by some inserted … as a true story… should there be any thing like truth in it, i should think that you should have heard something at least about it, & therefore i should be glad to hear from you, whether that report may be founded in truth, or falsehood.”

a seventy-year-old tailor in london, reading a cheap weekly, declines to believe a sensational story about africa and writes to the one person he knows who is actually there to ask whether it is true. there is no better description of what this archive tries to do, and it was in the first document it ever found that he wrote. the mirror of literature, amusement, and instruction ran from 1822 and is digitised; the number carrying this is now on the work list. to find

what it still does not say. no street address, as before — the margins of pages two and four carry notes about how to direct the box, naming the revd mr murray and dr philip, and they are written across the fold and are partly illegible. they are the only lines in four pages this archive has not been able to read, and they are not guessed at here.
the second attachment — a historian’s draft, and the two things in it that are wrong

melanie geustyn sent two files. the first was msb 751 itself. the second was a two-page afrikaans typescript headed msb 751 … for dsab / voorlopige teks — a draft entry for the dictionary of south african biography, initialled and dated 18/2/92. it is a secondary work, and this archive does not take secondary works as evidence. it is something better: a reading list, by somebody who had been to the archives this family has never reached.

the typescript carries no name, only the initials ks and the date 18/2/92. this archive worked out from the inside that it had to be karel schoeman — the bethanie claim in it has one published source, schoeman’s die huis van die armes (1985), and the paper was typed at the south african library where schoeman worked — and then published that as an inference it would not assert.

it did not need to. the library had already said so, in the email that carried the file. melanie geustyn, who had the background file open in front of her: “i am also sharing with you a two page document that was written for the dsab (dictionary of south african biography) which was in the background file. the author, ks, would be dr. karel schoeman who worked here at the national library. he includes a list of bronne (sources).” this archive read the two attachments and not the sentence they were attached to. corrections →

note her “would be”. it is a librarian’s hedge and it is the right one: the initials are an identification, not a signature, and she is reading them the same way this archive did — only with the institution’s own knowledge behind her. so: written by karel schoeman, on the word of the library that holds the file, and still not signed. the background file, she adds, holds nothing further about the donation or about any other deposit by dr griffiths — which closes a question the enquiry asked.
what matters even so is not who wrote it but how it behaves when it is checked, and this archive is in the rare position of being able to check it.
nine things it says that this archive already knew — by nine other roads
¦the entry this archive held on
¦born 7.12.1802; “his death notice and his gravestone both confirm” 1802 born 7 dec 1802, baptised 2 feb 1803 — the same day, to the day the westminster register and the karoo gravestone
¦j.g.e. kolbe (1822–68) born 7 jul 1822, died 3 apr 1868 the grahamstown journal obituary
¦j.g.e. at leeuberg, famed as a commandant “death of commandant kolbe”; farm fixed two hours from bloemfontein an 1870 auction advertisement
¦margaret downing (1803–1867) born 23 feb 1803, died 25 nov 1867 the monument, and her death notice for the day the stone has lost
¦married at london, 1819, very young the 1819 allegation — married at sixteen on a sworn falsehood the marriage allegation
¦trade on the settler roll: apothecary “george augustus kolbe, pharmacist” the nlsa catalogue
¦the farm wurthemberg, dist. colesberg “his farm, wirtemberg, near the orange river” the obituary
¦ten children “has left a widow and ten children” the obituary
¦at philippolis from march 1831 a daughter born at philippolis in 1831 the register
nine agreements, every one reached from a different direction. it is careful work, and that is what makes the tenth line worth the whole exercise.
the first error — “a german apothecary resident in london”

he was a tailor. not by inference — by one hundred and twenty-one westminster rate book entries, the printed roll of 234 master tailors of 1799, the master tailors’ list of april 1834, three london gazette partnership dissolutions every one of which reads tailors, the occupation column of the 1841 census, the westminster burial register, and his own son’s deposition on oath at the old bailey in 1819: “my father is a tailor, and lives in church-street, soho.”
the german is right. the london is right. the trade is the son’s, moved one generation up — george augustus sailed as an apothecary, and the apothecary has been handed to his father.

this is the whole value of the document. the entry is accurate wherever its author had a record in front of him. the single thing he had no record for is the thing he got wrong here — and this archive can only say so because it spent a day in the westminster rate books. a secondary work is a reading list, not a witness. church street south →
the second error — and it is in the source he lists first
“hy het tien kinders nagelaat, alhoewel sy sterftekennis slegs agt vermeld” — he left ten children, although his death notice records only eight.

the death notice names ten. this archive has read it, photographed the detail and the whole sheet, and published the transcription: kab mooc 6/9/35: 7698 (1845), made at colesberg in january 1845 and signed m. kolbe by his widow. it is source number one on his own list. the notice →

so the count of thirteen — ten left, eight on the notice, three dead as infants — rests on a miscount and does not stand as published. ten is what the notice says and ten is what the obituary says. whether three more died as infants is a separate claim, and this archive has no source for it either way. that the error sits in the one document he cites first, and that this archive could only see it because it had ordered the same document, is the argument of this whole page in a line.
what it settles, and what it corrects
wurtemberg is knapdaar
the entry’s heading kills him at knapdaar. its body explains why: “die plaas wurthemberg (soms ook aangegee as knapdaar)” — two names for one farm.

this archive had both names and did not know they were one place. the 1844 obituary says “his farm, wirtemberg”; his own death notice says he died “at knapdaar, in the field cornetcy of rhenosterberg”. two documents, two names, run together on this site into a single address that nothing actually supported. schoeman says in terms that they are the same farm — which is the difference between an assumption and a statement. resolved
msb 751 is not a letter “on his ordination”

the catalogue said it was, and this archive repeated the catalogue. the entry dates the ordination to 25 may 1833 — nearly three years after the letter — and the letter itself says he had been “fully accepted… as one of their missionaries”.
three steps, now in order: mission assistant 8 feb 1828 · accepted as a missionary aug 1830 · ordained 25 may 1833. the letter and the entry date each other. corrections →
nine years of his life that this archive did not have
published here as what the entry says, every line of it untested:
boesmanskool, 8 february 1828
accepted by the lms as a mission assistant and placed at the new station boesmanskool — the present bethulie — across the orange, with james clark, among the san.

boesmanskool is literally “bushman school”, which is what john montgomery called what he saw, in english, forty-five years afterwards. they are not the same place — montgomery’s was at koolskop where colesberg now stands, and this is across the river — and this archive is not going to weld them because the words match. open
among the slaves, from about 1824
four years with the graaff-reinetse zendelings genootschap, working among the slaves of the district, until the society could no longer afford him and merged with the lms.
this archive had nothing at all for 1820–1828 but one old man’s memory. untested
november 1828 — and it is in print
a journey with melvill to the caledon river valley, as far as present-day ladybrand: the earliest journey in the present free state of which a written record survives, and he wrote it.
the dsab cites it as an 1829 journal extract. it has now been run to ground, and the hunt turned up more than the citation. found
1836 — the accusation, the inquiry and the acquittal

at philippolis, with the station split between griqua and baster and his marriage under strain, kolbe was accused in 1836 of adultery with the wife of one of his congregation — a charge, the entry says, “often used as a means of revenge against missionaries of the period”. h. hendricks, secretary of the griqua council, led the agitation. an inquiry by the neighbouring french missionaries acquitted him. his younger colleague t. atkinson went on opposing him from august 1836; he left the station in march 1837, and on 19 june 1837 the lms dismissed him.

this archive held none of it. it is one sentence in a draft, about a man who cannot answer, and it is set down here in full because the alternative — keeping the founding of bethanie and quietly dropping the accusation — would be the worst thing this archive could do with a source. he was accused, he was investigated, and he was cleared. all three belong on the page. the captaincy’s own papers now say it too

the papers that would test it are the griqua council’s own — and they are printed: karel schoeman (ed.), griqua records: the philippolis captaincy, 1825–1861, van riebeeck society ii/25, 162 documents including the correspondence between the captaincy’s officials and the missionaries. it was published after this typescript was typed, which is why its own author could not cite it. this page said “two years after” until 11 october 2026, when the catalogue record was read: it gives 1996, which is four.
the journal of 1828, run to ground — and the man it is addressed to

the dsab gives it as “extract from the journal of messrs melvill and kolbe…”, transactions of the missionary society (1829), and searching under kolbe found nothing at all. the reason is that the printed version is filed under the other man’s name.

“extracts of the journal of messrs melvill and kolbe, addressed to the rev. richard miles, superintendent of the society’s missions in africa, philippolis, 25 nov. 1828”, council for world missions (london missionary society) archives. an edited version, dated 18 nov. 1828, appears in melvill (1829).
the citation as it is given in the scholarship — eldredge, sources of conflict in southern africa, c. 1800–30 (1992), and again in eldredge and morton, slavery in south africa.

so: the manuscript is at soas, in the cwm archive — which is source 4 on the dsab’s own list, two lines above source 6, and the entry never says they are the same document. and legassick quotes it: melvill and kolbe travelled to the caledon and met refugee groups with “no other means of subsistence than the wild animals found in these parts” — the first words of george augustus kolbe’s that this archive has ever read. they are about famine.

and the journey is printed in full, in english, in a book still in the shops. karel schoeman (ed.), early white travellers in the transgariep, 1819–1840 (pretoria: protea book house, 2003), page 30: “the journey of john melvill and g.a. kolbe from philippolis to the caledon (1828)”. an edited collection of the travellers’ own texts. that is the fourth schoeman title standing behind this one one typescript, and it is the one that would put his own account of the journey on this page. to buy
“mr miles had called at our house”
the letter of 23 august 1830, in the tailor’s own hand, opens by telling his son how the news reached london:
“mr miles had called at our house & informed me that you had been fully accepted by the [l.m.s.] as one of their missionaries…”

this archive read that as a name and moved on. the journal of 1828 is addressed to the rev. richard miles, superintendent of the society’s missions in africa — and richard miles, formerly pastor of brigg in lincolnshire, was sent to cape town to act as dr philip’s substitute while philip was in england. philip was in england from 1826; miles was acting superintendent at the cape in 1828, which is why kolbe addressed his journal to him there; and by 1830 philip was back and miles was in london, where he called at a tailor’s house in soho.

the lms official kolbe reported to from philippolis is, very probably, the man who knocked on his father’s door with the news. the 1830 letter says only “mr miles” and gives him no forename, so this is an identification and not a document — but the office, the continent and the dates all fit, and the same letter has dr philip carrying the previous letter out. two documents six thousand miles and two years apart, and the same two men are moving between them. inference, stated as one
and there may be a face
this archive holds no likeness of anybody in it born before 1850. the entry ends by naming two:

a portrait of kolbe as a young man, in 1992 in the possession of a descendant, c.j. du plessis of ruigtevlei, district bethulie, and reproduced in burger olivier, so onthou ons die oewerbewoners van ou “grootrivier” (bloemfontein, 1973).

a watercolour by charles bell of a church service at philippolis in 1834 with kolbe in the pulpit — africana museum, johannesburg, reproduced in the journal of andrew smith, ed. william f. lye (cape town: balkema, 1975).
a book of 1973 and a museum catalogue are both reachable. the second would be a picture of this family’s ancestor at work, drawn from life, in the year after he was ordained.
and it is catalogued in edinburgh, under the wrong denomination

the entry sends the reader to johannesburg. the picture is also in scotland. the university of edinburgh, centre for the study of world christianity, holds cswc 60 — five photographs, 1834–1840, “photograph copies of sketches by the south african artist c. bell of african congregations”. item 3 is “mr. kolbe”, “at philippolis in 1834”.

the five are james archbell (wesleyan), william edwards (london missionary society), kolbe, jean-pierre pellissier (paris mission), and a service at ebenezer on the elephants river. pellissier is source 9 on the dsab’s own list — the bethulie missionary whose biography the entry cites. the same small circle, a hundred and ninety years later, five photographs in a scottish archive.

edinburgh calls him “a moravian missionary?” — with the question mark, so the catalogue already doubts itself. he was london missionary society, and this archive holds two independent documents that say so: the catalogue of msb 751 at the national library of south africa, and his own father’s letter of 23 august 1830, which reports him “fully accepted by the [l.m.s.] as one of their missionaries”. this archive can correct a university catalogue, and intends to write and do it. the work list →
edinburgh holds photograph copies; the dsab puts the original watercolour in the africana museum, johannesburg. two institutions, one picture, and neither catalogue mentions the other.

the story the tailor asked his son to check — found, and it is a novel

two of the four pages of the letter of 23 august 1830 go on a story its writer had read and did not believe. this archive searched for it on google books, on the open web and on the internet archive, five ways, and recorded a clean negative. on 21 september it was found by downloading the volumes and reading them.
spirit of the public journals
a singular letter from southern africa.
communicated by mr. hogg, the ettrick shepherd.
the mirror of literature, amusement, and instruction, volume xiv (1829), pages 313–318.

it is fiction, and by a famous hand. “mr hogg, the ettrick shepherd” is james hogg — the author of the private memoirs and confessions of a justified sinner, walter scott’s friend and rival. the mirror reprinted his tale as though it were a letter home from a settler, which is exactly how the tailor read it, and exactly why he wrote to the one man he knew who was actually there.
every detail in the letter is in the story
¦the letter, 23 august 1830 hogg, 1829

¦“a caffre chief who had sent… for his wife, offering in exchange some oxen, & 2 or 3 of his finest caffre women” the chief karoo offers four oxen, then “ten cows and a bull for my wife, and a choice virgin to boot”
¦the messenger said “you will repent of your obstinacy” “telling me i was the son of foolishness, and that he foretold i should repent it”
¦“capt johnson the officer” and a company of soldiers captain johnstone, and “nine british soldiers” in a party of nearly a hundred
¦mrs w. carried off across the river by orang-outangs “he himself saw my wife carried across the river by a band of pongos, (ourang-outangs)”
¦found “as the queen” of the animals, with the son also taken “the great spirit had sent them a queen from the country beyond the sun” — and the boy william is with them

and the one detail he got wrong explains itself. he wrote: “a scottish colonist … i believe his name to have been either williams, or williamson.” the narrator has no name at all — the piece is addressed “my dear friend” and signed by nobody. his son is called william. a man recalling a magazine story a year later took the child’s name for the family’s, which is the most ordinary mistake a reader can make and is the reason five searches for williams and williamson found nothing.

he was right, and he was right for the right reason. “here we look upon the story as a fictious & romance, but it is by some inserted… as a true story… i should be glad to hear from you, whether that report may be founded in truth, or falsehood.” a seventy-year-old tailor in soho, reading a cheap weekly, declined to believe a sensational story about africa and wrote to the one person he knew who could check it. it was by one of the most celebrated authors in britain, printed as a genuine letter, and he was not taken in. this archive spent a day and five failed searches proving he was right. found
the tailor’s own marriage — searched properly, and it is not there

this archive has said for a fortnight that “her surname before marriage is not known and no marriage has been found”, and separately carried “mary larman” off the family tree. on 20 september it corrected a page that had welded the two together. then it went and looked, with a tool it did not have before.
findmypast’s spouselastname filter, both directions, whole life events collection:
¦kolbe × nonsense (control) 0 — the filter is working
and the control that makes the nil mean something

a nil return is worth nothing until a control shows the search works — which is this archive’s own rule, written on /method/. the control here is a marriage this archive already knows about: the eldest kolbe daughter married george kottlich kohlbeck at st anne’s, soho in 1811.
1810 · kohlbeck · st anne, soho, middlesex, england · westminster banns
the banns are indexed, a year before the wedding, in the family’s own parish. so findmypast’s coverage reaches this household, this church and this period. the larman zero is not a hole in the index.
which leaves three doors, and one of them is closed by an act of parliament

the obvious thought is that a german family buried its dead in the german lutheran church — this archive has five of them in tna rg 4/4631 — so perhaps it married there too, outside the anglican indexes.

it could not have. under hardwicke’s marriage act of 1753 — the same act this archive already invokes for the sworn ages at shoreditch in 1819 — every marriage in england except those of quakers and jews had to be performed in an anglican parish church to be legal at all. foreign protestant congregations were not exempt. a german lutheran couple marrying in england between 1754 and 1836 married in a parish church, and the entry is in a parish register.
the savoy congregation could bury them and baptise them. it could not marry them.
so three possibilities remain, and they are not equally likely:
the marriage is in an english parish findmypast does not index. possible — the london coverage is wide but not complete.

“larman” is wrong. the archive’s own person record has always said her surname is not known, and the name comes from the family tree and from nowhere else read here. today the same tree was caught giving margaret downing’s mother two different surnames in two different versions, so it is not a careful witness about maiden names.

they did not marry in england. he was born in württemberg in 1765 and his birth county is entered as “foreign” in the 1841 census in his own words. the first child of the house was baptised in london in 1792, when he was twenty-seven. where he was before that, this archive does not know — and a marriage in a german state would be in a german register, indexed nowhere this archive has looked.

the gain is not a fact, it is a narrowing. before today “no marriage has been found” was a shrug. it is now a negative with a control behind it and three named doors left, one of which — the german lutheran register — has been closed by reading the law rather than by searching anything. the next place to look is not another english index. it is württemberg. narrowed
looking for a downing–pooley marriage — and finding that two trees cannot agree what she was called

the familysearch tree gave margaret downing’s mother as mary king pooley, a name this archive had never held. the obvious thing to do with a new name is look for a marriage under it, so findmypast’s whole life events collection was swept for one.
devon marriages and banns · gbprs/m/514168016/1
john downing married mary pooley
10 may 1802 · welcombe (bishop’s transcripts), devon · anglican
transcriptions © devon family history society

it is the only downing–pooley marriage before civil registration in the entire collection — against 231,425 downing records and 65,460 pooley records. twelve records match the pair at all; three are indexed marriages, and the other two are 1882 and 1955.
the date works, and only just. margaret georgina elizabeth downing was born 23 february 1803. a marriage on 10 may 1802 is nine months and thirteen days earlier — exactly right for a first child.

the county is the right one. this archive’s own family tree puts the downings in devon: edward downing (1700–1792) m. mary heard; thomas downing (1736–1801) m. mary trick; john trick m. margaret hooper. trick, heard and hooper are devon names, and welcombe is a north devon parish on the cornish border. the tree and the register agree about the county without either knowing about the other.

margaret was born in london. a couple married in a remote north devon parish in may 1802 with a child in london nine months later is possible — people move — but it is not what the record says, and nothing here shows them moving.
john downing and mary pooley are not rare names, and this is a name match and a date. it is what this archive calls a candidate, not a finding.

no baptism has been found for margaret downing in london in 1803. the collection was searched and returns nothing of the kind — which matters, because a baptism naming both parents is the document that would settle this outright, and its absence is why the marriage cannot be tied to her.

and then the archive’s own tree contradicted the one that started this. the familysearch family tree calls her mary king pooley. the family tree this archive was built from calls her mary p king — surname king, with an initial.

so the “p” may be pooley, or “pooley” may be a later reading of the “p”. two collaborative trees, one woman, and they cannot agree whether she was a king or a pooley. neither can settle it, and the search that was launched on one of them was looking for a surname that may not be hers.
they disagree about her husband too: john paul downing is 1769–1839 in one and 1765–1839 in the other.
the baptism that would settle it — and why its absence proves little

one document ends the welcombe question: a london baptism for margaret georgina elizabeth downing in 1803, naming both parents. her monument at burgersdorp says she was “born in london 23 february 1803”, so it should exist.
¦margaret downing, baptism, 1801–1805 5 — two in edinburgh, three at madeley, shropshire (one event indexed three times)
¦nonsense forename (control) 0 — the filter restricts

this archive first published the wrong conclusion here, within the hour, and the way it went wrong is worth more than the result. widen the search to every downing baptism in england for 1800–1806 and findmypast returns 1,131, of which almost none are in london. that was read as a failure of coverage — “a picture of the index, not of london” — and the nil was declared worthless.
that was the wrong control. counting one surname by county tests where the downings were. it does not test whether the index covers london at all. the right control is a common name.
¦baptisms, 1800–1806 in the collection london in a sample of 100

thirty-seven per cent of smith baptisms in those seven years are london, middlesex or westminster. the coverage is excellent. so the near-absence of london downings is not the index failing — it is that there were very few downings in london.

which means the nil is real, and it points the other way from the one this archive published. margaret downing was born in london on 23 february 1803, the index covers london baptisms well, and there is no baptism for her. either she was not baptised in an anglican london parish, or her family was not a london family.

and that strengthens welcombe rather than weakening it. a couple married in a north devon parish in may 1802, with a child born in london in february 1803 and no london baptism and no london kin in the registers, is exactly what a family newly arrived from the country looks like. candidate, strengthened
and a check on this archive’s own reasoning, which failed

the welcombe case rested partly on county: the family tree puts the downings in devon through trick, heard and hooper, and welcombe is a north devon parish. it was worth asking whether the surname itself is a west country surname, because if it were, that would strengthen the case considerably.

it is not. a sample of 160 of those 1,131 baptisms, tallied by county: yorkshire (west riding) 20, suffolk 16, norfolk 16, cornwall 14, staffordshire 9, yorkshire 9, shropshire 7, devon 5. downing is a national name, and the west country is about an eighth of it, behind yorkshire.

so the devon argument stands only on the tree’s own specific ancestry — edward downing and mary heard, thomas downing and mary trick — and gains nothing at all from the geography of the surname. this archive tested its own inference and took half of it back.
withdrawn — they stayed in devon
the candidate raised this morning, strengthened at lunchtime, is dead by the evening, and it was killed by the simplest question available: did the welcombe couple stay?
every downing record in the parish of welcombe, in order:

1792 ann burial · 1792 william marriage · 1793 thomas baptism · 1795 damaris baptism · 1798 mary baptism · 1800 peter burial · 1801 philip baptism · 1802 john marriage · 1803 john baptism · 1806 william baptism · 1809 emmey baptism · 1810 elizabeth baptism · … · 1834 mary burial · 1839 john burial

they married at welcombe in may 1802 and baptised a child at welcombe in 1803, and more in 1806, 1809 and 1810. margaret georgina elizabeth downing was born in london on 23 february 1803. the welcombe couple never went anywhere. the pooleys are equally rooted there — baptisms in 1792, 1801 and 1813, a burial in 1810. withdrawn
and the last line of that list is the interesting one: a mary downing buried at welcombe in 1834. both family trees give margaret’s mother as dying in 1834.

that is almost certainly where “pooley” came from. a researcher looking for margaret downing’s parents finds one downing–pooley marriage in all of england, and a mary downing burial in the very year they wanted, in the same small parish — and attaches both. it is exactly the search this archive ran today, reaching exactly the same two records, and stopping one question earlier.

so “mary king pooley, 1768–1834” is most likely not a record at all. it is a previous researcher’s reconstruction — which would also explain why this archive’s own copy of the tree calls her mary p king instead: two compilers, the same fragments, two different guesses. margaret downing still has no mother, and the position is now better understood than it was this morning.
so the other surname was swept too — and a better tool was found

if she may have been a king rather than a pooley, the same sweep had to be run under king. searching for “king” as a keyword returns 144 records for 1790–1806 and almost every one of them is king’s lynn — a surname that is also half a place-name poisons the field completely.

the marriage transcripts carry spousefirstname and spouselastname, and spouselastname turns out to work as a real filter — a nonsense value returns nothing, which is the test this archive insists on before trusting a narrow count. run properly:
¦downing × pooley, all years 3 — welcombe 1802, penzance 1882, birmingham 1955
¦downing × king, 1790–1806 3 — and all three are one norfolk event indexed three times: a mary downing, at king’s lynn and norwich in 1790
¦either surname, nonsense control 0

a mary downing marrying a king in norfolk in 1790 is the wrong person in the wrong county in the wrong direction. under either surname, there is no london marriage for a john downing in the years this family needs. the welcombe entry of 1802 remains the only candidate in england.

her own death notice is still the only document in this archive that was ever asked about her parents, and it answered “both dead” and gave no names. that remains the position. a welcombe marriage of 1802 is now on the work list as a candidate to be tested — by the welcombe register itself, by a london baptism for margaret in 1803, or by a burial for a mary downing at the right date. nothing has been adopted, and the person record still has no mother. candidate
a collaborative tree names the commandant’s twelve — and two of its claims are already on this site

this archive does not take family trees as evidence, and it is not about to start. but there is a difference between a tree that is your own work read back to you and a tree compiled by strangers that turns out to agree with documents you hold — and the test for the second is the same as for a historian’s draft: check it where you can, before you believe it anywhere.
frederik fortunatus kolbe · birth 22 october 1857, bloemfontein · death 18 december 1930, bloemfontein
son of commandant.gen. john gherson eliezer kolbe and anna jacoba kolbe
husband of maria petronella elizabeth antoinette kolbe

father of maria francina; annie nelson marais; john gerson eliezar; francis elizabeth krone; rosa magdalene styger; magdalena jacoba; ada francis styger; petronella antoinetta botha; maria margaretha downing rousseau; frederik fortunatus; andries rowan
brother of catharina wilhelmina magdalena pienaar anderson; george augustus kolbe; general willem johannes kolbe; jan hendrik kolbe; petrus jacobus (pieter) kolbe and 6 others
geni, added 2014, four profile managers, one source attached. it is a collaborative tree and nothing about it is documentary.
why this is not the same as the last tree

a search on another member of this family returned her parents through myheritage, and that was this family’s own tree handed back to it — circular, and worth nothing as corroboration. this is not that. the commandant’s twelve children have never been in this archive at all; his obituary counts them and names none, and the work list has carried a row for two weeks asking for vab mhg m777, his widow’s estate, on the ground that it is “the document that would name the twelve”. a stranger’s tree naming them is independent of anything here.
and it agrees with two documents this archive reached by another road
a baptism register, 1890
this archive holds, from the bloemfontein register: a rosa magdalena kolbe baptised in 1890 to frederik fortuna kolbe and maria petronella elizabeth antoinetta mccabe.

the profile gives this man’s wife as maria petronella elizabeth antoinette and his daughter as rosa magdalene. wife and daughter, both, against a register entry the tree’s compilers are most unlikely to have seen.
an estate index, 1968
this archive holds tab mhg 5450/68 — rousseau, surviving spouse maria margaretha downing rousseau, picked up in a sweep for the downing forename and never attached to anybody.
the profile lists maria margaretha downing rousseau as his daughter. that is an orphan reference in this archive acquiring a father.

two independent hits is not proof and this archive is not adopting twelve people on it. what it is, is the same thing schoeman’s bibliography was: a list worth working. the difference between a tree and a source is not that one is always wrong — it is that one has to be tested and the other has already been.
what it would answer, if it holds

the twelve. the commandant died on 3 april 1868 leaving eight sons and four daughters, and this archive could put a hand on two. the profile names six siblings and says there are six more — among them a general willem johannes kolbe, which is a rank, and therefore findable in a way a farmer is not.

the kolbe–mccabe question, which this archive raised and could not settle. it wrote of the 1890 baptism: “a second kolbe–mccabe marriage in the same small free state world, and this archive does not yet know whether that is a coincidence.” if this profile is right, it is not a coincidence: the commandant’s widow anna jacoba van der merwe married francis mccabe, landdrost of bloemfontein, about april 1871 — and her son married a mccabe. stepmother and daughter-in-law out of the same family.

a fourth frederik fortunatus. this one is born 1857 at bloemfontein and dead there in 1930. he is not the settler’s tenth child (born 1839 at bethulie, died 1929 at utrecht), and not frederick fortunatus downing kolbe (died 1918, tab mhg 40293). this archive has already had to withdraw a claim once over two men sharing a name in one town, and it is going to be slower this time, not faster.

the document that tests all of it is still the one on the work list. vab mhg m777 at bloemfontein — the 1896 estate of anna jacoba van der merwe, filed under her second husband’s name mccabe, which would name her surviving children as of that year. a tree says twelve names; an estate file proves them. what has changed today is that the file now has something to be checked against, which is a better position to order a document from than an empty page. the work list →
the kolbe–mccabe “coincidence” is a stepbrother marrying a stepsister

this archive raised the question itself and could not answer it. of a baptism at bloemfontein it wrote: “a second kolbe–mccabe marriage in the same small free state world, and this archive does not yet know whether that is a coincidence.” the answer was already in two of its own files, and it took a stranger’s tree to make them speak to each other.
¦held here what it says
¦a baptism register bloemfontein, 1890 — rosa magdalena kolbe, to frederik fortuna kolbe and maria petronella elizabeth antoinetta mccabe
¦an estate index vab mhg c129 — francis mccabe, landdrost of bloemfontein, 1872, naming both his wives: maria petronella elisabetha antoinetta raath and anna, born van der merwe

¦an obituary mccabe “married his second wife about ten months since — the widow of the late commandant j.g.e. kolbe”, and died on 23 february 1872 leaving “four sons and two daughters, besides a large family of step-children”

read those three together and the four-part name does the work. maria petronella elisabetha antoinetta is not a name that recurs by chance. francis mccabe’s first wife was a raath of that name; a mccabe of that same name married a kolbe and had a child baptised at bloemfontein in 1890. she is his daughter, named for her mother entire — which is the naming habit this archive has documented across four families.

so the sequence is this. commandant j.g.e. kolbe dies on 3 april 1868, leaving anna jacoba van der merwe and twelve children. she marries francis mccabe, a widower with six children of his own, about april 1871. he dies ten months later. and on 8 november 1880, at bloemfontein, one of her sons marries one of his daughters.

two households were one household for less than a year, and a marriage came out of it nine years afterwards. that is not a coincidence in a small world. it is what happens when children are thrown together and then orphaned twice over.

what is documented and what is not. the 1890 baptism is a register entry; c129 is an estate index; the obituary is a newspaper. all three are held here. the one link that is not documented is that the frederik fortunatus who married her is the commandant’s son — that comes from user trees and is not adopted. vab mhg c129 would settle it by naming mccabe’s daughters, and it has just become a more valuable document than it was this morning. one link from a tree
two marriages, not one — and the widow’s own is now dated

the kolbe–mccabe question was answered above from an estate index and a baptism register, with one link borrowed from a user tree. on 21 september it was searched in the civil and church registers directly, and it turns out to be larger than the thing this archive was arguing about.
¦date entry collection
¦13 july 1871 anna jacoba kolbe, bride, born 1825 — spouse francis mccabe, free state south africa, civil marriage records, 1801–1974
¦4 june 1872 jan hendrik kolbe, groom, born 1849 — spouse rose maria mccabe, bloemfontein south africa, civil marriage records, 1801–1974

¦— john henry kolbe and rosa maria mccabe, as parents of john gerson eliezer, elizabeth magdalena, ada francis, anna jacoba free state dutch reformed church records, 1848–1956

two of the commandant’s sons married two of francis mccabe’s daughters. this archive wrote of one such marriage that it “does not yet know whether that is a coincidence”. two is not a coincidence. it is a stepfamily marrying within itself, and the household that produced it lasted seven months.

and jan hendrik married four months after his stepfather died. francis mccabe died on 23 february 1872; the marriage is 4 june 1872. john henry is jan hendrik anglicised — the same man under two spellings, as this archive has seen across four families — and his eldest son is named john gerson eliezer, which is the commandant’s name entire. that is the strongest thing yet said, from a register rather than a tree, that these are the commandant’s sons.

and a date this archive had only by inference is now written down. it had the remarriage from mccabe’s obituary, which said he “married his second wife about ten months since” before dying on 23 february 1872 — giving about april 1871. the civil register says 13 july 1871. seven months, not ten. a journalist rounding, again, which is the second time on this site that an obituary’s interval has been out by the same kind of margin. dated
these are index entries from named collections, not images read. the images would give ages, fathers and witnesses, and are the obvious next step.
and the familysearch family tree, which this archive had never opened

it uses familysearch constantly and had never once looked at the tree. every familysearch citation on this site is a record — an indexed register entry with an ark. the family tree is a different thing, a single collaborative tree the whole site edits, and /sources/ lists it among the leads. nobody here had opened it. david did, and sent the link.

the pedigree at ljny-blp runs straight up this archive’s own spine: frederick fortunatus kolbe (1859–1930) → john gerson eliezar kolbe, 1822–1868 → george augustus kolbe, 1802–1844 → john gottlob kolbe, 1765–1845. three generations whose dates this archive established from an obituary, a death notice, a census, a will and a burial register — and the tree has them right.
