¦pieter gerhardus cloete rousseau, 1898–1968, husband of margaretha maria downey kolbe tab mhg 5450/68 — rousseau, surviving spouse maria margaretha downing rousseau, 1968. the estate year is his death year.
¦rosa magdalena kolbe, 1890–1946 her baptism at bloemfontein in 1890, to frederik fortuna kolbe and maria petronella elizabeth antoinetta mccabe

two orphan index references in this archive have just acquired people, and a baptism has acquired a death. none of that makes the tree evidence — it makes it a lead list that has now passed the same test three times.
and two places it disagrees, one of which it loses
mary larman, and a burial register
familysearch gives her as 1768–1819. this archive holds tna rg 4/4631 folio 62: died 2 august 1814, buried 5 august, aged 46.

the register wins, and it is not close. a tree’s death year against a burial entry that gives the day, the burial and the age is no contest — and her surname remains tree-only in any case, which this archive corrected itself about earlier today.
two trees, two birth years
geni gives frederik fortunatus kolbe as born 22 october 1857. familysearch gives 1859. two collaborative trees, two years, and no document behind either of them here.

which is the useful thing to notice: they are not independent witnesses corroborating each other. where they agree it may be because one copied the other; where they differ, neither can settle it. only the register can.

one genuinely new name, and it is tree-only. familysearch gives margaret downing’s mother as mary king pooley, 1768–1834, and her father as john paul downing, 1765–1839. margaret’s own death notice of 1867 says her parents were “both dead” and gives no names at all, so this archive has never had a mother for her. it still does not. but it now has a name to look for in the london registers, which is not nothing — and a downing–pooley marriage in the 1790s would be a document. from a user tree, not adopted
four journals in his own hand — and the catalogue names every one

this archive has spent the day working a historian’s reading list, and every road on it ended at the same door: the council for world mission archive at soas. the door turns out to be open, and the catalogue item-level.

until this afternoon, the sum of george augustus kolbe’s own words in this archive was one sentence, quoted at second hand in legassick. the soas catalogue returns sixty-two records on the surname, and among them:
¦reference what it is
¦cwm/lms/05/05/100 extracts from the journal of john melvill and george augustus kolbe, during a tour to the north-eastwards of philippolis, 13–22 nov 1828
¦cwm/lms/05/05/102 extracts from the journal of george augustus kolbe, philippolis, 1828–1831
¦cwm/lms/05/05/106 journal of george augustus kolbe, philippolis, 1831–1834
¦cwm/lms/05/05/108 journal of george augustus kolbe, philippolis, 6 oct 1832 – sep 1833

six years of a man’s life in his own writing, in a building in russell square. the first of them is source 6 on schoeman’s list — the printed extract this archive hunted all morning and could not find — and here is the manuscript behind it, with the days of the journey on it: 13 to 22 november 1828.
and the year of the accusation is a single box
¦cwm/lms/05/02/02/044 south africa, 1835 — the catalogue lists “george augustus kolbe, philippolis” among the correspondents. box 14b
¦cwm/lms/05/02/02/046 south africa, 1836, 4 jan – 29 dec. box 15
¦— the 1837 file, in the same box

1836 is the year of the adultery charge; 1837 is the year of the dismissal. the society’s incoming correspondence for southern africa is filed by year, and 1836–1837 is box 15. whatever the directors were actually told about h. hendricks’s agitation, about the french missionaries’ inquiry and about the acquittal, it is in that box — and this archive has been repeating a one-sentence summary of it since breakfast.
what else the search turned up

a portrait. cwm/lms/01/09/02/01/525, in the missionary portraits series — “sykes, charlotte née kolbe (s. africa 1858–1887)”. she is not this family’s charlotte: she is the sister of the rhenish missionary friedrich wilhelm kolbe, and the same afternoon’s work put that whole household outside this tree. recorded so that nobody here mistakes her for the settler’s daughter, as sibree did.

and friedrich wilhelm kolbe’s own career, in the society’s files: reports from paarl in 1867, 1868, 1870, 1871, 1872, 1873 and 1875 and from stellenbosch in 1876; incoming letters from him from george in 1854, paarl from 1858, cape town to 1899; and, in the file for 1893, “frederick kolbe, cape town — death of mrs kolbe [née isabella maria elliott]”, which matches the s2a3 entry to the person. a wrong man, confirmed wrong from four directions in one afternoon.

the letter is written. seven references, a stated reason for wanting 1836 and 1837, an offer to start with one item, and one question that needs no searching — whether candidate papers survive as a class, since frederick william kolbe’s would settle sibree’s error outright. drafted, not sent. the letters →
owen’s party on the nautilus — and the lie was still running
source 7 on schoeman’s list is m.d. nash, the settler handbook. its entry for owen’s party is published in full online, and it gives the roll as the colonial department had it.
kolbe, george augustus 20. chemist. w margaret 19.

he was sixteen. born 7 december 1802, he sailed from gravesend on 3 december 1819 — four days before his seventeenth birthday. she was sixteen, born 23 february 1803. the roll adds about three years to each of them.

and it is the second sworn falsehood about their ages in eleven months, and the two do not even agree with each other. at shoreditch on 20 january 1819 both swore they were “of the age of twenty-one years and upwards”, because under hardwicke’s act a minor could not marry by licence without a parent’s consent. anybody twenty-one and upwards in january 1819 is not twenty in december.

so they were not keeping a story straight. they were saying, each time, whatever the paper in front of them needed — old enough to marry without a father, old enough to be counted as a man on an emigration list. he was a sixteen-year-old married to a fifteen-year-old, and by the time they reached algoa bay they had told the british government two different untruths about it. the allegation →
what kind of party he joined

fifty-two people, no. 3 on the colonial department list, led by thomas owen of 9 carey street, horseferry road, westminster — a joint-stock party, probably recruited in london, whose correspondence with the department was handled by owen’s father, the rev j owen of fulham.

deposits were paid for eleven men. sailed gravesend 3 december 1819, table bay 17 march 1820, algoa bay 14 april 1820. located near the kap river, at a place they called spanish reed place, between the wellington and kap rivers.

a london tailor’s son joined a london party got up by a clergyman’s son from westminster. he did not go out among farmers. the trades in the list are a bricklayer, a ropemaker, a goldsmith, two edged-tool makers, a smith, three farmers — and one chemist.
and it fell apart almost at once

thomas owen — “this querulous man”, in special commissioner hayward’s words — refused to draw rations for his people, and his brother w.s. owen was appointed director in his place. thomas owen left the location early in 1821 and the party dispersed soon afterwards.

which is the whole explanation of the gap this archive has never been able to fill. he was eighteen, in a party that had lost its leader and its rations, on a location that no longer existed — and the next thing anybody records of him is the graaff-reinet mission, working among slaves, about three years later.

three cape archives references, and this archive is already writing to that building. nash’s sources for the party list are co 6137/1,4 (the list of settlers under thomas owen’s direction), co 8543 (special commissioner hayward’s notes) and co 3917 — the memorial of independent settlers aboard the nautilus. a memorial is a petition, and a petition is signed. that last one could carry george augustus kolbe’s signature at seventeen, which would be the earliest thing of his own hand anywhere. no agent of transports’ return has ever been traced for the nautilus, so the roll as it stands is the best there is.
the society’s own register — and it had been free all along

source 5 on schoeman’s list is james sibree, a register of missionaries, deputations, etc., from 1796 to 1923, 4th edition, london missionary society, 1923. this archive searched the internet archive for it, failed, and wrote it up as not found. it is a free pdf, 225 pages, at missiology.org.uk. the failed search looked in one place and reported a negative about the world.

278. kolbe, george augustus (8). was previously connected with the graaff reinet missionary society, and laboured among the slaves around graaff reinet. was accepted provisionally by mr. miles, feb. 8, 1829, which action was confirmed by the directors, july 29, 1829. first laboured with mr. clark, at the bushman station, caledon river. thence proceeded to philippolis, arriving there, march 13, 1831. on may 26, 1833, he was ordained by the french missionaries, messrs. lemue, pellisier, and arbousset. his connection was dissolved by the directors, june 19, 1837.
the whole of his mission life, in eight lines, compiled by the society that employed him. the index gives his service as 1829 – 1837.
it settles mr miles, and it settles the word “fully”

the letter of 23 august 1830 says “mr miles had called at our house & informed me that you had been fully accepted by the [l.m.s.] as one of their missionaries”. this archive published that identification as an inference two hours ago, on the ground that a rev. richard miles — acting superintendent of the lms at cape town from 1825, sent out to stand in for dr philip while philip was in britain — was the man kolbe addressed his 1828 journal to.
miles did not merely carry the news. miles is the man who accepted him. “accepted provisionally by mr. miles, feb. 8, 1829, which action was confirmed by the directors, july 29, 1829.”

and the father’s adverb is not decoration. provisionally by miles at the cape; confirmed by the directors in london; and a father told that his son had been “fully accepted”. the letter is using the society’s own vocabulary, correctly, because the officer concerned was standing in the room explaining it. settled
where the register and the dsab draft disagree

both are printed works and neither is the manuscript. but sibree is the society’s own record of its own officers, and schoeman was working sixty-nine years later. where they differ this archive gives both and prefers neither in print:
¦schoeman, 1992 sibree, 1923
¦graaff-reinet society, among the slaves of the district the same, in almost the same words
¦accepted 8 february 1828 accepted provisionally 8 february 1829, confirmed 29 july 1829
¦boesmanskool, the present bethulie, with james clark, among the san “mr. clark, at the bushman station, caledon river”
¦philippolis, march 1831 philippolis, 13 march 1831 — to the day
¦ordained 25 may 1833 by arbousset and casalis ordained 26 may 1833 by lemue, pellissier and arbousset — three men, and no casalis
¦dismissed 19 june 1837 “dissolved by the directors, june 19, 1837”
pellissier is source 9 on schoeman’s own list — s.h. pellissier’s life of jean pierre pellissier van bethulie. sibree puts pellissier at the ordination and schoeman does not.
and then the line that stops the page

522. kolbe, frederick william (22). born, nov. 3, 1821, in south africa. son of rev. g. a. kolbe (no. 278). had been connected with the rhenish mission in s. africa. in 1853 he was accepted by the l.m.s.… removed to paarl in 1856… retired from the pastorate at paarl in 1875… mr. kolbe died at cape town, dec. 25, 1899, aged 78. books written: an english-herero dictionary. cape town: j. c. juta, 1883.

schoeman writes: “f.w. kolbe (1821–99) van die rynse sendinggenootskap was nie aan hierdie familie verwant nie” — was not related to this family. he names the same man, the same society and the same two years, and cuts him off. the london missionary society’s own register makes him the settler’s son.

he is not the settler’s son. sibree is wrong, and schoeman is right. this archive published the contradiction as open two hours ago and then went and worked it, and it came apart quickly — because the register’s own arithmetic was already against it.

the chronology. sibree gives his birth as 3 november 1821, and his age at death agrees. the settler’s known eldest, john gerson eliezar kolbe, was born 7 july 1822, and his age at death agrees. eight months apart. they cannot both be margaret downing’s sons, and that alone meant the claim could not simply be believed.
and three independent works say who he actually was.
¦source what it says
¦new catholic encyclopedia, on his son mgr f.c. kolbe “he was the son of a westphalian (german) protestant missionary who had married the daughter of a member of the london missionary society.”
¦s2a3 biographical database, on his wife isabella maria elliott, daughter of rev. william elliott, “married reverend friedrich wilhelm kolbe, missionary and herero scholar, in cape town in 1849”.

¦dictionary of south african biography, vol. 5 (hsrc, 1987) carries its own entry on f.w. kolbe — which is why schoeman’s draft marks him with an asterisk, and it was in print five years before he wrote.

friedrich wilhelm, not frederick william. a rhenish missionary of the german form of the name, married at cape town in 1849, at okahandja in present namibia by april 1850, fled to otjikango when jonker afrikaner attacked the hereros in august 1850, back in the colony from 1852 — george, paarl, stellenbosch, cape town — and the father of monsignor f.c. kolbe. he has nothing to do with this family, and schoeman knew it because the dsab had already published him.
how the society came to misfile one of its own

sibree’s register has two kolbes in south africa: entry 278, rev. g. a. kolbe, and entry 522, frederick william. a compiler joined them. it is the same species of error as the one this page spent the morning on — schoeman giving the father the son’s trade — two adjacent facts welded because they looked like they belonged together.

and the lesson runs the other way from this morning’s. at breakfast this archive proved a historian wrong from primary documents it had ordered itself. by the afternoon it had proved the society’s own register wrong and the historian right. neither is a witness. both are reading lists. the only reason the claim was not swallowed is that this archive checked an arithmetic it could do from its own records before it checked anything else.
sibree’s charlotte kolbe, born 25 december 1829, “sister of rev. f. w. kolbe”, who married rev. william sykes at paarl in 1860, goes with him. she is not the settler’s daughter either. resolved
indwe and barkly east past 1910 — and most of what came back was already here

a work-list row has stood since 15 september: “the archive stops where its leads stopped… nobody has read what the register says after that.” it has now been read. the honest result is a small one, and the reason it is small is the interesting part.
indwe is a membership register, not a baptism register

the two entries this archive already had at indwe — willem hermanus booijzen confirmed 31 may 1907 and a mountjoy dying in 1911 — sit in the lidmate roll, the list of who joined the congregation. that is a different book from the baptisms and it is where a colliery town’s incomers are written down.
knowing which register holds your people is half of knowing where to read next.
the mountjoy has a joining date
johanna catharina mountjoy — membership at indwe, 23 july 1907. this archive had her death there in june 1911 and nothing before it.
she joined seven weeks after willem hermanus booijzen was confirmed in the same congregation, on 31 may 1907. two families this archive follows, in one small coal town’s register, in one winter.
it does not make them relatives. it makes them neighbours, which is a fact and was not one before.
a married surname for a barry daughter
catherine mary sophia barry baxter — born 1883 at barkly east, died 18 november 1914, probate 1916.
the forenames are this family’s exactly — there are already two women of that name here, of 1855 and 1859. a third, born 1883 at barkly east, who married a baxter.
probable, not proved. nothing read here names her parents.
and the rest of it was already in this archive

the barkly east sweep returned thirty-six entries dated after 1910 across five surnames. checked one by one against the register here, nearly all of them were already held: harriet louisa barry, dead at manor owen on 7 september 1912; henry james kolbe barry, whose 23 june 1939 is already on his record; john gerson eliazer barry; james jonathan mountjoy, dead at barkly east on 22 december 1937; and margaretha wilhelmina elizabeth mary kolbe, dead at manorowen on 2 august 1912.

that is worth saying rather than quietly not saying. a sweep that returns almost nothing new is a measurement of how thoroughly the ground was already worked, and this ground was worked properly. the work-list row assumed otherwise.

one discrepancy, recorded and not adopted. the index gives the matriarch as “margaret louisa elizabeth kolbe barry, birth 1831 believe colesberg”, where this archive has 1826. the hedge is the index’s own word. the death date agrees to the day. 1826 stands until something better than a hedged index entry moves it.

a booysen cluster at indwe, and it is not claimed. four booysen men join that congregation between 1925 and 1931 — david schalk (2 may 1925), piet frederick (14 may 1927), petrus jacobus (16 may 1931) and willem adriaan — and three couples baptise children there between 1929 and 1932. the forenames are this family’s forenames and the town is the town its miner worked in. but not one of the wives — rachel margarita marais, aletta fredrika jacoina coetzee, johanna catharina aletta greyling — is a name this archive holds, and a booysen at a cape colliery is not evidence of anything. written down so that somebody with a reason can come back to it, and claimed by nobody.

a near-miss worth recording, because it nearly went the other way. a first pass matched rachel margarita marais against this archive and reported her as already held. she is not. the match was on the fragment “rachel marg” hitting rachel margaretha williamse, a different woman on a 1900 death notice at pretoria. had it stood, an unrelated indwe household would have been welded to this family on three letters of a forename.
8 december 1956 · phthisis was not what killed him. it was what he was paid for.

this archive carried two causes of death for henry james booyzen and had read the document behind neither. a correspondent on g2g reported phthisis; the johannesburg burial register gave “coronary pulmonary sclerosis”. the note said, in terms, “the two causes are not the same word and this archive has read only one of the two documents.” here is the other one.
form of information of a death · aangifte van ’n sterfgeval
1. identity number — 331-452322
2–3. surname, first names — booyzen, henry james
4. date of death — 8th december, 1956
6. place of death — florence nightingale nursing home, johannesburg
10. occupation — retired miner of langlaagte
11. pensioner or recipient of maintenance allowance — phthisis
12. causes of death — cor pulmonale with silicosis.
contributing cause:— broncho pneumonia
13. duration of last illness — 2 years : 7 days
14. medical practitioner — dr. a. l. agranat
15. place of birth — cape province
16. residential address — 3 fifteenth avenue, mayfair, johannesburg
17. intended place of burial — west park cemetery, johannesburg
20–21. informant — “person causing burial”, 6 jorissen street, braamfontein
both reports were wrong, and both came from this page

phthisis is on line 11, not line 12. it is not the cause of death — it is the allowance he drew. he was a certified miners’ phthisis pensioner, which is a category of compensated men on the rand, and the form has a line for it.

and “coronary pulmonary sclerosis” is a mangling of what line 12 actually says. cor pulmonale became coronary pulmonary; silicosis became sclerosis. one document, two wrong readings, and this archive was carrying both.
what actually killed him
cor pulmonale with silicosis, with broncho pneumonia as contributing cause, after an illness of two years and a final seven days.
silicosis is rock dust. cor pulmonale is the right side of the heart failing because the lungs have stopped letting blood through. it is the same disease the pension was for, arriving.
he was sixty-nine, and a retired miner of langlaagte estates.
and four things nobody had
his identity number, 331-452322. his own date of birth written on the form — 12-8-1887, which is now the fourth independent statement of it, after a family tree, a gravestone and a church register.

his address: 3 fifteenth avenue, mayfair. seven years earlier his niece catherine mary sophia booyzen married nuno fernando lerena at st joseph’s, mayfair — the hinge between this archive and the lerena one. he was living in that parish.
and a doctor’s name, a. l. agranat, and an informant at 6 jorissen street who is described only as the person causing the burial — not a relative, on the form’s own wording.

why this was worth a morning. a cause of death is the kind of fact that gets repeated. it had been repeated twice, from two places, in two different wrong forms, and both were traceable to a single sheet of paper nobody had opened. the rule this archive keeps relearning is that a transcript is not a document — and the day before this was read, a findmypast reference carried here for weeks turned out not to resolve at all. the method →
1923 and 1929 · two estate files at pietermaritzburg name nine children, and the daughters by their married names

this archive knew that frederik fortunatus kolbe, the settler’s tenth child, married elizabeth johanna du toit and baptised eight children between colesberg, hopetown and bethulie; and that three of them turned up at wakkerstroom, four hundred miles north. it had no death for either parent and had followed three of the children nowhere at all. the natal estate index answers all of it in one search.
frederick fortunatus kolbe
born 1839, cape province — died 23 november 1929 at utrecht, natal
pietermaritzburg estate files, probate 1929 · 1:1:qlr2-xfjc
ninety years old. born at a mission station on the orange river the year his father was working it; dead on a farm in the eastern transvaal borderlands.
elizabetha johanna du toit kolbe
born 1845, bredasdorp, cape province — died 12 july 1923 at “saxony”, utrecht, natal
probate 1923 · 1:1:qlrl-hrqv
her record here read “not yet found: her marriage, her parents, her death.” two of the three, and a birthplace nobody had.
and the estates name the children — which is how you follow daughters
a cape or natal estate file lists the heirs, and it lists a married daughter under both names. nine appear across the two files.

five confirmations, three people followed out of the font at last, and a ninth child. the archive’s own note was careful and said “eight of their children are in the dutch reformed registers” — the ninth was not, and he is named for his father.
the angeline question, answered by exclusion

martha angelina kolbe’s record carried a warning: an angeline kolbe died at wakkerstroom in 1900, and a martha angeline kolbe was buried at volksrust in 1901 aged two months, and “neither can yet be attached to her, and this archive will not guess.”

it does not have to guess now. martha angelina is named as an heir on her mother’s estate in 1923 and her father’s in 1929. she was alive for both. she is neither the woman who died in 1900 nor the baby who died in 1901 — and the volksrust infant has her own dates now: born 9 october 1901, died 8 december 1901.
and she is still written kolbe in 1929, where five of her sisters are written under married names. at sixty-one she had not married, or had been widowed back to her own name.

the town, and what it does to the wakkerstroom convergence. the estates are at pietermaritzburg and the deaths are at utrecht — on a farm called saxony — with one at vryheid. utrecht and vryheid sit either side of wakkerstroom on the natal–transvaal border. this is not three children who happened to marry in one town. it is a household that moved from the orange river to the natal border and stayed.

and one that reaches across to the other branch. the same index holds “anna maria viljoen kolbe” with a natal estate (1:1:qphz-23xs) — the woman found this morning in the burgersdorp baptism register as the mother of the other george augustus kolbe, the one born in 1861 and buried at wakkerstroom. both kolbe households ended up in the same corner of natal. sixty-four kolbe entries in that collection and this archive has read none of the files.
17 september · the rest of the burgersdorp register — 214 images, 2,046 baptisms, and three of the five were already here

the standing errand of this project. film 008039088, the burgersdorp dutch reformed baptism register, was swept by hand from image 338 to image 604 on 14 september and then stopped — twice — because a familysearch session is shorter than a 214-image sweep. it is finished.

what the last 214 images hold: 2,046 baptisms, running from 1858 to 1866 — 191 in 1859, 309 in 1860, 279 in 1861, 212 in 1862, 325 in 1863, 273 in 1864, 328 in 1865, 123 in 1866. 391 distinct parent surnames. no image failed and no image was skipped. it is a complete demographic slice of one karoo town across eight years, and this archive wanted five rows of it.

the one that lands on something published yesterday

on 16 september this archive read the wakkerstroom gravestones and separated two men of one name. one of them: george augustus kolbe, born 2 october 1861 at burgersdorp, died 8 november 1934 — and the age arithmetic made him the prisoner of war of wo 108/368 folio 709. the record then said, in terms, “the descent is not documented here and is not claimed”.
here is his baptism. 2 october 1861, burgersdorp, father g. a. kolbe, mother anna maria viljoen. the stone gave a date and a town; the register gives him parents.

whether his father is the settler’s twin son — the g.a. kolbe born 23 february 1836, who would have been twenty-five — is the next step and is not taken here. what is documented is a couple and three children.
a sentence withdrawn, which is the better kind of find

this archive already held a frederick fortunatus werdmuller — from a cape supreme court petition of 1907 and an estate of 1953 — with no birth, no parents, and a line saying “not shown to be her descendant” of augusta louisa kolbe.

image 673 shows it. fredrik fortunatus steenkamp werdmuller, born 25 april 1861, baptised 19 may, father c. j. o. werdmuller, mother augusta louisa kolbe. the settler’s fourth daughter gave her husband’s child her brother’s name — which is how frederik fortunatus reached a fourth surname.

it also dates her. c.j.o. werdmuller married again at burgersdorp in 1874, and this archive could not tell whether his son charles andrew belonged to that marriage or to augusta louisa. she was bearing his children in 1861. the werdmullers →

one step not taken: that the child of 1861 is the man of the 1907 petition. the name is rare and both are cape — but the 1907 man is of malmesbury and the child was baptised at burgersdorp, and nothing read here joins them.

two blank-name rows in 2,046, and neither is ours. image 666, a child baptised 17 february 1861 whose only named parent is fredrica geertruida elizabeth kezar; image 792, a child baptised 27 august 1865 whose only named parent is francina helena magda steenkamp. that failure — the empty name column — is the whole reason this register had to be swept rather than searched, because it is what hid catherine mary sophia barry in 1855 and the werdmuller child in 1857. twice more in this stretch, and both times to other families.
and the one that was not a find at all

johanna catharina mountjoy, born 28 january 1860, has been in this archive for days — a daughter of george mountjoy and maria sophia botha, baptised on a leap day, and the woman who married william henry keys. she is one of the thirteen mountjoy children.

the sweep reached her from the other direction and returned the same two dates. that is a confirmation and a citable reference, and it is not a discovery. the duplicate record this sweep created was caught by the build’s own name-collision check before it reached a page. the thirteen →

recorded so that they are not later adopted: two booysen entries at image 691 — jacobus alewyn, born 5 january 1862 to andries johannes daniel kruger and cornelia etresia booysen, and maria helena charlina, born 8 december 1861 to jan jonathan booysen and cornelia margaretha de villiers. neither couple is in this archive and neither is claimed. burgersdorp had booysens who were not these booysens.

a surname this rare can be measured rather than sampled. every kolbe in the british census, and every kolbe in the civil registers, for thirty years. it comes to eight records and four people, and the shape of it says something the individual records do not.

eight records in thirty years, all of them london.
and the thing the two tables say together

three women disappear from the census between 1841 and 1851, and at least two of them were demonstrably alive after it. amelia ann married at st pancras in 1854. a charlotte kolbe died at lambeth in 1867 — and the one kolbe in the whole 1851 census is at lambeth too.

so the 1851 blank is not a family ending. it is the record failing to hold them — mis-transcribed, or living in a household entered under somebody else's name. a census absence reads like an extinction and is very often an indexing accident.

this archive learned the same lesson about itself this morning, from the other side: seventeen of its own people had pages saying they were discussed nowhere, because a build step dropped them. an absence is a claim about the record before it is a claim about the person. the method →

one thing that got harder, not easier. the three women at conduit street — marianne, charlotte and amelia — match no baptism in the family’s own register run. their 1841 ages put them born about 1802–06, 1807–11 and 1812–16, and the eleven known children leave gaps at exactly 1808–1812 and 1814–1818. those are the same two gaps the three missing sons have to sit in. the 1841 census gives no relationships — that column starts in 1851 — so their place in this family is an inference from living in the house, and is recorded as one. the register that would settle it →
april 1834 · kolbe and fletcher, conduit-street, in a list of three hundred master tailors

this archive holds a printed line from december 1799: “kolbe, john, 18 broad-street, soho”, one of 234 master tailors who met over the combination act. it has just found the same man in the same kind of list thirty-five years later — and the second list closes a gap this archive had written down as unclosable.
morning post · wednesday, 30 april 1834
“meeting of master tailors. yesterday morning a meeting of considerably more than three hundred of the master tailors of the metropolis was held in willis’s rooms, st. james’s-street…”
…thomson and whitelaw · j. beaumont, finch-lane · kolbe and fletcher, conduit-street · w. pugh, regent-street…

the roll was reprinted across the london press over a fortnight and the entry survives in all of it, mangled differently each time by the scanner and identically by the compositor: globe 30 april and 10 may (“kerr, james, vine street · kolbe and fletch…”), old england 4 may, morning herald 10 may, london courier and evening gazette 10 may, true sun 10 may, public ledger and daily advertiser 12 may (“kolbs and fletcher”). seven newspapers, one line.

the westminster rate books have him at church street south, soho, to 1831. the london gazette has him at conduit street by september 1836. this archive wrote that the move happened somewhere in between and left it there.
he was at conduit street, with fletcher, by 29 april 1834. the gap is now 1831 to early 1834, and the partnership is two and a half years older than its dissolution notice.
what they were signing

not a trade directory. a side. the journeymen tailors had struck, and the masters met to resist the grand national consolidated trades’ union — in the masters’ own words, reprinted by the poor man’s guardian, “the present is not a contest between the master tailors and the journeymen, but the contest between the master tradesmen and the grand national consolidated trades’ union.”
spring 1834. the same season the tolpuddle labourers were transported.
and what it rhymes with
in december 1799 he is one of 234 masters over the combination acts, a young man at 18 broad-street with no partner and no bond street.
in april 1834 he is kolbe and fletcher of conduit-street, sixty-nine or seventy years old, a firm rather than a name.
two printed lists thirty-five years apart, the same trade and the same kind of fight — and this archive found the first one months ago and never thought to look for a second.
1824–1832 · four more things the london press says about this family
the newspaper archive was opened for one question and answered several. all four below come from the same search as the master tailors’ list, and none of them was looked for.
1 · the son’s trade, at last
law chronicle, commercial and bankruptcy register · 13 january 1825
“kolbe john henry, of norfolk-street, middlesex-hospital, last of mansfield-st., kentish town, tailor, draper…”

the gazette gave his addresses and not his trade. he was a tailor and draper on his own account — and the gazette’s “mansfield-place” is mansfield street, kentish town. he left his father’s firm in may 1824 and was in the insolvent debtors’ lists by october.
2 · the 1824 dissolution, in six papers

“j. h. kolbe and j. g. kolbe, church-street, soho, tailors” — the news 23 and 24 may, new times 17 may, nation 17 may, globe 17 may, sunday morning herald 16 may, fleming’s weekly express 16 may 1824.
a third independent witness to the soho address after the rate books and the son’s own deposition in the old bailey — and the papers put the son’s name first, where the gazette put the father’s.
morning herald · 6 june 1832
“…the most respectable references will be given. — letters addressed a. z., mr. kolbe, 5, church-street, soho, will be punctually attended to.”
a situations-wanted advertisement using the tailor’s shop as an accommodation address, which is what a respectable tradesman’s counter was for. the rate books give the street. this gives the number.
and it puts a kolbe still in church street in june 1832, after the last rate book entry.
4 · a boy who ran away, and the rejection that holds
morning advertiser · 31 december 1832

“left his home, monday, december 10, frederick kolbe, about 16, dark hair and eyes, with an impediment in his sight. any information addressed mrs. kolbe, no. 18, gerrard-street, soho, will be rewarded; if he will return, will…”

this archive rejected a frederick kolbe baptised at westminster on 16 december 1816 — father george, mother elizabeth — because the parents were wrong. “about 16” in december 1832 is exactly that boy, and gerrard street is two streets from church street.

so the rejection was right and it was not a dead end. there were two kolbe households in soho at once, and every soho kolbe record on this site has to be read against that. whether the two families were related is not known here.

and one for the settler. london courier and evening gazette, 12 november 1819, and the british press the next day: “the ministers are preparing to receive settlers proceeding to the cape of good hope. in the port of london — chapman, 558 tons; nautilus, 403; agamemnon, diadem, and ocean. at liverpool — thetis, 530 tons…” the ship george augustus kolbe sailed on, listed by tonnage in a london paper five months before it left, while he was still a boy in his father’s house in soho.
16 september 2026 · the savoy register is filmed, digitised, and padlocked

five of the eight sons are now named. three are not, and the gaps in the westminster baptism run — 1808 to 1812 and 1814 to 1818 — are where they must be. the burials of the ones who died are in the german lutheran church register at rg 4/4631. so the baptism register of the same church is the document that finishes the family, and this archive went looking for it.

it exists, and it is exactly what was wanted. familysearch catalogue entry koha:176759 — “church records of german lutheran church, 1694–1840”, author german lutheran church (savoy, westminster), filmed by the genealogical society of utah in 1967 from the original records at the public record office. the cover sheet calls it “die deutsche evangelisch lutherische s. marien kirche in der savoy”. text in german. all volumes have a name index.

why this is a good result and not a bad one

before today the three missing sons had no route at all. now they have one, and it is short: film 008004264, 537 images, a german-language register with its own name index, at any familysearch affiliate library. the index means it is a half-hour job at the machine rather than a page-by-page sweep.
and the same film holds the marriages to 1754 and burials to 1771, which would reach back past this family into whoever the kolbes were before broad street.
a seventh kind of shut door

this site keeps a list of the ways a source can be closed. this is a new one: digitised and withheld — not lost, not undigitised, not paywalled, not bot-blocked. photographed, catalogued, counted, and locked by contract, with the padlock drawn on every frame so you can see exactly what you are not allowed to read.
it is the most answerable of the seven, because the fix is a bus fare rather than a letter. the other six →
1901 · three booyzens on the city of cambridge — the war, at last with a document behind it

this archive has carried the family's own account of the anglo-boer war for the whole project and never had a record for it. it has also established, carefully, that no booysen is on a cape rebel roll. both of those things were true and neither was the answer, because the question was being asked in the wrong colony.
the list, as printed
¦no. surname christian name ship sailed age entered from
¦18463 booyzen stephanus francois city of cambridge 3-6-01 28 pretoria, pretoria
¦18464 booyzen petrus jacobus do. do. 29 do. do.

source. "de list", military records 1901–1903, south africa government archives (pretoria), volume no. 10469–32561, image group 008019246 (item 3 of 9), image 51 of 69. found through familysearch's full-text search, which reads the images themselves; read from the image, not from the transcript.

three consecutive numbers, one ship, one day, one district. that is what the list says and it is the whole of what it says — there are no parents on it, no farm, and no commando. but consecutive prisoner numbers on a single transport are not a coincidence of filing: these three men were taken together and processed together, and then put on the same ship out of the country on 3 june 1901.

the archive was asking the wrong question. the rebels page answers, correctly and at length, whether a booysen appears on a cape rebel roll. he does not. a cape rebel is a british subject who took up arms against his own government. these men were transvaal burghers fighting for their own republic, which is not rebellion and does not appear on that roll at all. months of careful negative work, all of it sound, all of it aimed one colony to the south.
what can be claimed, and what cannot
¦three men called booyzen were transvaal prisoners of war, deported 3 june 1901 documented — it is a printed government list and it is legible.
¦they were taken together inferred from consecutive numbering on one transport. strong, and an inference.

¦the david schalk is this archive's david schalk booysen, born cradock 1848 unproven. the age is given as 54; he would have been 52, six days short of 53, when the ship sailed. he was demonstrably at pretoria four years later, where he remarried. nothing on the list names a parent or a birthplace.

¦the stephanus francois is this archive's stephanus francois booyzen unproven. the age is 28; this archive has him born about october 1874, which would make him 26. he died at east lynne, pretoria — the district all three were entered from.
both testable ages run high by the same margin, one to two years. that is ordinary on lists taken in the field from men who had been on commando, and it is worth saying rather than smoothing.
and it touches the oldest dispute on the site

whether stephanus francois is a son of david schalk booysen is marked serious on disputed, and the three arguments for it have all been naming arguments — the marais forename, a bachelor of thirty at pretoria in 1905, an eldest son called david schalk. naming arguments in this family are weak, as the namesakes page keeps demonstrating.

this is the fourth argument and the first that is not about a name. he is 18463. david schalk is 18465. two apart, on one transport, on one day, out of one district — the district he would die in thirty-nine years later. he has not been moved on disputed, because a transport list is not a document that names a parent. but the dispute no longer rests entirely on what people were called.
where the ship went is not on the de list and has not been established here. the transports of 1901 carried transvaal prisoners to ceylon, india, bermuda and st helena.

all three lived at pretoria, all three rode with the pretoria commando, and all three were taken at tolosberg on 25 april 1901. six weeks later they were on a ship.

two booysens sit beside them and are not with them. 18462 adrian jacobus is a free state man of blaauwboschbank, fauresmith, edenburg commando, taken at springhaan nek in december 1900; 18466 gert is of bloemfontein, taken at kaffirskraal in october 1900. neither shares the district, the commando, the place or the date. the register separates those two as cleanly as it groups our three, which is what makes the grouping worth anything.

stefanus francois is exact. david schalk is within weeks of his fifty-third birthday. the note published earlier that "both ages run one to two years high" described the de list and not the record, and is withdrawn on corrections. the identification is no longer strained by the arithmetic — it is supported by it.

and the group is now hard to read as strangers. a man of fifty-three and two men in their twenties, one address, one commando, taken in one action on one day, numbered consecutively, shipped together. whether stephanus francois is david schalk's son is still not settled by a document naming a parent — and this is the nearest thing to one this archive has.
what happened at tolosberg — and who stephanus francois turns out to be

tolosberg is not in any gazetteer this archive could reach, nor in the standard battle lists, nor in a day-by-day war diary of 1901. it is in one place: the medal-roll database at angloboerwar.com, kept by dr david biggins — and the entry there is about this man, by this prisoner number.
"booysen was one of 42 boers captured on 25 april 1901 at tolosberg in the waterval valley, eastern transvaal, together with 2 guns and much stock. he was sent to india as pow no 18463."
18463 is the number in the register above. two record series, compiled for different purposes, agree on the man, the day, the place and the number.
the same entry, drawn from a city coins auction catalogue of november 2020 describing his medal, says what he was:
¦unit a member of the zarps — the zuid-afrikaansche republiek politie, the zar's police. based at pretoria, which is the home address the register gives all three men.
¦commanding officer commandant j. p. de la c. schroeder, who completed booysen's medal applications in full.
¦in action at talana · modder spruit · colenso · platrand (wagon hill) · spion kop · dalmanutha — the last of these the famous last stand of the zarps.
¦wounded at platrand (wagon hill), in the right leg above the knee.
¦decorations the abo, named burger s. f. booysen, with the lint voor verwonding — the wound ribbon.
¦after capture sent to india.

what this is and is not. it is a specialist database entry quoting an auction catalogue describing a medal and the papers that came with it. this archive has not seen the medal, the abo application, or schroeder's signature. it is strong secondary evidence, and the prisoner number is what ties it to the register rather than to a name alone.

the family's own war testimony now has something to be tested against. this archive has quoted tersia booyzen's account in full for the whole project and measured it only against surname distributions and rebel district figures, because there was no record. there is one now: a policeman of pretoria who was at talana in the first week of the war, wounded at wagon hill, present at spion kop and at the zarps' last stand, taken at tolosberg with forty-one others and two guns, and shipped to india.
tolosberg is still not on the atlas — "the waterval valley, eastern transvaal" is the only location this archive has for it, and no map consulted so far carries the name.

born at the cape of good hope, dead at johannesburg in 1918. that is the migration of every one of kathleen barry’s children — born in the north-eastern cape, dead on the rand. with the forename that is her own brother’s, and a birth about 1894 that falls exactly in the gap between her daughter of 1891 and her son of 1901, the inference is now a good deal firmer than it was at lunchtime. it is still not documented: this form names no parents, because a transvaal death registration does not ask.

this archive has an open question — why was kathleen barry a “military pensioner” at her death in 1940? her husband died in 1905 of a stomach ulcer, so the pension is not his, and the page has said for months that “no son of hers is among the first world war dead”.
a son of hers dead in october 1918 looked like the answer. enormous numbers of south african servicemen died in that epidemic and their dependants were pensioned.

he was not a soldier. occupation: a trade. condition: married — so he had a wife, and a married son’s death does not pension his mother in any case. he died in his own house in turffontein of influenza and pneumonia after eleven days, and the man who reported it gave an address in market buildings in town.

the theory is rejected. it was a good theory — the right son, the right age, the right month — and the document says no. the open question stands, and it is now better specified: the pension belongs to a son who served and survived, which is exactly what the letter already sitting at the sandf documentation centre asks about. open question →

this archive carried a contradiction marked serious: margaretha kolbe appeared to marry george frederick enslin in 1850 while married to john barry, and to bear barry and enslin children three and a half months apart in 1851. it was resolved from margaret downing’s 1867 death notice, which lists among her children “mary elizabeth (dead) who was married to george f. enslin”. the enslin marriage belongs to margaretha’s sister.

and it puts them at burgersdorp. the 1915 death notice says the marriage was at “burghersdorp (probably)” — a son guessing, sixty-five years on, at something nobody had told him. they were baptising a child in that church in 1853, and the godparents were her own brothers. the guess was right.

three more kolbes come out of these two entries — john kolbe and george kolbe, godfathers at the barry font, and catharine kolbe, godmother at the enslin one. margaretha and mary elizabeth had a family around them at burgersdorp, and this archive has been treating margaretha as though she arrived alone.

why neither could be found by name

margrith louisa maria has no surname in the index. two separate index passes of the same register give “margrith louisa maria” and “margreth louisa mary”, and the name column stops there. it is the blank name column again — the same failure that hid catherine mary sophia of 1855 until a fortnight ago.

william frederick thomas is invisible for the opposite reason. he is not missing a name; he has the same one as his brother. a search for william barry returns the 1853 child and stops, and nothing about the result says there is a second.
both were found by asking the index for a relationship — father john barry, mother a kolbe — and letting it return whatever the child was called. the method →
and the count comes right

nine baptisms in the registers, plus hendrik nicholaas and richard peter — both named on their parents’ death notices and in no register this archive can find — makes eleven, which is exactly the number the 1903 death registration gives.

margaret mary, named on the death notices and never placed, is almost certainly margrith louisa maria: it is her mother’s name, and there is no other candidate in the sibling group. inferred from the count and the name

and two williams eight years apart means, by this family’s own practice, that the first william died — which is what the archive concluded about the two catherine mary sophias. a baptism is not done twice. the “william who appears on nothing else” on the wife’s death notice is one of these two, and the notice does not say which.

the citations. margrith louisa maria: ark:/61903/1:1:6vyg-ss94 and 1:1:6f4l-76pk, images 3:1:3q9m-csvc-xpsy and 3:1:3q9m-csfq-qlqn — the second of which is on film 008039088, the burgersdorp register this archive has been sweeping by hand. william frederick thomas: 1:1:623r-9mm9 and 1:1:62gj-sd8z, images 3:1:3q9m-csk6-9s81-j and 3:1:3q9m-csvd-5vnz. each child is indexed twice, and neither index pass agrees with the other about the spelling.
and a trap in the tool, which is worth as much as the finding

the search api accepts q.filmnumber, and for film 008039088 it reports 22,059 records — the whole indexed film, which would have made the hand sweep unnecessary. it also accepts an offset, and pages correctly to offset 1000.
at offset 1001 it silently returns page one again. no error, no warning, no change in the reported total. the response still says "results": 22059 and still says "index": 0.

an unchecked sweep would have re-read the first thousand records twenty-two times and reported the film as holding 1,400 entries. it was caught by comparing the first name returned at offset 0 against offset 1400 — they were identical — and then bisecting to find the edge. this is the fourth undocumented boundary this archive has hit in a week, after the church films beginning in 1843, the estate inventories stopping in the 1830s, and naairs defaulting to or. it is the only one so far that answers wrongly rather than emptily.

which is why the film sweep is not abandoned. the api will show 1,001 of 22,059 records and no more, so the remaining 214 images of the hand sweep still have to be stepped. what the api is good for is exactly what it did here: a targeted relationship query, where the answer is small enough to fit inside the first thousand.

cradock in january 1822, because he counted it

this archive keeps saying it names the people documents leave out. here is a town, complete, in one sentence — five years after james mountjoy married in it and fifteen before the booyzens arrived to marry there too.

at that time there were only about half a dozen inhabitants in the place. all that i can remember are messrs. solomon and s.m. de beer, the rev. mr. evans (d.r. church), mr. [p. gie], james mountjoy (a saddler, who was discharged from the 21st light dragoons), the two messrs. ziervogel (one was secretary to government), mr. heilberg, fieldcornet b.j. vorster, and gert van deventer.

nine names and a constable who demanded his pass in the street. solomon is the constable — montgomery refuses to show him the pass, walks to the landdrost’s office four miles out at driefontein across the fish river, and arrives “just in time to prevent myself being brought up a prisoner”, because solomon already had the warrant. captain harding is the landdrost, “a little cross-grained irishman”. it is the only picture this archive has of the place its people were living in.
and what a memoir is worth — a position, since two of them cost walls

john montgomery was recalling forty-seven years back when he wrote that, and forty-five when he placed george augustus kolbe at a mission school. this archive has taken two substantial claims from him. it should say what that kind of source is.

a memoir is a witness, not a record. it has no clerk, no form, no oath and no date of composition close to the event. what it has instead is circumstantial specificity — montgomery does not say “a saddler lived there”, he says which regiment, and he slept in the man’s house and ate his breakfast.
the test this archive is using: does the memoir claim something it had no reason to invent, and does anything independent touch it?

on koolskop, something does. a cape town library catalogue written from the papers themselves calls george augustus kolbe an lms missionary, and this page had already deduced a mission circuit from where his children were born. three lines of evidence, none of them aware of the others. that one is as good as an unverified claim gets.

on the 21st dragoons, nothing does — yet. the regiment is real, it was at the cape from 1806 to 1816, and the man married there in 1817. but he is not in any name-catalogued discharge series at kew, and the reason may be structural or may be that montgomery misremembered a regiment forty-seven years on. both remain open, and the site says so rather than letting a good sentence do the work of a document.
the asymmetry is the point. one memoir claim is corroborated and one is not, and they are written up differently on this site for exactly that reason — not because one is a better story.
december 1819 · what the voyage was like, from a man on the same deck

this archive has had the nautilus as a set of dates since the settler roll was checked: gravesend on 3 december 1819, table bay on 17 march 1820, algoa bay on 14 april. george augustus kolbe was sixteen and his wife was sixteen, and the roll says twenty and nineteen. what none of it said was what the crossing was.

john penny mandy led another party on the same ship and wrote home to his mother in kent. his letters survive in a descendant's copy — the originals went to the albany museum at grahamstown and were destroyed in a fire in the 1920s — and a newspaper printed them in 1970.

in one letter, written in january 1820, he describes the nautilus disaster in the downs. after they dropped anchor in the queen’s channel, a day after leaving gravesend, “it came on to blow tremendously hard, the sea running mountains high. we could not weigh anchor till sunday afternoon, when our troubles began, the sea breaking over us in all directions, tables, chairs, boxes, plates and dishes; men, women and children all mixed together, tumbling over one another, and all dreadfully seasick, except myself and smith, who was on deck working the ship; i below, basin holder.”

“in the midst of this the sea broke into our cabin windows, dashing glass and frame in, the things that were below rolling and sliding, took to swimming.” … when the ship struck on the sands all was confusion and dismay — “even the sailors seemed panic struck.” after an hour and a half a heavy sea set them afloat without much damage, and five or six boats went to their help.

then another storm, which lasted three days. “the sea was running as high as our masthead, and two of the waves broke over us; the forepart of the ship had three tons of water in, which swamped almost every person in their beds, joseph was washed out of his cot.”
what this is, and what it is not
it is not about this family. mandy led a different party and there is no evidence he and kolbe ever spoke. ships carried several parties and a hundred people apiece.

they were on the same deck in the same storm, a day out of gravesend, and the ship went aground on the sands before it had properly started. a boy four days short of his seventeenth birthday and a girl of sixteen, both of whom had sworn on paper that they were older than they were, were somewhere in that cabin among the tables and chairs.
and it dates the voyage properly

mandy's party reached algoa bay in april 1820, and he writes from there on 20 april: “i landed on sunday night to get ready for mary anne and the children.” this archive has the nautilus at algoa bay on 14 april. they agree.

and a child was born aboard. william nautilus mandy, on 1 march 1820, “in latitude 18 degrees, longitude six degrees” — a fortnight short of table bay, and named for the ship. he died at lushington valley in 1887 in his sixty-seventh year.

a note on how this was found, because it closes an item rather than opening one. the plan was to read john montgomery's serialised memoir entire — it had already produced the koolskop mission school and the 21st dragoons, and it runs through the friend across 1868, 1869 and 1870 under two titles. that turns out to be unnecessary. both finds came out of sweeping a surname across the whole newspaper collection, and those sweeps are done: kolbe returns 43 documents and mountjoy six, across every paper in the archive. koolskop appears exactly once in the entire collection — in the passage already read. reading a long memoir to find what a name search has already found is work that looks like diligence. this was found instead by searching for the ship.
the natal depot, opened — and a connection this archive nearly invented

nab had never been searched. it had only ever been asked for six references somebody else had found. opened properly it holds thirty-nine kolbes, nine mountjoys, four booyzens and no daschners at all — and one document that looked for ten minutes like the link this archive has been hunting for a fortnight.
the one that was not what it looked like
ck barry, wakkerstroom. mr. gs kolbe asks to be supplied with a copy of the road board law.

a barry and a kolbe in one sentence, at wakkerstroom, in 1908. wakkerstroom is the district whose kolbes this archive has spent weeks trying to attach to the 1820 settler. this archive holds three barrys carrying kolbe as a forename — henry james kolbe barry, richard pieter kolbe barry. c.k. barry read, for about ten minutes, like a fourth.

he is cyril kershaw barry, and he is an attorney. four further documents settle it: he asks about the appointment of a commissioner of oaths at wakkerstroom; he enquires whether a certificate of domicile has been issued to mahomed mamoojee motala of ladysmith; he forwards quitrent on behalf of mr moll; he writes about the division of ground in natal. that is a country solicitor’s week, and g.s. kolbe is a client. the k is kershaw. nearly published as a family link

it is set down at length because the mistake was a good one to almost make: two surnames from this archive, in the right district, in one line of a catalogue — and the thing joining them is a professional relationship that would have been invisible if the other four documents had not been read.

and two court cases from before the republic
illiquid case. petrus gerhardus booyzen versus david schalk van der merwe.
illiquid case. andries evert gouws… versus petrus gerhardus booyzen.

1846 is the oldest booyzen document this archive has found outside the cape. and the defendant's name is the one this site spent yesterday proving is a van der merwe name that entered the booyzen line by marriage — here the two surnames are on opposite sides of a lawsuit two years before this family's own david schalk turned forty. no connection is claimed. petrus gerhardus is not a name in this archive, and a booyzen in natal in 1846 is more likely one of the trekker families than one of ours. recorded because it is early and because the pairing is worth somebody's attention, not because it is a lead.

and the kolbes of wakkerstroom kept stock. six veterinary files, 1905–1912: f.f. kolbe refusing a cheque for sixteen shillings for the rent of a sheep kraal; a claim for £25 for a cow lost to poisoning; g.s. kolbe asking permission to move two bulls; scab in j. kolbe's sheep; and permission to move one bull from wakkerstroom to saxony, utrecht. it is the most ordinary material in this archive and it is the first time these people appear doing their actual work.

and a sweep that was abandoned, deliberately. the plan was to put this family's farms through the education series as well as its surnames. brakfontein returns 77 documents, koedoesfontein 188, goedehoop 41 — they are among the commonest farm names in the country and the results are other people's schools in other districts. one is worth keeping: od or150/95, “cab meyer, koedoesfontein, wyk zwartruggens, rustenburg”, is unmistakably this archive's koedoesfontein — the farm where hendrik stefanus booijsen died in 1908, in the ward of zwartruggens. it had a school in 1895 and no booyzen is anywhere on its papers. a farm-name sweep without a surname is not a search, and the rest of it is recorded as void.
the free state depot, swept at last — and the settler was a missionary

vab had been opened twice in this project's life, both times for a single reference. swept properly it holds 146 kolbe documents and thirteen mccabes, and among them is the catalogue entry that turns this morning's inference into a fact.
first, the thing nobody was looking for
sa library, cape town · manuscript · msb751
ga kolbe collection. donated by dr jean griffiths, somerset west, 1985. photocopy, 4 pages.
“george augustus kolbe, pharmacist, 1820 settler, missionary, married margaret downing. + letter, 1830 aug. 23, from johan kolbe, london, to his son, george augustus kolbe on his ordination.”
and on the second entry: “george augustus kolbe, 1802–44. lms missionary. + letter from his father, jg kolbe, london.”
it corroborates a memory this archive published as an inference

this morning john montgomery’s reminiscence put the settler at a bushman mission school at koolskop about 1824, and this archive published it hedged: a man recalling forty-five years back, naming somebody only as a commandant’s father.

a library catalogue, written from the papers themselves, calls him an lms missionary. two sources that have nothing to do with each other — an old man’s memoir in a bloemfontein newspaper and a manuscript donated to a cape town library in 1985 — and they agree. the inference stands up.

it also settles the occupation. the 1820 settler roll entered him as a chemist; the catalogue says pharmacist; the 1844 obituary describes a medical practice. they are one man and one trade, and the missionary work is the part nobody had.
and it is the london end, in four photocopied pages

a letter from johan kolbe in london to his son at the cape, dated 23 august 1830, written on his ordination. this archive has spent a fortnight failing to connect the tailor of conduit street to the settler of colesberg by way of directories, census returns and a newspaper obituary.

the two men wrote to each other, and the letter survives. a letter from london in 1830 is very likely to carry an address at the head of it — which is the exact question the brunswick square muddle turns on, and which google books, hathitrust and archive.org between them could not answer.
it is a photocopy of something. where the original is, and whether more of it survives with dr griffiths’s descendants, the catalogue does not say.

this archive recorded, and flagged as unresolved, that a rosa magdalena kolbe was baptised at bloemfontein in 1890 to frederik fortuna kolbe and maria petronella elizabeth antoinetta mccabe — “a second kolbe–mccabe marriage in the same small free state world, and this archive does not yet know whether that is a coincidence.”
