six people of one surname applying to a court together is a sibling group. four married daughters, two sons, and among the six forenames are margaret downing, george augustus and georgina augusta. it is a generation too late to be the commandant’s twelve — these are more likely his grandchildren — but it is the first free state kolbe sibling group this archive has been able to name at all, and the file will say what they were applying about, which is usually a parent’s estate. on the errands list →
1780–1810 · anna catharina slier gets parents, and this archive had two men under one name

volume 3 of the cape genealogies was opened to look up the six slier entries the index reported. one of them is a whole family, and it answers a woman who has been on this site as a birth year and five spellings. it also shows that what this archive has been calling her first husband is two people.
willem slier, van hamburg, gehuwd 19 november 1780 met anna catharina fortman.
(b) 1 anna catharina, gedoopt 14 october 1787, gehuwd met hermanus pieterse
2 wilhelmina christina, gedoopt 27 december 1789, gehuwd 5 januari 1811 met jan abraham van wijk, van amsterdam
3 geertruida johanna, gedoopt 2 juli 1791
4 wilhelmus josephus, gedoopt 5 maart 1797

this archive has carried her as “anna catharina sleer — slier · schleher · sher · hier, five renderings, five sources”, born 1787, died 1885 aged ninety-eight, first the widow of a pietersen and then the wife of james montjoy. every one of those facts holds and three more arrive. she was baptised on 14 october 1787. her father was willem slier of hamburg and her mother anna catharina fortman. and she had three siblings, one of whom married an amsterdammer.

the five spellings stop being a mystery. a hamburg name — schlier, schleer — written down by cape clerks who had never seen it, which is exactly how slier, schleher, sher and hier all come out of one family in one generation. this archive has a whole page arguing that a spelling is whatever the clerk had, and here is the argument again, on a different surname, from a different country. the name →
and then the pietersens, two pages later
hermanus pietersen, namen van ouders onbekend, gehuwd 5 april 1807 met anna catharina slier.
(b) 1 willem hermanus, gedoopt 12 maart 1809
2 johan christiaan, gedoopt 28 april 1810

this archive has been running a father and a son together. the entry here reads “willem hermanus pieterzen — anna catharina slier’s first husband”, built out of two documents that spell him differently: the 1817 marriage register, which calls him harmanus pieterze, and the 1840 death notice, which calls him william pietersen. two spellings looked like one man with a long name. they are two men. the husband is hermanus, married on 5 april 1807. willem hermanus is his son, baptised 12 march 1809 — and this archive already half knew it, because its own note says the 1851 godfather who carries both forms in full was his son.
johan christiaan pietersen, baptised 28 april 1810 — a second son, and a second half-brother to the montjoy children. he is on nothing else this archive holds.

and the marriage is dated. she married hermanus pietersen on 5 april 1807, at nineteen; was a widow by 9 march 1817, when she married james montjoy; was a widow again by september 1827; and lived until 1885. fifty-eight years a widow.
where “willem hermanus” comes from, at last

this site has said for weeks that the name willem hermanus — carried by two booyzens in the direct line — entered through a step-relation with no blood tie. that was right, and it can now be traced one generation further back.
the boy baptised in 1809 is willem, for his mother’s father willem slier of hamburg, and hermanus, for his own father. the whole name is accounted for, and half of it is german. namesakes →

one more, and it is a negative worth the space. the dormehls are in volume 2 at entry 393 — siebert dormehl, van marburg, married 29 january 1792 to johanna israel, widow of johan godlieb carstedt, and twice more after that. his sixth child is charlotta elisabeth, baptised 18 june 1802. this archive holds a charlotta elizabetha dormehl who married hendrik stefanus booijzen at zeerust in 1892. a woman baptised in 1802 cannot be marrying in 1892, so these are two women ninety years apart, and the only thing the book gives is that the name charlotta elisabeth was already in the founding dormehl household. not a link, and recorded so that it does not become one later.
january 1822 · a man who lodged in james mountjoy’s house says where he came from

question 12 on this site has been marked blocking since it was written: who were james montjoy’s parents? his own death notice answers not known. his marriage register leaves the column ruled through and empty. and the question’s own note concluded that “the way in is a cape arrival record, not an english birth record”. it is, and one has just been found in a newspaper.
the friend of the free state and bloemfontein gazette · thursday, 25 november 1869
“how i arrived in cradock in january 1822, and narrowly escaped incarceration…”
by mr. john montgomery, founder of burghersdorp, cape colony

i arrived in cradock, tired and jaded, on a knocked-up horse, on a very cold, stormy afternoon in january 1822. at that time there were only about half a dozen inhabitants in the place. all that i can remember are messrs. solomon and s.m. de beer, the rev. mr. evans (d.r. church), mr. [p. gie], james mountjoy (a saddler, who was discharged from the 21st light dragoons), the two messrs. ziervogel (one was secretary to government), mr. heilberg, fieldcornet b.j. vorster, and gert van deventer. after some trouble i obtained lodgings for the night from mr. mountjoy.

he goes on to be challenged for his pass in the street outside the house by solomon the constable, to be asked to breakfast by mountjoy, to be told by him that the landdrost’s office was four miles out at driefontein across the fish river, and to walk there and arrive “just in time to prevent myself being brought up a prisoner”.

this archive holds james montjoy, saddler, born in “europe” about 1782, who married anna catharina slier at graaff-reinet on 9 march 1817 and died at cradock in september 1827. montgomery names a james mountjoy, a saddler, at cradock in january 1822 — inside that window, in that town, in a place with six inhabitants.
there is no room in a village of six for two saddlers of one name. it is him.

a regiment. the 21st light dragoons were the cavalry of the cape garrison — they came out with the 1806 expedition and were not disbanded until the end of the 1810s. a man discharged from them at the cape is a man who arrived in uniform, which is why no cape document can say where he was from: he did not come as a settler and no ship’s list records him as a passenger.
it also dates him. discharge would put him a civilian in the colony by about 1817 — the year he married.

the document that answers the question is now named. british army discharge papers for the period are wo 97 at the national archives, kew — royal hospital chelsea soldiers’ documents, arranged by regiment before 1855 — and they give the man’s parish and county of birth, his age on enlistment, his trade and his service. the muster books and pay lists are wo 12. neither is digitised for this regiment. question 12 stops being unanswerable and becomes an errand at kew, which is a different kind of problem and a much better one. errands →

the same man, twice in one week. john montgomery’s serialised reminiscences in the friend have now broken two walls on this site that had nothing to do with each other. his “forty-five years ago” piece put george augustus kolbe at a bushman mission school at koolskop, on the ground where colesberg was later laid out. this one puts james mountjoy in the 21st light dragoons. neither was found by searching for a kolbe or a mountjoy. they were found by reading a surname sweep to the bottom instead of skimming it, and both were sitting in the memoir of one old man in burgersdorp who happened to write down who he met. the koolskop passage →
two others from the same sweep, neither of them this family
1859 · an intestate estate at middelveld

the friend: “in den intestaten boedel van wyle jan lodewyk booijsen, van het middelveld, district bloemfontein” — who married about 1819 christina magdalena de buijs, widow of cornelius faber of the cape colony, and whose estate had become mixed with faber’s. a jan lowies booijsen also has a cape inventory of 1831, at onder roggeveld. not connected here, and recorded because the forename pair jan lodewyk / jan lowies keeps appearing beside this family without joining it.
1862 · a trek-farmer near the orange river

the eastern province herald reports a booyzen, a trek-farmer digging for water at deep fountain between the hartebeest river and hope town, who recognised and seized a party of bushmen accused of shooting a farmer — “six men, seven women and seven children”. the dispute behind it was water: ground the bushmen had used “from time immemorial” and which the government had let to the dead man for £70 a year. nothing connects this booyzen to this family. it is set down because the paper recorded the numbers and this archive is not going to be the place that drops them.
three questions put to the same search engine, and what each one cost

the baptism finder, the land & deeds finder and the marriage transcriptions, asked in that order. one returned a hard negative that closes a route, one returned four exact dates for nothing, and one turned out not to be an index at all.
1. the 1788 baptism is not on this route, and now this archive knows why

the decisive errand on this site is the dutch reformed baptism entry of 21 september 1788, which would name petrus jacobus booijsen's father in a contemporary hand and end the oldest question here. the baptism finder lists, town by town, which registers the familysearch project holds. the three candidate congregations were asked:
¦congregation registers earliest held
¦paarl (drakenstein) — where b3c4 jan was a burgher 54 1843–1844
¦graaff-reinet 48 1843–1844
¦stellenbosch 55 1843–1844

every register in the collection begins in 1843, in every town, sorted earliest first. this is the post-1842 nederduitse gereformeerde kerk archive series, and it does not reach the eighteenth century at all. the 1788 baptism cannot be got from this collection, and neither can anything else this archive wants from before 1843 — which is a fact about the filming project and not about the registers, because the originals exist. it also explains, retrospectively, why weeks of familysearch work on this family has produced nothing older than the 1840s. the errand stands, and it is a cape town errand, not a screen one.
2. four mountjoy children, with the day of birth, for nothing
the baptism database — a different thing from the finder — holds six mountjoys, four of them nineteenth-century, and the free layer of each record gives an exact date of birth:
¦maria elizabeth mountjoy 12 june 1858 —
¦johanna catharina mountjoy 28 january 1860 —
¦georg herkules johannes mountjoy 16 january 1862 27 april 1862
¦elsje petronella frederika mountjoy 10 june 1864 17 july 1864

four children at roughly two-year intervals is a sibling group, and the names are the interesting part: georg herkules johannes and elsje petronella frederika are thoroughly cape dutch name-strings sitting on an english surname, baptised in the dutch reformed church. this archive already holds a hercules johannes mountjoy, born 16 july 1866 — the same forenames and the same day of the month, four years later.
and one of them may be the woman who died at indwe

this archive holds “johanna catharina mountjoy of indwe” with no birth date at all — she joined the dutch reformed congregation at indwe on 23 july 1907, arriving from barkly oost six weeks after willem hermanus booijzen was confirmed in the same church, and the register's last column records her dead there in june 1911. a johanna catharina mountjoy born 28 january 1860 would be fifty-one in june 1911.

it is a candidate and it is not being entered. this family already contains one johanna catharina mountjoy, born 1819 and dead in 1863, so the name repeats within it. what would decide it is the congregation the 1860 baptism was registered in — if it is barkly east or anywhere in that district, the two women are almost certainly one. and the congregation is the field the site charges for.
3. where exactly the paywall falls
worth setting down precisely, because it decides whether a subscription is worth buying for this project. on a baptism record the free layer gives:
father's names and surname
mother's names and surname

the free layer gives dates; the paid layer gives parentage and the citation. for a project that already has most of its dates and is short of parents, that is the wrong half — which is exactly why it is worth knowing before paying rather than after. nothing has been bought and no account has been made.
4. land & deeds turned out not to be an index

it was opened to look for vaalbank and kwaggafontein. it does not take a farm name or a surname: it takes a year and an area, and the areas are natal and the transvaal only — no cape, no free state, so leeuwberg and kaalspruit are out of reach by this road anyway.

what it returns for 1898, transvaal is fifty-seven registers — farm records, volumes rak 89, rak 243, rak 274, rak 275, rak 279, rak 281, rak 387 and more — each with a link to view the film online. it is a film finder, not a name index. to find vaalbank in it somebody has to open a volume and read. that is a real errand and it is now a specified one, which it was not this morning.
and the marriages, since they were free

mountjoy: twenty-two, 1895 to 1969. two are worth naming. 1937 — willem hermanus mountjoy × elsie susanna du plessis: willem hermanus is this archive's own name-string, carried by two booyzens in the direct line, here on a mountjoy. and 1919 — frank mountjoy-bentley × kathleen rita miley fitzpatrick — a second hyphenated compound in this archive's own surnames, after kolbe-booysen.

daschner: three. 1900 — carl axel martenson × minnie daschner; 1935 — joseph charles daschner × elizabeth hendrina murray; and 1935 — gert andries van jaarsveld × margaret wilhelmina elizabeth jeanette daschner. the whole surname holds forty-five records in the entire aggregate, which is the smallest of this archive's five families by a long way.

none of the above is entered as fact. every line is an index entry from a commercial aggregator, and the archive's rule has not changed for being given a better search box: a transcription is a lead, and the register is the record.
1781 · the people this family owned, and the fact that this archive had never looked

the mooc8 finder searches the inventories taken of cape estates at death. thirteen of them name a booijsen. the oldest belongs to gerrit booijsen — the man at the top of this archive's cape line — and like every inventory of its kind it lists the enslaved people of the household by name, because under cape law they were property and property is what an inventory is for.

this project has been running for weeks. it reaches back to a marriage of 1733. it has a page about who this family named their children after and a page about what its documents fail to record. until this afternoon the word slavery appeared nowhere on it, and that was not a judgement about the family — it was an artefact of which records had been read. estate inventories had never been opened.
mooc 8/18.11 · 13 december 1781
gerrit booijsen — st martijn, eselscloof, drakenstein
the eleven people named in it

the cape formula gives a name and where the person was taken from. it is set out here in full, because a list of eleven names is the only thing that survives of eleven people and shortening it would be the second theft.
¦silvia silvia van de caab
¦lena lena van de caab
¦sara sara van de caab
¦janna janna van de caab
¦dorinda dorinda van de caab
¦fortuijn fortuijn van de caab

¦februarij februarij van de caab

eight born at the cape, two taken from madagascar, one from the malabar coast. the names are the ones given to them, not the ones they were born with: fortuijn is fortune, februarij and meij are the months they were bought or landed in, achilles is the classical joke a slave-owner made. that is the whole vocabulary of the practice, in one column.
is this the right gerrit

de villiers has b3 gerrit booijsen, married johanna du rand in 1733, father of c4 jan, who was a burgher at drakenstein — and this inventory is at drakenstein. a man who married in 1733 and died in 1781 is seventy-odd, which is ordinary. the other gerrit in the printed genealogy, b3c4d1, was not baptised until 1771 and cannot have an inventory in 1781.

so it is almost certainly him, and it is published as almost certainly. what would settle it is the inventory itself, which names the heirs — and if the heirs include a jan, this archive's direct line runs straight through this document. it has gone on the errands page for cape town. the identification is the uncertain part. the eleven names are not.

a caution about the last one. the index line for mooc 8/46.59 runs personal names and farm names together in one string, so knue and onder roggeveld sit in the same list as eva and castoor. the ten names above are the ones that are unambiguously people. the document has to be read before anyone is counted. 1831 is three years before emancipation at the cape.
two things this archive owes
it did not find these people. it found them by accident.

the mooc8 finder was opened this afternoon to look for mountjoy inventories, because the mountjoy wills are on the cape town errands list. mountjoy returns zero. booijsen returns thirteen. nobody here went looking for the eleven names; they were on the way to something else, and that is worth admitting rather than dressing up.
and the zeros are not yet negatives

mountjoy 0 · montjoy 0 · slier 0 · kolbe 0. every one of those families arrived at the cape in the nineteenth century, and mooc8 as indexed here runs from the 1780s to the 1830s. a zero from an index that stops before your people arrive is not a finding. this archive published exactly that mistake this morning about luus and is not going to publish it again four hours later. recorded as untested.

where the full text is, and why it is not here. the mooc8 inventories were transcribed in full by the tanap project, and its database is off the air — databases.tanap.net does not resolve, and the internet archive was itself down when this was written. so what is above is read off index entries, not off the documents. the documents are at the western cape archives, 72 roeland street, and are already on the errands page. eleven people are named here on the strength of a catalogue line, and the line is not the record. what is wanted from roeland street is the inventory of mooc 8/18.11 entire: the heirs, and every name and valuation on the list.
a search engine this project had never opened, and a negative it took back in ten minutes

the user asked whether gendatabase.com had been tried. it had not. the word appears nowhere in this repository. it aggregates ten south african datasets in one query, four of which this archive has never touched at all — and inside the first half hour it produced a marriage this archive had published as not existing.
the withdrawal first
on 14 september this archive published, about the twelve household names on the silverton pillar:
“luus with booyzen returns nothing.” … five of the twelve silverton children remain unplaced and this archive would rather say so than fill them in.
the marriage transcription database on gendatabase:
1928 · cornelius abraham luus × susanna frederik alettha booyzen

the negative was true of naairs, which is the only index this archive had asked. it was published as though it were true of the record. a marriage register is not an estate index, and a sentence that says “returns nothing” has to name what was asked. withdrawn. whether this susanna is the “ousie” of the pillar is a separate question and is not being assumed — but she is a booyzen who married a luus, which is the thing this archive said did not exist. corrections →
what the site actually is
one search box over ten datasets, with facet counts returned before you pay for anything. for booyzen it gives 569 records:
¦database booyzen what this archive had been using instead
¦verified death database 190 nothing. post-war deaths, verified.
¦national archives 152 naairs itself — already swept, and this is a far better search over it.
¦estate file database 122 the estate indexes, reached the hard way.
¦marriage transcription database 54 nothing at all. this is the gap. fifty-four marriages with both spouses' full names and a year.
¦baptism database 22 nothing at all. 1812–1835.
¦familysearch 22 tree data. not evidence, and treated as such below.
¦concentration camps 3 reached once, through naairs, by accident.
¦1925–1931 voter database 2 nothing at all.
¦civil death / unconfirmed death 2 —

it also carries specialist finders this archive has not yet used: cape estates, transvaal estates, mooc8 inventories, land & deeds, old voter rolls, boer war soldiers, legal gazettes, and a baptism finder that lists which dutch reformed registers survive for each of 181 towns.

three booyzens in the camps, and two on a voters' roll

gert jacobus, gertruida magdalena and jan gerhardus lodewicus booyzen in the university of cape town's born in the camps database — this archive had reached one of them, once, through naairs. and on the 1925–31 voters' roll: jacobus nicolas booyzen and john barry booyzen, both of whom are on the list of six estate files now with a researcher in pretoria. a voters' roll gives an address.

a search for kolbe returns 2,308 records, and of those, thirty-one are people born between 1843 and 1869 — which is exactly the window of the commandant's twelve children, between his marriage on 3 april 1843 and his death on 3 april 1868. it looks for a moment like the answer to the oldest question on the kolbe side of this family.

every one of the thirty-one comes from the familysearch slice, which is tree data. not a register, not an estate, not a death notice — other people's trees, indexed. this archive does not take a child from a tree, and thirty-one plausible ones do not become evidence by being plausible together. they are worth exactly what they cost, which is a list of names to test against documents, and they are not being entered.

two of them are worth naming anyway, because they are testable. gersom eliezär kolbe, born 1868, died 1902 carries the commandant's own forenames and was born in the year he died — and the obituary says the youngest child was an infant. and the national archives rows, which are documents, show the name running on: a john gerson eliezer kolbe sued by e. wille and sons, by john william pearce and by the nelspruit roller mills, divorced by hester johanna catherina born hammon, and tried with one adam barnard in a criminal case. four generations of the same three names, and this archive has documents for the first and the last of them and none in between.

terms. it is a commercial service: the result lists are free, the documents behind them are not. nothing here was bought, no account was made, and everything quoted above came off the public result pages. what it is worth to this project is not the documents — it is that four of its ten datasets are sources this archive did not know it had not searched.
question 0, answered by two people who own the book this archive does not

the oldest open question on this site is one line of one form. the 1876 rustenburg sterfkennis of petrus jacobus booijsen names his father gerthardus lödewikus booijsen, and the printed cape genealogy of 1893 names him jan. one of them is wrong, and this archive could not say which without a book it has never seen.

the escape route was always the same: de villiers’s 1893 original was revised by pama in 1981, and a revision can move a man. if the 1981 edition had quietly relocated petrus jacobus, the death notice would stand and the 1893 entry would be a superseded reading. that was the question put to the wikitree forum, and it came back in nine words.
riël smit · 14 september 2026
“yes, de villiers & pama (1981) still place petrus jacobus (b3c4d7) b. 21 sept 1788 under jan b3c4.”
and in the same thread, from pieter van zyl, who had gone and looked at the notice:

i have seen death notices or “sterfkennis” where mistakes were often made with especially the parents. (i also had a look at the specific one that you mentioned.) the informant that gives the information to the person who writes the notice is usually a child or even a grandchild. his real dad, jan, was already dead for more than 40 years when petrus jacobus died. quite possibly, the informant “thought” the dad’s name was g l. normally the parents are not so important for the executor of the probate, especially if they were deceased. i searched for a marriage between a gerhardus lodewicus and magdalena de beer but could not find one. if i remember there was a child of petrus called gerhardus lodewicus on his sterfkennis.
riël smit, concurring, added his own case: “i have seen a mother on a death notice to be actually the wife — the son filling out the form confused his mother with his dad’s mother.”
he remembered right, and the proof is nine lines lower on the same sheet
line 3 of notice 678 gives the parents as gerthardus lödewikus booijsen and magdalena de beer. line 12 of the same sheet lists eight children, all of age, and the fifth of them is:
jan gerthardus lodewikus booijsen

the name written in the parents’ box is the back half of a son’s name, on the same page, in one clerk’s hand. and the half that was dropped is jan — which is the name the printed genealogy gives for the father, in both its editions. a grandson named for his grandfather is the ordinary thing in this family; this archive has spent a whole page demonstrating it. the old man’s father and the old man’s fifth son had the same first name, and an informant reaching for one of them arrived carrying too much of the other.

who was doing the remembering. the form is countersigned by h. s. booijsen — hendrik stefanus, the seventh child, whose own name is four lines above his signature. he was born about 1828. his grandfather jan had married in 1770, remarried in 1793, and was dead before he was ten. he was writing the name of a man he had almost certainly never met, about a father who was eighty-eight.
what this archive now holds, and what it still will not do
four things now point one way
1. de villiers 1893 puts petrus jacobus (bapt. 21 sept 1788) under jan, b3c4.
2. de villiers & pama 1981 still does — the revision did not move him.
3. no marriage of a gerhardus lodewicus to a magdalena de beer can be found, and a cape genealogist went looking.
4. the disputed name is on the same document, nine lines lower, as a son.

and the mother on line 3 — magdalena de beer — agrees with the book exactly. the informant got the woman right and the man wrong, which is what an informant reaching for a half-remembered pair of names would do.
and the spine is not being moved on this

the pedigree still shows gerthardus lodewikus booysen at the top, marked open, and it stays there today. everything above is secondary. de villiers is a printed genealogy of 1893; pama’s revision agreeing with it is one book agreeing with its own earlier edition, not two sources agreeing. against it stands a primary document, a death notice signed by a son, and this archive does not let a book overrule a page just because the book is tidier.

de villiers is not a source. he is an index to one. his entry for petrus jacobus was compiled from the dutch reformed baptism register, from the entry of 21 september 1788. that register entry names the father in a contemporary hand, written within days of the birth, by somebody with no reason to be confused about it. that single line ends this question outright, and it has gone to the top of the errands page.

this is the second time the forum has done in a day what this archive could not do in a fortnight, and both times what it supplied was not a document but access to a shelf. the 1981 edition exists in a number of south african houses and in none of this project’s. sources →
1893 · volumes two and three of the cape genealogies — where the name david schalk comes from

on 14 september riël smit posted links to all three parts of de villiers’ geslacht-register der oude kaapsche familien in the wikitree forum. this archive downloaded part 1, read page 78, and never went back for the other two. they were sitting there the whole time, and they answer a question the namesakes page has been asking since it was written.
first, a negative, and it is the useful kind
volume 2 has a kolbe entry, number a483, and it is not this family:
carel frederik kolbe, van anhalt dessau, burger te kaapstad, gehuwd 6 juni 1762 met maria magdalena de wens.

1 johannes marthinus, ged. 6 februari 1763 · 2 jacobus, ged. 13 januari 1765, gehuwd 6 juni 1799 met johanna magdalena paulsen · 3 johanna elisabeth, ged. 13 maart 1767 · 4 maria magdalena, ged. 21 mei 1769 · 5 marthinus, ged. 12 augustus 1770 · 6 carel frederik, ged. 11 augustus 1771 · 7 salomon, ged. 8 januari 1773.

a german kolbe family was at the cape fifty-eight years before the 1820 settler landed, from anhalt-dessau, burghers in cape town, and volume 3 confirms the marriage from the other side under paulsen. they are nothing to do with george augustus kolbe, whose father was a tailor in london and who came out on the settler ships. this archive spends a great deal of its time warning itself that a rare-looking surname is a trap; here is the trap, printed, in the standard reference, and it is being set down so that nobody — including this archive — walks into it later.
anna maria van der merwe, who was a name and is now a family
she has been in this archive as the mother on a baptism of 4 january 1807 and almost nothing else. volume 2 carries the van der merwe genealogy, and she is in it:
(e) 3 willem, gedoopt 30 september 1764, burger te stellenbosch, gehuwd 7 november 1784 met hester maria van der merwe
(f) 1 johanna catharina, gedoopt 8 maart 1787
2 anna maria, gedoopt 5 october 1788, gehuwd met petrus jacobus booijsen

4 hendrina magdalena, gedoopt 10 juli 1792
5 hester maria, gedoopt 3 november 1793, gehuwd met michiel van niekerk
6 hendrik petrus jacobus, gedoopt 21 februari 1796
two babies, fourteen days apart

volume 1, page 78, has petrus jacobus booijsen baptised 21 september 1788. volume 2 has anna maria van der merwe baptised 5 october 1788. a fortnight between them, in the same colony, and they married each other. this archive has never had a date for her of any kind.

the two volumes also confirm the marriage from both directions — volume 1 from his side, volume 2 from hers. that is one author being consistent with himself, not two sources agreeing, and it is worth exactly that much.
and the parents do not agree with the tree

this archive has carried, flagged as coming from wikitree and not from a document, that anna maria was a daughter of david schalk van der merwe and anna elizabeth louw, born 1785. de villiers makes her a daughter of willem van der merwe and hester maria van der merwe, baptised 1788. both cannot be right. neither is being adopted over the other here.

but look at what survives the disagreement. on the tree’s version, david schalk is her father. on de villiers’s, david schalk is her brother. two incompatible parentages, and in both of them the name sits one step from her. a conclusion that holds under either reading of the evidence is the only kind this archive gets to keep.
the claim is testable, so it was tested. the three volumes were downloaded as text and the string david schalk counted in each, allowing for the scanner’s misreadings.
¦volume “david schalk” where
¦part 1 (a–j, and it holds the whole booijsen genealogy) 1 and it is our man. “david schalk, gedoopt 4 januari 1807” — the son of petrus jacobus and anna maria. the only one in the volume.
¦part 2 15 thirteen of the fifteen are inside the van der merwe section, generation on generation of them — 1738, 1739, 1761, 1787, 1790, 1791, 1797, 1800, 1804…
¦part 3 3 scattered, none connected here.

david schalk is a van der merwe name. in the entire first volume of the cape genealogies — which contains every booijsen de villiers recorded — it occurs once, and it is the child born the year after a van der merwe married into the line. this archive holds three david schalks and has built a page around the way names descend in this family. it can now say where this one came in, and on what evidence. namesakes →
and david schalk booijzen married his first cousin
this one was not looked for. volume 3 holds the viljoens, under their older spelling:
1,008.—villion, thans viljoen.
(e) 12 hercules albertus, gedoopt 30 maart 1777, burger te graaff-reinet, gehuwd 26 februari 1797 met magdalena booijsen

(f) 1 jan wilhelmus, ged. 1799 · 2 magdalena, ged. 1801 · 3 henning jacobus, ged. 1803 · 4 anna cornelia, ged. 1805 · 5 hercules albertus, ged. 1807 · 6 pieter nicolaas, ged. 1808 · 7 adriana christina, gedoopt 19 augustus 1810
(e) 14 judith cornelia theresia, gedoopt 22 october 1782, gehuwd met jan jonathan booijsen
volume 1 gives the booijsen side of both marriages, and they are three children of one household — jan booijsen and magdalena de beer:
¦d5 jan jonathan, ged. 11 juli 1779, burgher at graaff-reinet 28 may 1797 — judith cornelia theresia viljoen
¦d6 magdalena, ged. 29 september 1782 26 february 1797 — hercules albertus viljoen
¦d7 petrus jacobus, ged. 21 september 1788 anna maria van der merwe

a brother and a sister married a sister and a brother, three months apart in 1797. magdalena booijsen married hercules albertus viljoen in february; her brother jan jonathan married hercules albertus’s sister judith cornelia theresia in may. two households became one twice over in a single year.

thirty-one years later, david schalk booijzen — son of the third of those children — married adriana christina viljoen at cradock on 3 november 1828. magdalena booijsen’s seventh child is adriana christina, baptised 19 august 1810, which makes her eighteen in 1828 and makes him her first cousin: his father and her mother were brother and sister.

what is proved and what is not. de villiers records adriana christina viljoen’s baptism and gives her no husband. the marriage date of 3 november 1828 at cradock is itself something this archive holds from wikitree and has never seen a document for. so the cousin marriage rests on a right name, a right age, a right district and a family already doubly tied — and on a date that is not yet a document. it is published as an inference and the weak join is named. the cradock marriage register would close it.

one more, for the same page. jan jonathan booijsen and judith cornelia theresia viljoen’s sixth child is judith cornelia theresia, baptised 16 august 1807 — which is b3c4d5e6, the code this archive resolved last week to settle a johannesburg gravestone. she has her mother’s three names entire, and her mother was a viljoen. the same mechanism, in the same generation, in the house next door.
1866–1872 · the widow remarried, and the farm was two hours from bloemfontein

the commandant’s estate file at bloemfontein is indexed under the name mccabe, and this archive has been saying for days that it did not know who mccabe was. he is in the newspapers, with a birth date, an office and a funeral. the same run of papers also settles where the farm was, names the first of the twelve children, and gives the settler an occupation nobody had.
the friend of the free state, 29 february 1872

died near modder-river district, bloemfontein, orange free state, suddenly, of heart disease, on friday evening, 23rd february, francis mccabe, esq., landdrost of bloemfontein, aged 54 years, deeply regretted by a sorrowing widow and large family of children and stepchildren, besides many attached friends and acquaintances, as well as by the public of this town and district whom he long and faithfully served.
and the obituary beneath it does the rest of the work:

the late francis mccabe was the son of dr. mccabe, a staff-assistant surgeon, attached to the british army on the cape frontier, and was born at one of the military posts, in what is now known as british kaffraria, on the 29th september 1817. he married his second wife about ten months since — the widow of the late commandant j.g.e. kolbe, of kafirberg, near this town. he leaves a widow, four sons and two daughters, besides a large family of step-children, to mourn their loss.
what that gives anna jacoba van der merwe

married 3 april 1843. widowed 3 april 1868, on the anniversary, with twelve children. married francis mccabe about april 1871. widowed again 23 february 1872. fifteen months. she then lived another twenty-four years and died in 1896, which is why the free state estate index holds her as mccabe, anna jacoba, nooiensvan van der merwe and why she was so hard to find.

the newspaper also counts for us. mccabe left four sons and two daughters of his own, and the step-children are “a large family” — the twelve. for about eleven months there were eighteen children attached to one household.

he had spent 23 february — the anniversary of the state’s independence — superintending the burghers’ annual target shooting for the government prize. at 5:15 in the afternoon he set off for the diamond fields by spring-cart with four horses, adjutant van rensburg of the free state artillery and a servant, meaning to sleep at his own farm “uitvlugt” on modder river. at about half past seven, in deceptive moonlight, one hour’s ride short of the farm of mr g.f. enslin, the cart went into a sluit washed out by the recent rains. he was dead that evening of heart disease.

g.f. enslin is already in this archive — he is the husband who placed the notice of 23 october 1863 saying that maria elizabeth kolbe had died intestate. he is used here as a landmark on a road at night, which is how a district knows a man.

he was buried in the public cemetery at bloemfontein on the sunday afternoon at six o’clock, the coffin carried from house to hearse and hearse to grave by the commandant of the district, the resident members of the volksraad, and the principal government officers, in the presence of the state president and upwards of two hundred who walked in the procession. his brother joseph mccabe, the well-known trader and traveller, had died in december 1865 in the interior; his brother john died at bloemfontein in 1860; their mother rose, relict of patrick mccabe, resident-surgeon, died on 1 august 1858 aged 72 years 3 months and 8 days. one sister only survived. four mccabe deaths and a surviving sister, all in the bloemfontein papers, and none of it was looked for.
the first of the twelve children to be named

the free state criminal court, reported in the friend in the second half of 1869. jochemus jacobus ackerman pleaded guilty to horse stealing at the farm springfield, ward upper modder-river, district bloemfontein, in the beginning of october 1868, and got three years’ hard labour. he had driven off three animals:

firstly: 1 black mare, with dark brown foal, the property of anna jacoba van der merwe, widow of late j.g.e. kolbe: secondly 1 blue schimmel mare, with foal, the property of john kolbe, jun.: and thirdly, a chestnut riding horse, the property of jephts, a man of color, now residing at leeuwberg.

three things at once. the widow is on springfield, ward upper modder river six months after her husband’s death, which gives the field-cornetcy. john kolbe, junior is holding stock in his own right beside her — a son, carrying the father’s name, and the first of the twelve this archive can put a hand on. and jephts, a man of colour living at leeuwberg, owned a chestnut riding horse and the court wrote his name down beside theirs. he is recorded here because he was recorded there. a great many people who lived on these farms are in no document at all; he is in one, and this archive is not going to be the second place that leaves him out.
where the farm was — and a pin that has to come out

an auction advertisement in the friend of 13 january 1870, placed by w.w. collins, general agent, dated bloemfontein 30 november 1869, selling the landed property of the insolvent estate of thos. heatly of worcester:

1. the farm, wildebeestkooi, adjoining the farm leeuberg, the property of the late j.g.e. kolbe, about two hours ride from the town of bloemfontein; this farm is well adapted for the breeding and depasturing of all kinds of live stock, being healthy and well situated.

two days ago this archive pinned leeuwberg at fauresmith, on a 1903 land file recording a “leeuwberg no 465, dist. faurismith”, and published the pin with its own objection attached: fauresmith is a hundred and thirty kilometres from where kaalspruit was pinned, and the obituary says he died at the one and lies at the other. the objection has now been answered, and it answered against the pin. leeuberg adjoins wildebeestkooi and is about two hours’ ride from bloemfontein — fifteen or twenty kilometres, not a hundred and thirty. the fauresmith farm is a different farm of the same name. withdrawn, and the pin moved. corrections →

everything else now agrees. the mccabe obituary calls him “of kafirberg, near this town”. his own 1864 advertisement signs “j.g.e. kolbe, kafferberg, kaalspruit”. his widow is at springfield in the ward of the upper modder river. kafferberg, kaalspruit, leeuberg, wildebeestkooi and springfield are one neighbourhood, an easy ride north-west of bloemfontein — and the soil-conservation district registered as kaalspruit – kafferrivier (bloemfontein), which was a guess when this archive used it, now has three documents standing behind it.
the settler kept a school for bushmen where colesberg now is

the friend of the free state, first half of 1869, printed a reminiscence headed “forty-five years ago”, by john montgomery, founder of burghersdorp. he is describing a journey from cradock made about 1824.

after visiting my friends i continued my journey towards the orange river, by koolskop, where the father of the late lamented commandant kolbe conducted a bushmen mission school, and which is now colesberg. from there i crossed the orange river, which was almost dry — the water being in pools only here and there. i then trekked on to philippolis, where old dam kok was in command of the bastards or griquas.

this archive had george augustus kolbe as a medical practitioner, from the 1844 obituary, and as a man who died on a farm in the colesberg district. here he is twenty years earlier, at a place called koolskop, running a mission school for bushmen on the ground where the town of colesberg was laid out in 1830. it explains what the family was doing in that corner of the colony at all — they were there before the town was.

what it is worth. montgomery is writing forty-five years after the fact and identifies the man not by name but as the father of a commandant who had died the year before he wrote. that is a recollection, not a register. it is also a specific one, from a man who founded a town in the same district and had no reason to invent a school. recorded as an inference with the source printed beside it, not as fact.
three smaller things out of the same run
foreman of the jury, 1866

a forgery trial at bloemfontein, before mr van soelen — the same official who spoke at kolbe’s graveside two years later. “the jury, through their foreman, mr. j.g.b. kolbe, of kafferberg, brought in a verdict of not guilty.” a fourth public office, and the initials printed j.g.b. for j.g.e., in the town paper, in his own lifetime.
a grandson, killed by lightning, 1884

“the eldest son of mr. john kolbe, ‘little jannie’, a promising youth ten years old, was struck dead by the electric fluid on his father’s farm five hours to the northward of bloemfontein.” the natal witness index carries the same death and names the father george. two papers, two fathers. if the john of 1884 is the john kolbe junior of 1868, this is the commandant’s grandson.
kolbe-booysen, in print

the name page carries kolbe-booysen as a compound the family tree records for the wife of david kolbe booyzen, married 1921 — and calls it a tree oddity. the eastern province herald prints it twice. it is a household in port elizabeth.
16 october 1944 · engagements

sawtelle – kolby-booysen. — the engagement has been announced between levina (finnie), only daughter of mr and mrs d. kolbe-booysen, of port elizabeth, to raymond patrick, only son of mrs d. sawtelle, of cambridge, england.
19 april 1945 · to be married

kolbe-booysen – kruger. to be married at st cuthbert’s church, bingley street, port elizabeth, to-day (thursday), april 19th, at 3.30 p.m., hilda (s.a.c.s.), only daughter of lieut. and mrs f. kruger, of heidelburg, transvaal, to william (s.a.a.f.), son of mr and mrs d. kolbe-booysen, of port elizabeth.

d. is david. david kolbe booyzen married maria jacoba smit in 1921 and the tree recorded her surname as kolbe-booysen; the compound had no document behind it. now it has two, six months apart, and with them a town and two children: levina, called finnie, the only daughter, marrying an englishman from cambridge in the last winter of the war, and william, of the south african air force. their father hyphenated the two surnames of this entire archive and used it as his name.
and the engagement notice spells the headline kolby and the body kolbe, four words apart, in one paragraph, in 1944. the name →
1897–1900 · a farm school in marico, and the man who countersigned it

the seven marico compensation claims were read today and gave up nothing but their own initials. the same search returned three files nobody had asked for, and those three turned out to be part of a bundle of forty-eight: the entire correspondence of a school on a farm, from the letter asking for a teacher to the last cheque before the war.

start with the negative, because it was the errand. seven booyzen men claimed compensation as burghers in the district of marico in 1903 and 1904. all seven detail records were pulled. every one of them reads, in full:

what came back instead

the query was booyzen and marico in the transvaal depot. ten documents. seven were the claims. the other three were from source od, the education files of the south african republic, and all three were about a school.
h de vries, jgl booyzen, kwaggafontein, distrik marico, pk kafferskraal.
zenden aanzoek om subsidie. — remarks: bij or13059/97

what jgl booyzen was

he is on eight of the forty-eight, and always in the same position: first or second name at the head of the letter, beside the teacher, on the documents that involve money and returns — the subsidy application, the book orders, the four quarterly statements, the explanation of the deficit, and the argument about the eight pounds. he is on none of the documents about holidays, forms, or railway certificates, which the teacher sent alone.

that is the shape of a school commission officer — on the evidence of the paper, its treasurer. the parallel file at vaalbank below names a penningmeester explicitly and puts him in exactly this slot.

he is not the teacher. the teacher is h. de vries, fetched by wagon from somewhere else in december 1897, and the department writes to him about his own salary certificates every month. booyzen is the local man who signs for the school.
and which jgl booyzen — not answered

this archive holds two men of those initials. jan gerthardus lodewikus booijsen, fifth of the eight children on the 1876 sterfkennis, born district graaff-reinet about 1818, died on the farm vaalbank in the district of lichtenburg on 25 may 1885 — so he is thirteen years dead and cannot be this man. his nephew and namesake jan gerhardus lodewicus booysen, born 4 december 1855, seventh on the 1863 list, is a man of whom this archive has said for months that nothing is known of what became of him. in 1898 he would be forty-two.

that is a candidate and not an identification. marico adjoins lichtenburg, this family is documented in marico from the 1892 zeerust marriage, and jan gerhardus lodewicus is the name at the top of this line. it is also one of the commonest name-strings in the whole surname. the index line gives initials, a farm and a post office, and no more. recorded open.
three spellings of one man, in ten months, by one department

this is worth setting down on its own, because this archive has an entire page arguing about the letter in the middle of the name. within a single register series, in a single government office, about a single man at a single farm school, the clerks wrote:
booyzen — january 1898 · or262/98, the subsidy application
booysen — 12 february 1898 · or2773/98, a book order
booysen — 9 may 1898 · or6919/98, the deficit
booyzen — 1 july 1898 · or9812/98, second quarter
booijzen — 20 october 1898 · or16104/98, third quarter
booysen — 15 december 1898 · or19636/98, fourth quarter

three spellings, one man, one office, ten months. nothing in this archive has ever shown the point so cleanly. the z is not a branch and the ij is not a generation. it is whichever clerk had the pen. the name →
and a second school, on this family’s own farm

searching the same series for the surname against onderwyzer returned sixteen documents, most of them other booysens running other farm schools across the republic — wonderboom, hartsenbergfontein, kareeboomputten, zeekoefontein. one of them is not somewhere else.

vaalbank in the district of lichtenburg is this archive’s own ground. jan gerthardus lodewikus booijsen died on that farm on 25 may 1885, and his daughter magdalena susanna maria died on the same farm on 1 may 1920. in between, in december 1898, a booysen on vaalbank is sending an unstamped power of attorney and eighteen pence in postage stamps to the government bookkeeper, co-signing the school’s quarterly returns with the teacher j.p. louw, and — in february 1899 — writing to ask how school materials can be provided to orphans, arising from a case among them.

and the initials will not be read from here. ds. may be a man with the forenames david schalk, which is this family’s most heavily used name-string and would put a named relative on the farm. it may equally be ds., the dutch abbreviation for dominee — and six weeks earlier, at this very school, or15594/98 names “jp louw ds van roojen” in exactly the same slot, where ds. van rooijen is far more likely a minister than a man with those initials. one abbreviation, two readings, and this archive cannot choose between them from an index line. the file itself would settle it in a sentence. it has gone on the errands page.

a correction while doing this. the atlas has carried, since it was built, an event under marico reading “1898 — jgl booyzen of kwaggafontein, district marico, in the field-cornet’s papers”. the papers are the education department’s, not the field-cornet’s. a field-cornet does appear in this bundle, once, valuing the teacher’s house — and that is a different document, sent by a different man. corrected in place. corrections →
1907–1953 · piet retief and wakkerstroom — a date for the twin, and a third stone that names children by nickname
two kolbe stones at piet retief and one at wakkerstroom, all located yesterday in an index line and read today. one of them may put a day on a birth this archive has only ever had as a year.
piet retief — g.a. and a.m. kolbe
aan … vader en moeder

the settler's ninth and tenth children were twins born at burgersdorp in 1836 — charlotte felicia and george augustus — and this archive has never had a day for either. a g.a. kolbe born 23 february 1836 is the right man in the right year, and would date his twin sister too. it is initials and a year, not a name and a parent. it would also give the other george augustus kolbe — born burgersdorp 2 october 1861, buried at wakkerstroom — a father aged twenty-five, which is the shape the eastern transvaal kolbes have been missing.
piet retief — p.j. kolbe

the day of birth will not resolve at any magnification and is not guessed. thirty years younger than the stone beside it; if g.a. is the twin, this is very likely his son, and nothing on the stone says so.

her birth is now a date, where this archive had only the year off an estate file. and six children are named — by what they were called, not by what they were registered as. she is george augustus kolbe's daughter, so these six are great-grandchildren of the 1820 settler, and they are new.

that is three stones now. the booyzens at silverton list twelve children on a centre pillar; the kolbes at wakkerstroom use the same double-stone-and-pillar form; and this one sets six household names under a mother's dates. two families, four hundred miles apart, burying their dead in the same grammar. this archive keeps finding children on gravestones that are on no register it can reach — and the reason is simple enough: a register records a birth, and a stone records who was left.
8 october 1831 – 3 september 1832 · “extracts from the journal of mr. george augustus kolbe”

until 11 october 2026 the sum of this man’s own words in this archive was one sentence, quoted at second hand. the london missionary society printed his journal in its own monthly — the evangelical magazine and missionary chronicle, 1833, pp. 410–412 — and the volume is out of copyright and free. all three pages have now been read from the page images and are transcribed from them. this page carried a caveat for six hours saying pp. 411–412 had been read only from the internet archive’s ocr; the images were then fetched and the caveat earned its keep, because the ocr text had silently dropped four words and this transcription had stopped before the document did. both are repaired below, and what the repair changed is stated rather than quietly absorbed. the page, and what else tests these years →
p. 410 — the end of his letter of 1 september 1832, and his signature

…our church at present consists of thirty members, who are all (as far as can be ascertained) walking worthy of the gospel of christ. there are also twenty-five candidates for baptism and church-fellowship. from 80 to 133 children daily attend the school.

you have been informed, from previous reports, that some griquas from this place, with others, had attacked the zoola king, mosselekaats. i feel happy in being able to state that none of our church members had any concern in this wicked transaction, and they all express their abhorrence of such deeds. our new chapel is completed. it can hold and seat about 500 persons.
we have commenced a temperance society, and it promises much success…
i remain, rev. and dear sir,
your obedient servant,
and fellow labourer in the gospel,
(signed) g. a. kolbe.
p. 410 — the journal begins

november 6th, sunday.—260 persons attended the different services of religion to-day. three candidates were admitted as church members. in the evening the lord’s supper was administered to fifteen persons. we trust the lord was with us. after the sacrament, two persons came to me, desiring to speak about their spiritual state before god. [mr. kolbe afterwards speaks of his weariness of body in the spiritually delightful duties of the day, and closes by remarking, in reference to the people among whom it is his privilege to labour, “it is now ten o’clock, yet we still hear prayers and hymns of praise ascending to god and our saviour jesus christ. may the lord bless his own work!”]
november 7th, monday.—100 persons attended the missionary prayer-meeting.
november 9th, wednesday.—the chief sent a letter to the veld cornet joubert, complaining of the intrusions of the farmers, especially of the colonists, who had insulted and beaten his people.
november 20th, sunday.—178 persons attended the services. proclaimed a solemn fast to the lord for the acknowledgment of sin, and deprecating his wrath…

november 24th, thursday.—visited the people in their houses. from this day’s experience we are constrained to praise god, who is doing great things for us… of many who we supposed never had a serious thought about their souls, we were constrained to say, behold, they pray!

january 14th, 1832, saturday.—in the evening twenty-nine waggons arrived, all loaded with people who came to attend the services of religion. mr. jenkins, of bootschaap, being here, addressed a crowded congregation.
january 18th, wednesday.—vaccinated twenty-six persons. the school increased to ninety children. service in the evening—102 attended.
january 22nd, sunday.—the number of candidates exceeding thirty, it was thought necessary to divide them into two classes…

january 29th, sunday.—this day being appointed as a day of thanksgiving to almighty god, for having mercifully delivered us from that dreadful disease, the small-pox, mr. jenkins preached to 400 persons…

february 5th, sunday.—two elders and two deacons were chosen by the unanimous votes of the members. our church discipline is as follows:—if a member conduct himself unbecomingly he is reprimanded; if this proceeding have no effect, two other members endeavour to convince him of his error. if their endeavours fail, the subject is brought before the missionary, elders, and deacons, and their conclusion is laid before the whole church. the votes of the members decide the questions brought forward.
pp. 411–412 — read from the images, 11 october 2026

february 15th, wednesday.—some bushmen having stolen two heifers belonging to our people, two parties went out last night in quest of the thieves. this morning many bushmen were brought to the station. the delinquents were discovered and whipped, and the other bushmen were sent away with presents of meat, &c. this is another proof that bushmen may be brought to punishment for their depredatory acts, and that in many cases (as in this) there is no need of discharging a gun, much less of shooting them.

april 1st, sunday.—…our new church being so far ready, we were able to hold service in it to-day. this building has been erected entirely by the inhabitants of the district of philippolis. the society assisted with 200 rix-dollars (£15), and some nails, hinges, screws, &c. it will contain 500 persons. the walls are of stone, two feet and a half thick, and twelve feet high. to-day the church was filled, and the aisles crowded, and 100 were obliged to remain in the street…
april 2nd, monday.—335 children in the school.

april 9th, monday.—rode to dice fountain (five miles distance from this place). all the scholars requested to go with me. i took as many as the waggon could contain. such affection is very pleasing. on my return they (the children in the waggon) sung many hymns, which quite excited my feelings. at five o’clock met the members of the church.

april 15th, sunday.—in the evening a griqua came, desiring to speak to me. he stated that for some time past he had had great prejudices against me and my preaching; that he was sorry for it, and begged my forgiveness… i advised him to refrain from commandoes, and to seek christ as his saviour.
may 8th, tuesday.—after dinner, rode to a horde of corannas, who were afflicted with the small-pox…

may 23rd, wednesday.—having preached various sermons against drunkenness, calling upon the chief and his council… to do all in their power to prevent the bad practice which the colonists have of bringing brandy into this country. i rejoice to hear that the chief has prohibited the sale of spirits at the station.

may 26th, saturday.—a griqua, who came from graham’s town with a load of goods to this station, stopped at okkert schalkwyk’s (a colonist residing near this station), where he had so much brandy given him to drink by the boor, that he was found dead in his bed the next morning.
june 2nd, saturday.—to-day we were informed that a person had shot a griqua in a fit of drunkenness…

july 21st, saturday.—the veld-cornet joubert (the nearest veld-cornet to this boundary), and two other farmers, arrived here this afternoon, for the purpose of obtaining medical advice, and also to attend the religious services of the station.

august 5th, sunday.—our chapel was filled—yea, literally crammed. 500 persons attended the various services of religion, among whom were a dutch colonist, three english traders, captain waterboer and his council from griqua town, and a few persons from bootschaap…
august 12th, sunday.—400 persons attended the services of religion, among whom were eighty bechuanas.
september 1st, saturday.—service as usual. 300 attended. after service, met the members for prayer and self-examination, preparatory to the sacrament.
september 2nd, sunday.—500 persons attended the different services of religion.

september 3rd, monday.—a meeting was called for the purpose of commencing a temperance society. several persons addressed the meeting, and eighty-three signed as members. joseph de bruin (a member of the church) proposed that the use of spirits should be entirely discontinued, even for medicinal purposes; for he observed, that under the name of using spirits as medicine, drunkenness would be secretly indulged in. this proposition was unanimously agreed to, with an amendment.

a memorial was also presented to the chief and council, signed by all the members, requesting him to issue an order that all spirits brought from the colony, for the purpose of trafficking in this district, should be considered as contraband and forfeited goods.
p. 411 — the heifers and the whipping, the chapel opened on 1 april 1832 with a hundred left standing in the street, and the children singing in the waggon.

p. 412 — the veld-cornet riding in for medical advice, captain waterboer down from griqua town, and the document’s real ending: eighty-three signatures and a memorial asking the chief to treat imported spirits as contraband.

what reading the type actually changed. two things, and one non-thing. the ocr had dropped “(the children in the waggon)” from the 9 april entry — four words, and they are the ones that make the sentence a picture. the transcription had also ended at 2 september, three sentences before the journal does, losing the temperance society entirely. and one suspected error turned out not to be one: a first pass at the page image read “four english traders” against the published “three”; magnified, the type says three, and nothing was changed.

why the july entry matters more than it looks. his 1844 obituary said he had been “for many years engaged in rendering them medical advice and assistance whenever called upon”, and this archive had only the obituary’s word for it. here is a veld-cornet and two farmers riding in for exactly that, sixteen years earlier, in his own hand.

he had refused public life for about twelve years after the abandonment — he was among those who protested the british withdrawal and applied to sir george clerk for compensation for his land so that he might leave with the troops. failing that, “he, like many more, had to cast his lot with the free state”. he took no office until the end of 1865.

a widow and twelve children. of four daughters, only one was married; the youngest was an infant. two of the sons had been serving with their father in the field and “have proved themselves to be amongst the bravest of our burghers”. not one of the twelve is named, and none of them is in this archive.
the deathbed, which is the part worth keeping

“on his death-bed, and while he still retained his full senses, he declared to the doctor, to mr. salzmann, and to others that were at his bed-side, that this state had taken too much land from the basutos, and that he had felt so all along, and had declared it as his opinion in the volksraad, in may 1867, at the time of the making of the ‘corn peace’; and now, on the bed from which he never expected to rise again, he wished by message to warn the raad, and to beg of them to rescind their resolution, annul their protest, and to treat with the governor for an equitable settlement of the boundary line.”
he was interred the monday following; mr. p. grobler, elder of the church, conducted the service in the minister's absence, and the president of the free state delivered an address.
and it describes his parents

“his parents came out with the settlers of 1820; his father was of german extraction, if not birth, but resided and married in london. his mother — a thorough-going and fine old english lady — it will be remembered died in burghersdorp about three months since.”

that is george augustus kolbe and margaret downing, described in 1868 by somebody who knew them, in a newspaper that had no genealogical interest whatever. german extraction, if not birth is exactly right for a man born in westminster to a württemberg father — and this archive worked that out from a soho baptism, a london gazette notice and a census, none of which this writer had. it also confirms from a fourth direction that the father became a missionary to the griquas at philippolis, and that most of the family grew up there — which is what the children's baptism places already said.

one date does not fit, and it is left not fitting. this archive has margaret downing dying in 1867, on the strength of her death notice. this obituary, printed 15 april 1868, says she died at burgersdorp about three months since — which is january 1868. a death notice is a form with a date on it and a newspaper’s “about three months” is a journalist rounding, so the notice should win; but this archive has already been caught once by an estate filed thirteen years after the death it records, and will not simply wave this away. her place of death is new either way: burgersdorp.

and one small thing, from the same search. grahamstown journal, 9 february 1872, quoting the colesberg advertiser under the heading “terrible warning”: an action before the resident magistrate between mr. geo. kolbe, plaintiff, and mr. t. nelson, watchmaker, defendant — kolbe “sought to recover a watch which had been entrusted to defendant for repair, but which, despite repeated promises, the latter neglected to repair or to deliver”. a kolbe of colesberg, in court, over a watch.

read in order they make a family. charles andrew, of steynsburg in 1884, is charles werdmuller, j.p. of hoopstad by 1909 — the same town his wife died in. the two little girls left in 1891 are the reason the 1909 notice can call amy a second daughter. and a child of charles andrew's father was baptised at burgersdorp in april 1857 to a mother named augusta louisa kolbe.

the link that is not proved, and this archive will not pretend otherwise. nothing read here names charles andrew's mother. his father remarried — or a man of exactly the same name married — at burgersdorp in 1874, to elizabeth johanna catharine vorster. if charles andrew is the child born 14 february 1857 he was twenty-seven when he married and augusta louisa kolbe is his mother; if he belongs to the later marriage he is no relation to this family at all, and the 1874 date makes that impossible for a man marrying in 1884 as a second son. the dates favour kolbe strongly and the documents do not say it. set down as a chain with a gap in it.

if the chain holds, amy werdmuller is a great-granddaughter of the 1820 settler, and in 1909 she married a holder of the victoria cross. this archive records the two letters exactly as the journal printed them and has not gone looking for which action he won it for; that is somebody else's page, and the temptation to borrow it is exactly the temptation this archive is built to resist.

why no search would ever have found her — and this is the finding that outlasts her. the familysearch film viewer carries an index panel under each image, listing every entry on that page: name, birth date, both parents, event, place. on image 427 the row reads | 10 jul 1855 | john barry | margaret louisa kolbe | baptism | — the name column is empty. the child is indexed with no name at all. her forenames are written plainly on the register page and simply were not keyed. no search by surname, forename or spelling variant can return a record that has neither, which is why nine separate attempts here — barry, berry, barrie, bary, barrey, barri, bari, and the mother under kolbe, kolber and colbe — all came back with the same seven children. the parents are indexed. the child is not. searching by the parent is the only thing that reaches her, and a parent search only works if you already know to run it on a page you cannot see.

the same sweep caught a second nameless row, on image 513: a child born 14 february 1857, baptised 10 april 1857 at burgersdorp, to augusta louisa kolbe and coenraad johannes otto werdmuller. she is the settler's fourth daughter, born at graaff-reinet in 1829, and this is the first of her children this archive has ever seen. two nameless entries in 267 images, and both of them belong to this family.

19 december 1844 · the grahamstown journal buries the settler — and names a london square and eight sons

printed eighteen days after he died, four hundred miles from the farm, and never read here until today. it is the fullest contemporary account of george augustus kolbe that exists, and almost every line of it says something this archive did not have.

died at his farm, wirtemberg, near the orange river, december 1st, the rev. george augustus kolbe, aged 44 years, a man possessed of a most amiable temper, and of more than ordinary abilities. he was the last remaining of eight sons of john godloff kolbe esq. of brunswick-square, london, has left a widow and ten children to lament their loss, and to whom he has been a most affectionate husband and father. the inhabitants of the district of colesberg, and the surrounding districts, will sustain a heavy loss, he having been for many years engaged in rendering them medical advice and assistance whenever called upon. his very long affliction for nearly a year has been borne with exemplary patience and resignation. his disease was an affection on the lungs, which brought on extreme weakness and debility. he died in peace, in sure and certain hope of a glorious immortality, through the merits of his redeemer, jesus christ.
grahamstown journal, thursday 19 december 1844, transcribed in the eggsa newspaper extracts.

this archive knew john gottlob kolbe of conduit street through a census, a gazette notice, a burial and a death index, and knew of one son — the one who sailed. the obituary says george augustus was the last remaining of eight.

seven brothers, all dead before december 1844, and not one of them is in this archive. the three women in the 1841 conduit street household — marianne, charlotte and amelia — are sisters or daughters; the sons are simply absent, because dead men do not appear in a census.
brunswick square, not conduit street

the 1841 census has john gottlob kolbe at conduit street, mayfair, and he died at number 34 in 1845. the obituary — written from the son's side, and printed while the father was still alive — places him at brunswick-square, in bloomsbury, a mile and a half away.

both can be true: the family may have been at brunswick square when george augustus sailed in 1819 and at conduit street twenty years later. this archive has already had to move this man once, off the family tree's lamb's conduit street and onto conduit street proper, and it is not going to move him again on one line of print. recorded as a second address and not as a correction. corrections →
a doctor, in everything but the word

his death notice calls him an agriculturist. the trades this archive had were reverend missionary, chemist, tailor. the obituary says he had for many years rendered medical advice and assistance to the inhabitants of the district of colesberg and the surrounding districts, whenever called upon.
that is the difference between a trade listed on a form and what a man actually did for thirty years. it also explains the chemist: on that frontier, in the 1830s, the chemist was the doctor.
what he died of, and what does not fit
ill for nearly a year, of an affection on the lungs — consumption, in the language of the time.

two things in the notice are wrong and are printed here anyway. aged 44: he was born 7 december 1802 and died 1 december 1844, five days short of forty-two. and ten children: this archive counts twelve born, one of whom died an infant, which leaves eleven. a death notice in a newspaper is written by the grieving and set by a compositor four hundred miles away. it is the best kind of source and it is not a register.
